# Part 10 — AI Operating System Roadmap

The AI Operating System Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will design, build, govern, operate, measure, secure, and continuously improve the intelligence layer that coordinates the complete AI Workforce.

The AI Operating System is not a chatbot layer.

It is not a collection of disconnected prompts.

It is not a single large language model.

It is the governed enterprise execution system responsible for:

- Understanding work
- Creating tasks
- Selecting agents
- Selecting models
- Retrieving knowledge
- Applying policies
- Coordinating workflows
- Managing approvals
- Tracking evidence
- Monitoring performance
- Controlling cost
- Preserving memory
- Learning from outcomes
- Supporting multiple products and projects

Every major AI capability inside MianX.ai should operate through this shared operating system.

---

# AI Operating System Roadmap Statement

> **Build one secure, model-flexible, memory-enabled, policy-governed, observable, and multi-project AI Operating System capable of coordinating specialized AI agents across every MianX.ai department, product, client, and enterprise workflow.**

---

# AI OS Vision

The long-term vision is to create an intelligence operating layer capable of coordinating humans, AI agents, enterprise systems, organizational memory, business rules, and reusable workflows through one governed execution model.

The target architecture is:

```text
Human Direction

↓

Enterprise Request

↓

Context and Policy Validation

↓

Planning

↓

Task Generation

↓

Agent and Model Selection

↓

Tool Authorization

↓

Execution

↓

Review and Approval

↓

Evidence Capture

↓

Knowledge and Memory Update

↓

Performance Measurement

↓

Continuous Improvement
```

The AI OS should enable useful autonomy without removing accountability.

---

# AI OS Mission

The mission of the AI Operating System is to transform unstructured business requests into controlled, traceable, verifiable, and reusable enterprise execution.

The AI OS must:

- Standardize AI behavior
- Coordinate the AI Workforce
- Preserve project and tenant isolation
- Route work to appropriate agents
- Select appropriate models
- Enforce security and governance
- Integrate enterprise memory
- Support human approvals
- Produce verifiable evidence
- Measure quality and cost
- Recover from failure
- Improve through validated learning
- Operate across multiple projects simultaneously

---

# AI OS Strategic Objectives

The AI OS Roadmap exists to:

- Establish one shared AI execution architecture
- Standardize agent behavior through Prompt OS
- Maintain a central Agent Registry
- Convert requests into structured tasks
- Execute repeatable multi-step workflows
- Route work by capability, permission, cost, and availability
- Coordinate multiple agents safely
- Retrieve trusted enterprise knowledge
- Preserve organizational and project memory
- Support multiple model providers
- Control tool access
- Enforce AI governance
- Embed human approval
- Evaluate output quality
- Measure cost and performance
- Support concurrent products and projects
- Enable controlled continuous improvement
- Prevent uncontrolled AI autonomy

---

# AI OS Core Principles

Every AI OS capability must follow these principles:

- Governance Before Autonomy
- Context Before Execution
- Identity Before Permission
- Planning Before Action
- Evidence Before Completion
- Human Authority Before High-Risk Decisions
- Shared Services Before Independent AI Implementations
- Model Flexibility Before Provider Lock-In
- Tenant Isolation Before Knowledge Reuse
- Measurable Quality Before Scale
- Cost Visibility Before Uncontrolled Usage
- Recovery Before Full Automation
- Documentation Before Production
- Continuous Evaluation Before Trust Expansion

---

# AI Operating System Scope

The AI Operating System includes:

- Prompt OS
- Agent Registry
- Department Registry
- Role Registry
- Skill Registry
- Tool Registry
- Model Registry
- Task Engine
- Workflow Engine
- Agent Router
- Orchestration Layer
- Context Manager
- Memory Engine Integration
- Knowledge Retrieval
- Policy Engine
- Permission Evaluation
- Human Approval
- AI Audit
- Evidence Management
- Evaluation Framework
- Cost Management
- Performance Analytics
- Failure Recovery
- Multi-Project Context
- Multi-Tenant Isolation
- Learning and Improvement

---

# AI OS Non-Scope

The AI OS should not:

- Replace human enterprise ownership
- Approve its own high-risk actions without independent controls
- Store unrestricted customer context inside shared memory
- Allow agents to access tools without explicit permissions
- Depend permanently on one model provider
- Treat generated content as automatically correct
- Execute financial, legal, security, or destructive actions without required approval
- Create hidden workflows outside governance
- Bypass platform access controls
- Learn directly from unvalidated outputs
- Present simulated completion as verified work

---

# AI OS Layer Architecture

The AI Operating System should follow a layered architecture.

```text
Experience and Request Layer

↓

Identity and Authorization Layer

↓

Context and Knowledge Layer

↓

Planning and Task Layer

↓

Routing and Orchestration Layer

↓

Agent, Model, and Tool Layer

↓

Execution and Workflow Layer

↓

Review and Approval Layer

↓

Evidence and Audit Layer

↓

Analytics and Learning Layer
```

Each layer must have clear ownership and documented contracts.

---

# Layer 1 — Experience and Request Layer

This layer receives work from:

- Humans
- Products
- APIs
- Workflows
- Events
- Schedules
- Enterprise Systems
- Other Authorized Agents

A request should include appropriate context such as:

- Requester
- Tenant
- Organization
- Workspace
- Project
- Product
- Priority
- Purpose
- Data Classification
- Desired Outcome
- Required Deadline
- Approval Requirements

Unstructured requests should be normalized before execution.

---

# Layer 2 — Identity and Authorization Layer

Every AI action must have an identifiable actor and authority chain.

The layer should validate:

- Requester Identity
- Agent Identity
- Tenant Scope
- Project Scope
- Role
- Permissions
- Tool Permissions
- Data Access
- Model Policy
- Approval Threshold
- Action Risk

Anonymous or untraceable production AI execution should not be permitted.

---

# Layer 3 — Context and Knowledge Layer

This layer assembles the information required for accurate execution.

Context sources may include:

- User Request
- Current Task
- Product Documentation
- Project Documentation
- Enterprise Standards
- Governance Policies
- Previous Decisions
- Approved Memory
- Knowledge Base
- Customer Configuration
- Industry Knowledge
- Tool Results

Context must be permission-aware and source-aware.

---

# Layer 4 — Planning and Task Layer

This layer converts requests into executable work.

It should support:

- Intent Classification
- Goal Definition
- Scope Definition
- Constraint Identification
- Task Decomposition
- Dependency Mapping
- Priority Assignment
- Risk Classification
- Review Planning
- Evidence Requirements
- Completion Criteria

Complex work should not be executed as one uncontrolled prompt.

---

# Layer 5 — Routing and Orchestration Layer

This layer selects:

- Department
- Agent
- Model
- Tool
- Workflow
- Reviewer
- Approval Path
- Execution Order
- Retry Strategy
- Escalation Path

Routing decisions must be explainable and auditable.

---

# Layer 6 — Agent, Model, and Tool Layer

This layer contains approved execution resources.

It includes:

- AI Agents
- Agent Skills
- AI Models
- APIs
- Code Tools
- Search Tools
- Repositories
- Databases
- Enterprise Services
- Communication Tools
- Deployment Tools
- Monitoring Tools

Agents should access only the resources required for assigned work.

---

# Layer 7 — Execution and Workflow Layer

This layer performs structured work through:

- Sequential Steps
- Parallel Steps
- Conditional Branches
- Retries
- Timeouts
- Approvals
- Compensating Actions
- Human Escalation
- Tool Calls
- Agent Collaboration

Every workflow should have a defined lifecycle.

---

# Layer 8 — Review and Approval Layer

This layer validates output before release or action.

Possible reviews include:

- Self-Check
- Peer Agent Review
- Specialist Review
- Security Review
- Quality Review
- Compliance Review
- Human Review
- Executive Approval

Review depth must match risk.

---

# Layer 9 — Evidence and Audit Layer

This layer stores evidence that work occurred correctly.

Evidence may include:

- Inputs
- Plan
- Agent Assignments
- Model Used
- Tool Calls
- Output
- Tests
- Review Results
- Approval
- Logs
- Files
- Checksums
- Deployment Results
- Failure Records

Evidence should be protected against unauthorized modification.

---

# Layer 10 — Analytics and Learning Layer

This layer measures:

- Task Completion
- Quality
- Cost
- Time
- Failures
- Escalations
- Agent Performance
- Model Performance
- Tool Reliability
- Human Override
- Knowledge Reuse
- Workflow Efficiency

Validated learning may improve future execution.

Unvalidated output must not automatically update trusted enterprise knowledge.

---

# Prompt OS Roadmap

Prompt OS defines the standard behavioral system for AI agents.

It should replace disconnected prompt files with a governed layered prompt architecture.

---

# Prompt OS Objectives

Prompt OS must:

- Standardize AI behavior
- Preserve enterprise principles
- Define authority boundaries
- Reduce prompt duplication
- Support role specialization
- Support department specialization
- Support task-specific context
- Improve maintainability
- Enable versioning
- Support model portability
- Maintain human-readable governance

---

# Prompt OS Layer Model

A recommended structure is:

```text
L0 — Founder and Enterprise Direction

L1 — Executive Operating Layer

L2 — C-Suite and Enterprise Function Layer

L3 — Department Director Layer

L4 — Manager and Team Layer

L5 — Specialist or Worker Layer

Task Prompt

Project Context

Runtime Context
```

Each lower layer should inherit approved higher-level constraints.

---

# Prompt OS Base Layer

The Base Layer should define:

- Enterprise Identity
- Mission
- Core Principles
- Security Rules
- Documentation Rules
- Honesty Requirements
- Evidence Requirements
- Escalation Rules
- Prohibited Actions
- Communication Standards
- Completion Standards

The Base Layer should remain stable and centrally governed.

---

# Prompt OS Role Layers

Role layers should define:

- Role Purpose
- Responsibilities
- Authority
- Inputs
- Outputs
- Allowed Tools
- Required Reviews
- Escalation
- Metrics
- Knowledge Requirements
- Collaboration Rules

Roles should not depend on informal personality prompts.

---

# Prompt OS Runtime Composition

Runtime prompts should be composed from approved sources.

```text
Enterprise Base

+

Governance Policy

+

Department Layer

+

Role Layer

+

Project Context

+

Task Context

+

Tool Instructions

+

Output Contract
```

Prompt composition should be traceable.

---

# Prompt OS Versioning

Every prompt layer should include:

- Prompt ID
- Version
- Owner
- Status
- Effective Date
- Dependencies
- Model Compatibility
- Change Summary
- Reviewer
- Approval

Prompt changes should be tested before broad release.

---

# Prompt OS Testing

- Instruction Following
- Policy Compliance
- Output Structure
- Hallucination Risk
- Escalation Behavior
- Tool Use
- Security
- Context Handling
- Model Compatibility
- Cost
- Latency
- Quality

Prompt changes should not be judged only by one successful example.

No production agent should operate outside the registry.

# Agent Status Model

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Proposed | Under design |
| Draft | Initial configuration |
| Testing | Under evaluation |
| Approved | Authorized for controlled use |
| Active | Available for production work |
| Limited | Restricted execution |
| Suspended | Temporarily disabled |
| Deprecated | Replacement planned |
| Retired | No longer operational |
| Revoked | Disabled due to risk or violation |

# AI Task Lifecycle

```text
Requested

↓

Validated

↓

Planned

↓

Approved Where Required

↓

Queued

↓

Assigned

↓

In Progress

↓

Blocked or Escalated

↓

Review

↓

Approved

↓

Completed

↓

Knowledge Capture

↓

Archived
```

---

# Task Priority

Recommended priorities:

## P0 — Critical

Security, legal, data integrity, production outage, or enterprise continuity.

## P1 — High

Major customer, platform, or delivery impact.

## P2 — Standard

Normal planned enterprise work.

## P3 — Low

Useful but non-urgent work.

## P4 — Experimental

Research or validation work.

Priority should influence routing, cost limits, review, and escalation.

---

# Task Risk Classification

Tasks should be classified by risk.

| Risk | Description |
|---|---|
| R0 | Read-only, low-impact |
| R1 | Internal reversible action |
| R2 | Controlled production or customer impact |
| R3 | Financial, security, legal, or destructive impact |
| R4 | Enterprise-critical or irreversible impact |

Higher risk requires stronger approval and evidence.

---

# Task Evidence Standard

Evidence requirements may include:

- Source References
- Output File
- Test Result
- Validation Report
- Code Diff
- Deployment Log
- Approval
- Screenshot

- Measurable
- Continuously Improving

The objective is not maximum autonomy.

The objective is maximum useful enterprise capability within clear, auditable, and responsible boundaries.

# Part 11 — AI Workforce Roadmap

The AI Workforce Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will design, create, organize, govern, deploy, measure, improve, scale, and retire its enterprise AI workforce.

The AI Workforce is not a collection of unrelated assistants.

It is a structured digital organization made up of specialized AI agents operating through:

- Defined Roles
- Department Ownership
- Permission Boundaries
- Shared Enterprise Standards
- Prompt OS
- Task Engine
- Workflow Engine
- Agent Routing
- Memory and Knowledge
- Human Oversight
- Independent Review
- Performance Measurement
- Auditability

The workforce must increase enterprise execution capacity without weakening security, quality, accountability, or human authority.

---

# AI Workforce Roadmap Statement

> **Build a governed, measurable, multi-department AI Workforce capable of supporting multiple products and projects concurrently through specialized roles, verifiable work, shared knowledge, bounded autonomy, and structured collaboration with humans.**

---

# AI Workforce Vision

The long-term vision is to operate an intelligent digital workforce capable of assisting every major enterprise function.

The AI Workforce should support:

- Leadership
- Product
- Engineering
- Platform
- DevOps
- Security
- Infrastructure
- Data and AI
- Design
- Quality Assurance
- Research
- Documentation
- Operations
- Customer Support
- Customer Success
- Marketing
- Sales
- Finance
- Human Resources
- Legal
- Analytics
- Shared Enterprise Services

The objective is not to maximize agent count.

The objective is to create dependable enterprise execution capacity.

---

# AI Workforce Mission

The mission of the AI Workforce is to expand human capability by executing clearly defined, governed, and measurable work.

The workforce must:

- Perform specialized enterprise tasks
- Collaborate across departments
- Follow approved governance
- Use authorized tools
- Preserve evidence
- Escalate uncertainty
- Support multiple projects
- Reuse enterprise knowledge
- Improve through validated learning
- Remain within assigned authority
- Produce outputs that humans and systems can verify

---

# AI Workforce Strategic Objectives

The AI Workforce Roadmap exists to:

- Establish one AI organizational model
- Define enterprise AI departments
- Define agent hierarchy and authority
- Create reusable agent roles
- Maintain an authoritative Agent Registry
- Measure real workforce capacity
- Standardize agent onboarding
- Establish training and evaluation
- Enable multi-agent collaboration
- Enable multi-project staffing
- Maintain project and tenant isolation
- Separate execution from review
- Integrate humans into approval and escalation
- Measure quality, cost, reliability, and impact
- Improve agent performance through governed learning
- Retire weak or unsafe agents responsibly
- Scale without uncontrolled duplication

---

# AI Workforce Principles

Every AI workforce capability must follow these principles:

- Organization Before Individual Agents
- Capability Before Agent Count
- Role Before Tool Access
- Permission Before Execution
- Context Before Action
- Evidence Before Completion
- Review Before High-Impact Release
- Human Authority Before Strategic Decision
- Shared Knowledge Before Repeated Discovery
- Tenant Isolation Before Cross-Project Reuse
- Measured Performance Before Increased Autonomy
- Governance Before Scale
- Retirement Before Permanent Weakness
- Long-Term Enterprise Value Before Novelty

---

# AI Workforce Scope

The AI Workforce includes:

- Executive AI
- C-Suite AI
- Department Directors
- Department Managers
- Team Leads
- Specialists
- Workers
- Reviewers
- Auditors
- Coordinators
- Researchers
- Monitors
- Incident Responders
- Knowledge Agents
- Operational Agents
- Project-Specific Agents
- Shared Service Agents

---

# AI Workforce Non-Scope

The AI Workforce should not:

- Replace legal human accountability
- Make unrestricted strategic decisions
- Create its own unlimited authority
- Access unrelated client information
- Approve its own high-risk output without separation
- Operate outside the Agent Registry
- Use unapproved tools
- Hide uncertainty
- Claim completion without evidence
- Learn from unvalidated outputs automatically
- Create uncontrolled duplicate agents
- bypass enterprise security or governance
- become dependent on one model provider
- operate without monitoring or suspension controls

---

The AI Workforce should mirror a disciplined enterprise organization.


The hierarchy exists to provide:

- Accountability
- Delegation
- Coordination

- Separation of Duties
- Performance Ownership
- Enterprise Scalability

# AI Workforce Ownership Model

The workforce is owned by MianX.ai.

The operating model is:

```text
MianX.ai Owns the Workforce

AI OS Owns Execution

Departments Own Capabilities

Projects Own Business Context

Products Own Product Outcomes

Clients Own Their Restricted Data

Governance Owns Enterprise Boundaries

Humans Own Final Accountability
```

This ownership model prevents project-specific AI teams from becoming isolated or duplicated organizations.

# Evaluation Stages

## Stage 1 — Unit Evaluation

Tests isolated skills.

## Stage 2 — Role Evaluation

Tests role-level responsibilities.

## Stage 3 — Workflow Evaluation

Tests the agent inside multi-step work.

## Stage 4 — Adversarial Evaluation

Tests security, manipulation, and failure handling.

## Stage 5 — Pilot Evaluation

Tests controlled real-world use.

## Stage 6 — Production Evaluation

Measures ongoing real performance.

# Capacity Formula Concept

A simplified capacity model may consider:

```text
Verified Capacity

=

Available Execution Time

×

Quality-Adjusted Throughput

×

Successful Completion Rate

–

Review Load

–

Retry Load

–

Failure and Escalation Cost
```

The exact model should be validated through production data.

# Collaboration Patterns

## Sequential Collaboration

One agent's approved output becomes the next agent's input.

```text
Researcher

↓

Planner

↓

Builder

↓

Reviewer
```

## Parallel Collaboration

Several agents execute independent work simultaneously.

```text
Security Review

Design Review

Architecture Review

Market Review
```

## Hierarchical Collaboration

Managers delegate to specialized agents.

## Peer Review

One specialist independently reviews another specialist.

## Consensus

Several agents provide independent analysis before a human or governed process decides.

# Agent Suspension

- Policy violations occur
- Quality drops below threshold

- Model behavior changes materially

- Cost becomes uncontrolled
- Owner is unavailable

- Performance remains unacceptable
- Security risk cannot be mitigated
- Tooling is obsolete
- Department structure changes
- Cost is unjustified
- Duplication is identified
- Product or project is retired

# Part 12A — Engineering Strategy & Foundation

Engineering is the execution engine of MianX.ai.

While the AI Operating System defines intelligence, and the AI Workforce defines execution capability, Engineering transforms validated ideas into secure, scalable, maintainable, production-ready enterprise systems.

Engineering is responsible for designing, building, testing, deploying, operating, maintaining, and continuously improving every technical capability across the MianX.ai ecosystem.

The Engineering Roadmap establishes the long-term strategy, governance model, organizational structure, engineering standards, execution methodology, and cultural principles that will guide engineering teams for the next decade and beyond.

The objective is not simply to write code.

The objective is to build one of the world's most disciplined AI-first engineering organizations capable of creating Industry Operating Systems at enterprise scale.

---

# Engineering Roadmap Statement

> **Build an AI-first engineering organization capable of designing, developing, securing, operating, and continuously improving enterprise-grade software platforms through standardized architecture, reusable engineering systems, governed AI collaboration, and measurable engineering excellence.**

---

# Executive Summary

Engineering is the permanent production capability of MianX.ai.

Every product...

- RestaurantOS

- SDK

...will be designed, implemented, tested, deployed, operated, and evolved by the Engineering Organization.

Engineering must support:

- Long-Term Maintainability

The Engineering organization should be built around systems rather than individuals.

Processes should be repeatable.

Knowledge should remain inside the organization.

Quality should be measurable.

Security should be continuous.

Documentation should be complete.

Every engineering decision should strengthen the platform instead of increasing long-term complexity.

# Engineering Vision

The Engineering Vision is to build one of the world's most scalable, reusable, AI-native enterprise engineering organizations capable of creating, operating, and continuously improving intelligent business platforms.

The vision extends beyond software development.

Engineering should become a strategic capability that enables:

- Enterprise Innovation

without losing quality, consistency, or governance.

# Engineering Mission

The mission of Engineering is to transform validated business requirements into secure, scalable, maintainable, observable, and production-ready software systems.

Engineering exists to:

- Design enterprise architecture
- Build reusable platforms
- Deliver reliable software
- Maintain engineering standards
- Protect system quality
- Reduce technical risk
- Improve developer productivity

- Enable continuous delivery
- Preserve organizational knowledge

Engineering should maximize long-term enterprise value rather than short-term feature delivery.

# Engineering Philosophy

Engineering at MianX.ai follows a platform-first philosophy.

Software should never be treated as disposable.

Every component should become part of a reusable ecosystem.

The engineering philosophy is based on the following beliefs:

- Every system should solve real business problems.
- Reuse is better than duplication.
- Simplicity is better than unnecessary complexity.
- Security must exist from the beginning.
- Documentation is part of engineering.
- Architecture should guide implementation.
- Automation should eliminate repetitive work.
- AI should amplify engineers rather than replace engineering discipline.
- Knowledge belongs to the organization.
- Quality is everyone's responsibility.
- Engineering decisions should remain understandable years later.

---

# Engineering Principles

Every engineering activity should follow these core principles.

## 1. Platform Before Product

Build shared capabilities first.

Avoid rebuilding common functionality across products.

---

## 2. Architecture Before Code

Engineering begins with architecture.

Implementation should follow approved architecture.

---

## 3. Security By Design

Security is part of engineering.

Not an afterthought.

---

## 4. Documentation First

Every important engineering decision must be documented.

Knowledge should survive personnel changes.

---

## 5. Reuse Before Rewrite

Prefer extending reusable modules instead of rebuilding them.

---

## 6. Configuration Before Customization

Use configurable systems whenever possible.

Avoid product forks.

---

## 7. Automation Before Manual Work

Manual engineering work should continuously decrease over time.

Automation should increase.

---

## 8. AI-Assisted Engineering

AI should accelerate engineering while remaining governed.

AI never removes accountability.

---

## 9. Observable Systems

Every production system should be measurable.

Nothing should become a black box.

---

## 10. Continuous Improvement

Engineering never becomes "finished."

Every release should improve the platform.

---

## 11. Enterprise Thinking

Engineering decisions should consider:

- Future Products
- Future Teams
- Future Clients
- Future Industries
- Future Scale

---

## 12. Long-Term Maintainability

Every engineering decision should remain understandable and maintainable after many years.

---

# Architecture Principles

Every architectural decision follows these principles.

## Platform First

Shared capabilities come before product-specific implementations.

---

## Modular Design

Every component should be independently maintainable.

---

## Separation of Concerns

Responsibilities should never overlap unnecessarily.

---

## High Cohesion

Related functionality belongs together.

---

## Low Coupling

Dependencies between components should remain minimal.

---

## API First

Every reusable capability should expose well-defined interfaces.

---

## Security By Design

Security must exist in every layer.

---

## AI Native

Architecture should support AI integration from the beginning.

---

## Event Driven

Support asynchronous enterprise workflows.

---

## Configuration Driven

Behavior should be configurable before customizable.

---

## Observable

Everything should be measurable.

---

## Scalable

Architecture should support growth without redesign.

---

## Resilient

Systems should recover from failures gracefully.

---

## Backward Compatible

Breaking changes should be minimized.

# Part 12B-2 — Core Engineering Disciplines

The Core Engineering Disciplines define how MianX.ai designs, builds, tests, secures, operates, and evolves its primary software delivery capabilities.

These disciplines include:

- Backend Engineering
- Frontend Engineering
- Mobile Engineering
- API Engineering

Each discipline has a different responsibility, but all must follow the same enterprise architecture, security, documentation, testing, observability, and governance standards.

No discipline should operate as an isolated technical team.

All engineering disciplines must collaborate through approved contracts, shared platform services, common standards, and documented ownership.

---

# Core Engineering Discipline Statement

> **Build every backend service, frontend experience, mobile application, and API as a secure, reusable, observable, testable, accessible, and maintainable component of the wider MianX.ai enterprise platform.**

---

# Core Engineering Objectives

The Core Engineering Disciplines exist to:

- Translate approved architecture into production systems
- Maintain clear technical ownership
- Standardize implementation patterns
- Reduce duplicated engineering
- Improve delivery predictability
- Maintain secure coding practices
- Support multi-product development
- Protect tenant and project isolation
- Improve customer and developer experience
- Produce reusable platform capabilities
- Maintain test coverage
- Support reliable deployment and recovery
- Preserve engineering knowledge
- Integrate AI-assisted engineering safely
- Support ten-year maintainability

---

# Shared Engineering Principles

Backend, frontend, mobile, and API teams must follow these shared principles:

- Architecture Before Implementation
- Security by Design
- Reuse Before Rebuild
- Configuration Before Customization
- API Contracts Before Integration
- Documentation With Delivery
- Testing Before Release
- Observability Before Production
- Accessibility by Default
- Tenant Awareness by Design
- Evidence Before Completion
- Backward Compatibility Where Required
- Controlled Dependencies
- Automated Validation
- Human Accountability for Final Approval

---

# Shared Engineering Responsibilities

Every engineering discipline is responsible for:

- Understanding approved requirements
- Following architecture decisions
- Maintaining documentation
- Producing testable implementation
- Protecting data and access
- Supporting observability
- Managing errors safely
- Recording technical decisions
- Participating in reviews
- Supporting deployment
- Supporting production operations
- Tracking technical debt
- Preserving backward compatibility where required
- Improving shared engineering systems
- Escalating uncertainty and risk

---

Every discipline should define:

- Executive Owner
- Engineering Director
- Technical Lead
- Architecture Owner
- Security Reviewer
- Quality Reviewer
- Documentation Owner
- Operational Owner
- AI Engineering Owner
- Escalation Path

No critical component should exist without clear ownership.

# Backend Engineering

Backend Engineering is responsible for server-side systems, business logic, domain services, platform services, data access, integrations, background processing, security enforcement, and enterprise workflow execution.

The backend is the operational foundation behind every MianX.ai product.

It should remain:

- Modular
- Secure
- Scalable
- Observable
- Testable
- Tenant-Aware
- API-Driven
- Event-Ready
- Recoverable
- Long-Term Maintainable

---

# Backend Engineering Mission

The mission of Backend Engineering is to build dependable enterprise services that enforce business rules, protect data, coordinate workflows, expose stable interfaces, and support every current and future MianX.ai product.

---

# Backend Engineering Scope

Backend Engineering includes:

- Domain Logic
- Application Services
- Platform Services
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Tenant Management
- Organization Management
- Workspace Management
- Project Management
- Task Management
- Workflow Execution
- API Implementation
- Database Access
- Caching
- Event Processing
- Background Jobs
- File Processing
- Billing
- Payments
- Notifications
- Search Integration
- Reporting Services
- Audit Logging
- AI Service Integration
- External Integrations
- Operational Tooling

---

# Backend Architecture Model

The backend should follow a layered and modular architecture.

```text
Transport Layer

↓

Application Layer

↓

Domain Layer

↓

Infrastructure Layer

↓

Data Layer

↓

External Services
```

---

# Transport Layer

The Transport Layer receives and returns requests.

It may include:

- REST Controllers
- GraphQL Resolvers
- Webhook Handlers
- Event Consumers
- Queue Consumers
- Scheduled Jobs
- Internal Service Endpoints

The Transport Layer should:

- Validate input
- Establish request context
- Authenticate requests
- Call application services
- Return standardized responses
- Avoid complex business logic

---

# Application Layer

The Application Layer coordinates enterprise use cases.

Responsibilities include:

- Use Case Execution
- Command Handling
- Query Handling
- Transaction Coordination
- Policy Evaluation
- Workflow Invocation
- Service Coordination
- Audit Event Creation

The Application Layer should remain independent from user interface concerns.

---

# Domain Layer

The Domain Layer contains core business rules.

It may include:

- Entities
- Value Objects
- Domain Services
- Business Rules
- Domain Events
- Validation Rules
- State Transitions
- Invariants

Domain logic should remain understandable without requiring knowledge of infrastructure implementation.

---

# Infrastructure Layer

The Infrastructure Layer implements technical capabilities.

Examples include:

- Database Repositories
- Cache Adapters
- Message Brokers
- File Storage
- Email Providers
- Payment Providers
- Search Engines
- AI Providers
- External APIs
- Logging
- Metrics

Infrastructure dependencies should be abstracted where long-term portability or testing requires it.

---

# Data Layer

The Data Layer manages persistent and transient data.

It may include:

- PostgreSQL
- Redis
- Search Indexes
- Object Storage
- Data Warehouse
- Event Storage
- Audit Storage
- Vector Storage

Data access must remain:

- Tenant-Aware
- Permission-Aware
- Transaction-Safe
- Observable
- Tested
- Documented

---

# Backend Modular Design

Backend systems should be divided into bounded modules.

Example:

```text
backend/

├── identity/
├── organizations/
├── memberships/
├── roles/
├── permissions/
├── workspaces/
├── projects/
├── tasks/
├── notifications/
├── files/
├── search/
├── reporting/
├── audit/
├── billing/
├── integrations/
├── workflows/
└── ai/
```

Each module should define:

- Purpose
- Public Interface
- Data Ownership
- Events
- Dependencies
- Security Rules
- Tests
- Documentation
- Operational Ownership

---

# Backend Service Boundaries

A backend module or service should own one coherent enterprise capability.

A boundary should be reviewed when:

- Several products require the capability
- Data ownership differs
- Scaling requirements differ
- Security boundaries differ
- Independent deployment is justified
- Operational ownership differs
- Failure isolation is required

Services should not be separated only to create a microservice appearance.

---

# Modular Monolith Strategy

During early platform development, a modular monolith may be preferred when it provides:

- Simpler operations
- Lower infrastructure cost
- Easier transactions
- Faster development
- Clear module boundaries
- Controlled future extraction

A modular monolith must still enforce:

- Module Ownership
- Internal Contracts
- Dependency Rules
- Data Boundaries
- Testing
- Documentation

Poorly structured monoliths must not be accepted as temporary architecture.

---

# Microservice Adoption Criteria

A service should be separated when evidence shows a meaningful need.

Possible reasons include:

- Independent Scaling
- Strong Security Isolation
- Separate Team Ownership
- Different Reliability Requirements
- Different Technology Requirements
- High Failure Isolation Need
- Independent Release Need
- External Platform Consumption

Microservices introduce operational cost and should not be adopted without justification.

---

# Backend Request Lifecycle

A standard backend request should follow:

```text
Request Received

↓

Request ID and Context Created

↓

Authentication

↓

Tenant Resolution

↓

Authorization

↓

Input Validation

↓

Application Service

↓

Domain Rules

↓

Data Transaction

↓

Domain and Audit Events

↓

Response Mapping

↓

Metrics and Logging

↓

Response
```

---

# Backend Authentication

Backend authentication should support:

- User Sessions
- Access Tokens
- Refresh Tokens
- Service Accounts
- API Keys Where Approved
- Enterprise Identity Providers
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Session Revocation
- Token Rotation
- Authentication Audit

Authentication does not automatically grant resource access.

---

# Backend Authorization

Authorization should evaluate:

- Identity
- Tenant
- Membership
- Role
- Permission
- Resource
- Ownership
- Policy Conditions
- Action Risk
- Approval Requirements

Authorization checks should not exist only in the frontend.

The backend remains the authoritative enforcement layer.

---

# Backend Tenant Isolation

Every tenant-aware backend operation must:

- Resolve Tenant Context
- Validate Tenant Membership
- Scope Queries
- Scope Cache Keys
- Scope Search
- Scope Events
- Scope Files
- Scope AI Context
- Scope Audit Logs
- Prevent Cross-Tenant References

Tenant isolation must be covered by automated tests.

---

# Backend Validation

Input validation should include:

- Required Fields
- Types
- Formats
- Lengths
- Ranges
- Enumerations
- Business Rules
- Tenant Scope
- Resource Existence
- Permission
- File Type
- Data Classification

Validation errors should return controlled and consistent responses.

---

# Backend Error Handling

Errors should be classified.

```text
Validation Error

Authentication Error

Authorization Error

Not Found Error

Conflict Error

Rate Limit Error

Dependency Error

Business Rule Error

System Error
```

Error handling must:

- Avoid exposing secrets
- Include correlation identifiers
- Preserve debugging evidence
- Use consistent error codes
- Support retry guidance where appropriate
- Record operational metrics
- Escalate critical failures

---

# Backend Transactions

Transactions should be used where data consistency requires atomic operations.

Transaction design should define:

- Transaction Boundary
- Isolation Requirement
- Retry Behavior
- Idempotency
- Failure Handling
- Event Publication
- Audit Creation
- Compensation Where Required

Long-running external calls should not remain inside database transactions without strong justification.

---

# Backend Idempotency

Idempotency should be implemented for operations where repeated requests may occur.

Examples include:

- Payments
- Webhooks
- Order Submission
- Workflow Execution
- Job Processing
- Data Import
- Retryable Commands
- External Integration Calls

Idempotency keys should be tenant-aware and time-bound where appropriate.

---

# Backend Event-Driven Engineering

Backend systems may emit events when meaningful state changes occur.

Examples:

```text
organization.created

membership.invited

project.created

task.completed

invoice.paid

workflow.failed

ai.task.reviewed
```

Events must have:

- Event ID
- Schema
- Version
- Producer
- Consumers
- Tenant
- Correlation ID
- Timestamp
- Delivery Policy
- Retention
- Security Classification

---

# Background Processing

Background jobs should be used for:

- Email Delivery
- File Processing
- Report Generation
- Data Synchronization
- Notifications
- Search Indexing
- AI Processing
- Scheduled Workflows
- Cleanup
- Analytics Processing

Every job should define:

- Job ID
- Queue
- Priority
- Retry
- Timeout
- Idempotency
- Dead Letter Handling
- Monitoring
- Ownership

---

# Backend Caching

Caching should improve performance without weakening correctness.

Cache design should define:

- Cached Data
- Source of Truth
- Key Strategy
- Tenant Scope
- Time to Live
- Invalidation
- Stale Data Tolerance
- Failure Behavior
- Security
- Monitoring

Cache should never silently become the permanent source of truth.

---

# Backend Security Standards

Backend security should include:

- Secure Authentication
- Least Privilege
- Input Validation
- Output Encoding
- Parameterized Queries
- Secret Management
- Dependency Scanning
- Rate Limiting
- Audit Logging
- Data Encryption
- Tenant Isolation
- File Validation
- Webhook Verification
- SSRF Protection
- Injection Protection
- Safe Deserialization
- Security Headers Where Applicable

---

# Backend Observability

Every critical backend service should provide:

- Structured Logs
- Request Metrics
- Error Metrics
- Latency Metrics
- Throughput
- Dependency Metrics
- Queue Metrics
- Database Metrics
- Cache Metrics
- Business Metrics
- Audit Events
- Distributed Traces

Logs must include enough context for investigation without exposing sensitive data.

---

# Backend Performance

Backend performance should be measured through:

- Response Time
- Throughput
- Query Time
- Queue Delay
- Cache Hit Rate
- Error Rate
- Resource Usage
- External Dependency Time
- Concurrency
- Data Volume

Optimization should follow evidence rather than assumption.

---

# Backend Testing

Backend testing should include:

- Unit Tests
- Domain Tests
- Application Service Tests
- Repository Tests
- Integration Tests
- API Tests
- Authorization Tests
- Tenant Isolation Tests
- Event Tests
- Queue Tests
- Migration Tests
- Performance Tests
- Security Tests
- Recovery Tests

---

# Backend Quality Gates

Before release:

- [ ] Architecture follows approved boundaries
- [ ] Business rules are tested
- [ ] Authorization is tested
- [ ] Tenant isolation is tested
- [ ] Inputs are validated

# Backend Documentation

Every backend module should document:

- APIs

# Frontend Engineering

Frontend Engineering is responsible for building the user-facing web experiences through which customers, employees, partners, administrators, developers, and AI operators interact with MianX.ai.

The frontend must transform complex enterprise capabilities into understandable, efficient, accessible, responsive, and secure user experiences.

---

# Frontend Engineering Mission

The mission of Frontend Engineering is to provide consistent, accessible, high-performance enterprise interfaces that expose platform capabilities without duplicating or weakening backend business rules.

---

# Frontend Engineering Scope

Frontend Engineering includes:

- Public Websites
- Authentication Interfaces
- Customer Applications
- Admin Applications
- Enterprise Dashboards
- Developer Portal
- Partner Portal
- Marketplace
- AI Workforce Control Center
- Reporting Interfaces
- Configuration Interfaces
- Internal Operations Tools
- Shared Component Library
- Design System Implementation

```text

↓

Routing

↓

Page or Feature Modules

↓

Shared UI Components

↓

Client Services

↓

API Layer

↓
```

# Frontend Application Shell

- Authentication State
- Tenant Selection

- Product Selection
- Theme

- Global Error Handling
- Notifications

The application shell should not own feature-specific business logic.

# Frontend Feature Modules

Example:

```text
frontend/

├── auth/

├── workspaces/
├── projects/
├── tasks/
├── files/
├── notifications/
├── reports/
├── billing/
├── settings/
├── ai/
└── shared/
```

Every feature module should define:

- Routes
- Components
- Data Requirements
- Permissions
- State
- Validation
- Tests
- Analytics
- Documentation

---

# Frontend Design System

Every MianX.ai product should use the shared Design System.

The Design System should provide:

- Color Tokens
- Typography
- Spacing
- Layout
- Icons
- Buttons
- Forms
- Tables
- Navigation
- Modals
- Notifications
- Loading States
- Empty States
- Error States
- Charts
- Accessibility Patterns
- Responsive Patterns

Shared components should be reused before product-specific components are created.

---

# Frontend Component Categories

## Primitive Components

Examples:

- Button
- Input
- Label
- Checkbox
- Radio
- Select
- Icon
- Text
- Container

## Composite Components

Examples:

- Form Field
- Search Input
- Data Table
- Date Picker
- File Uploader
- User Selector
- Permission Selector

## Product Components

Examples:

- Task Board
- Order Timeline
- Poultry Ledger
- Kitchen Queue
- Agent Activity Panel

Product-specific components should remain outside generic primitives unless broadly reusable.

---

# Frontend State Management

Frontend state should be classified.

## Server State

Data owned by backend services.

Examples:

- Users
- Projects
- Tasks
- Reports
- Notifications

Server state should use approved query and caching patterns.

## Local UI State

Examples:

- Modal Open State
- Selected Tab
- Form Draft
- Temporary Filter

## Global Client State

Use only when several unrelated areas require the same client-side state.

Examples:

- Current Tenant
- Current Workspace
- Theme
- Locale

Global state should not become a second backend.

---

# Frontend Data Fetching

Frontend data access should:

- Use approved API clients
- Include tenant context
- Handle loading
- Handle empty states
- Handle errors
- Support cancellation
- Avoid duplicate requests
- Respect caching rules
- Support retries where safe
- Record telemetry
- Avoid exposing secrets

---

# Frontend Authorization

The frontend may hide or disable actions based on permissions, but it must never be the only enforcement layer.

Frontend authorization should:

- Improve usability
- Prevent unavailable actions from being presented
- Explain missing permissions where appropriate
- Refresh after role changes
- Handle expired sessions
- Avoid exposing restricted metadata

The backend remains authoritative.

---

# Frontend Form Engineering

Forms should support:

- Clear Labels
- Validation
- Accessible Errors
- Loading States
- Success States
- Unsaved Change Protection
- Submission Prevention During Processing
- Server Error Mapping
- Keyboard Navigation
- Mobile Responsiveness
- Localization
- Audit-Sensitive Confirmation Where Required

---

# Frontend Error Handling

Frontend errors should provide:

- Clear User Message
- Recovery Action
- Correlation ID Where Helpful
- Retry Where Safe
- Support Guidance
- Logging
- Error Boundary
- Graceful Degradation

Internal technical details should not be exposed to users.

---

# Frontend Accessibility

Frontend Engineering must follow approved accessibility standards.

Requirements include:

- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard Navigation
- Focus Management
- Screen Reader Support
- Sufficient Contrast
- Accessible Forms
- Text Alternatives
- Responsive Zoom
- Reduced Motion Support
- Error Announcement
- Logical Heading Structure

Accessibility is a release requirement, not an optional improvement.

Every supported interface should define behavior for:

- Laptop
- Desktop
- Large Displays

Responsive design should preserve:

- Core Workflow
- Readability
- Navigation
- Touch Targets
- Table Usability
- Form Completion
- Accessibility

Not every desktop feature must be copied unchanged to mobile layouts.

- Server Rendering Where Appropriate
- Static Generation Where Appropriate
- Streaming Where Appropriate

Optimization should remain evidence-based.

---

# Frontend Security

Frontend security should address:

- Cross-Site Scripting

- Open Redirects

- Third-Party Scripts

Secrets must never be embedded in client code.

- Performance Tests

Analytics collection must remain purpose-driven and privacy-aware.

# Frontend AI Experience

- What data is being used

AI interfaces should not create false confidence.

# Mobile Engineering

Mobile Engineering is responsible for building secure, reliable, accessible, and platform-aligned mobile experiences for supported MianX.ai products.

Mobile applications should not be created only to duplicate the complete desktop application.

They should focus on mobile-relevant workflows, field operations, notifications, data capture, approvals, and time-sensitive work.

---

# Mobile Engineering Mission

The mission of Mobile Engineering is to make important MianX.ai workflows available securely and effectively on mobile devices while preserving shared platform rules, data integrity, and enterprise governance.

---

# Mobile Engineering Scope

Mobile Engineering may include:

- Customer Mobile Applications
- Staff Applications
- Field Operations
- Delivery Applications
- Sales Applications
- Approval Applications
- Support Applications
- Mobile Notifications
- Mobile Reporting
- Offline Data Capture
- Barcode or QR Workflows
- Camera and File Capture
- Location-Aware Workflows Where Approved
- Mobile AI Assistance

---

# Mobile Product Decision

A mobile application should be created when:

- Users perform work away from desktop devices
- Real-time notifications are important
- Camera, GPS, barcode, or device capabilities add value
- Field data capture is required
- Mobile approval improves operations
- Offline or low-connectivity workflows are required
- Customer usage patterns support mobile

A mobile application should not be built only for product appearance.

---

# Mobile Architecture Model

```text
Mobile Application Shell

↓

Feature Modules

↓

Shared Mobile Components

↓

Local State and Secure Storage

↓

API Client

↓

Offline Synchronization

↓

Telemetry and Crash Reporting
```

---

# Mobile Shared-Core Principle

Mobile applications should reuse:

- Backend APIs
- Authentication
- Roles and Permissions
- Business Rules
- Workflows
- Notifications
- Files
- Reporting
- AI Services
- Audit

Business rules should not be independently recreated inside mobile clients unless offline requirements demand controlled duplication.

---

# Mobile Technology Strategy

The mobile technology choice should evaluate:

- Product Requirements
- Team Capability
- Performance
- Native Device Needs
- Code Reuse
- Accessibility
- Security
- Release Process
- Long-Term Support
- Ecosystem Maturity

Possible strategies may include:

- React Native
- Native iOS
- Native Android
- Progressive Web Application
- Hybrid Approach

Technology selection requires architecture review.

---

# Mobile Authentication

Mobile authentication should support:

- Secure Login
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Biometric Unlock Where Approved
- Secure Session Storage
- Token Rotation
- Session Revocation
- Device Registration
- Device Risk
- Logout
- Account Recovery

Sensitive credentials must not be stored insecurely.

---

# Mobile Secure Storage

Secure storage should be used for:

- Tokens
- Device Credentials
- Encryption Keys Where Appropriate
- Limited Offline Data
- User Preferences

Sensitive business data should be minimized on the device.

---

# Mobile Offline Architecture

Offline support should define:

- Which Data Is Available Offline
- Read-Only or Editable Behavior
- Local Encryption
- Synchronization
- Conflict Resolution
- Retry
- Expiration
- Device Loss Handling
- Audit
- Data Deletion

Offline behavior must never silently weaken tenant or permission controls.

---

# Mobile Synchronization

Synchronization should support:

- Incremental Sync
- Retry
- Idempotency
- Conflict Detection
- Version Comparison
- Server Authority
- User Resolution Where Required
- Audit
- Network Awareness
- Background Processing

---

# Mobile Permissions

Device permissions may include:

- Camera
- Location
- Notifications
- Files
- Microphone
- Contacts

Applications should:

- Request only necessary permissions
- Explain purpose
- Handle denial
- Respect operating-system controls
- Avoid background access without need
- Record consent where required

---

# Mobile Notification Engineering

Push notifications should be:

- Relevant
- Permission-Aware
- Tenant-Aware
- Configurable
- Rate-Controlled
- Secure
- Deep-Link Safe
- Localized
- Auditable Where Required

Notification content should avoid exposing sensitive data on locked screens.

---

# Mobile Deep Links

Deep links should validate:

- Destination
- Authentication
- Tenant
- Permission
- Resource Existence
- Expiration
- Source

A deep link must not bypass authorization.

---

# Mobile Accessibility

Mobile applications should support:

- Screen Readers
- Dynamic Text
- Contrast
- Touch Target Size
- Orientation Where Appropriate
- Keyboard Access Where Applicable
- Clear Focus
- Reduced Motion
- Accessible Forms
- Error Announcements

---

# Mobile Performance

Mobile performance should measure:

- Startup Time
- Screen Load
- API Latency
- Memory Usage
- Battery Impact
- Network Usage
- Crash Rate
- Freeze Rate
- Offline Sync Time
- Application Size

---

# Mobile Security

Mobile security should address:

- Insecure Local Storage
- Token Leakage
- Reverse Engineering Risk
- Rooted or Compromised Devices Where Relevant
- Screenshot Exposure Where Relevant
- Clipboard Exposure
- Unsafe Deep Links
- Untrusted Certificates
- Dependency Risk
- Sensitive Logs
- Device Loss
- Offline Data Leakage

# Mobile Testing

# API Engineering

API Engineering is responsible for designing, implementing, securing, documenting, versioning, monitoring, and operating the interfaces through which MianX.ai services, products, partners, plugins, agents, and external systems communicate.

APIs are enterprise contracts.

They must remain stable, predictable, secure, and understandable.

---

# API Engineering Mission

The mission of API Engineering is to provide reliable and governed interfaces that expose MianX.ai capabilities without exposing internal complexity or weakening security and platform ownership.

---

# API Engineering Scope

API Engineering includes:

- Internal APIs
- External APIs
- Public APIs
- Partner APIs
- Product APIs
- Service APIs
- AI APIs
- Webhooks
- GraphQL Where Approved
- Event Contracts
- SDK Contracts
- Plugin Interfaces
- Marketplace Interfaces
- API Gateway
- API Documentation
- API Analytics

---

# API-First Development

Reusable capabilities should define their interface before implementation.

The API-first lifecycle is:

```text
Business Capability

↓

API Requirements

↓

Contract Definition

↓

Security Review

↓

Consumer Review

↓

Mock or Prototype

↓

Implementation

↓

Contract Testing

↓

Documentation

↓

Release
```

---

# API Design Principles

Every API should be:

- Consistent
- Predictable
- Secure
- Tenant-Aware
- Permission-Aware
- Versioned
- Documented
- Observable
- Testable
- Backward-Compatible Where Required
- Idempotent Where Required
- Developer-Friendly
- Performance-Aware

---

# API Categories

## Internal Service APIs

Used between trusted platform services.

Internal does not mean unauthenticated.

## Product APIs

Used by MianX.ai web and mobile applications.

## Partner APIs

Used by approved enterprise partners.

## Public APIs

Used by external developers under published contracts.

## Administrative APIs

Used for high-privilege operations and require stronger controls.

## AI APIs

Used for agent tasks, model access, memory, knowledge, and AI workflows.

---

# REST API Standards

REST APIs should define:

- Resource Naming
- HTTP Methods
- Status Codes
- Request Schema
- Response Schema
- Error Schema
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Pagination
- Filtering
- Sorting
- Idempotency
- Versioning
- Rate Limits
- Documentation

---

# Resource Naming

Recommended:

```text
/organizations

/organizations/{organizationId}

/projects/{projectId}/tasks

/users/{userId}/memberships
```

Avoid action-heavy routes where a resource or command model is more appropriate.

---

# HTTP Method Standards

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| GET | Retrieve |
| POST | Create or execute approved command |
| PUT | Replace complete resource where appropriate |
| PATCH | Partially update |
| DELETE | Delete or request deletion |

Operations must remain idempotent according to their documented behavior.

---

# Status Code Standards

Common responses may include:

| Status | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 200 | Successful request |
| 201 | Resource created |
| 202 | Accepted for asynchronous processing |
| 204 | Successful with no response body |
| 400 | Invalid request |
| 401 | Authentication required or invalid |
| 403 | Authenticated but unauthorized |
| 404 | Resource not found within authorized scope |
| 409 | Conflict |
| 422 | Valid request format but invalid business data |
| 429 | Rate limit exceeded |
| 500 | Internal server failure |
| 502 | Upstream dependency failure |
| 503 | Temporarily unavailable |

Error behavior must remain consistent.

---

# API Response Standard

A successful response may include:

```json
{
  "data": {},
  "meta": {
    "requestId": "req_123"
  }
}
```

A list response may include:

```json
{
  "data": [],
  "meta": {
    "page": 1,
    "pageSize": 25,
    "total": 250,
    "requestId": "req_123"
  }
}
```

The exact standard should remain centralized and versioned.

---

# API Error Standard

An error response may include:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "TASK_VALIDATION_FAILED",
    "message": "The task could not be created.",
    "fields": {
      "title": [
        "Title is required."
      ]
    },
    "requestId": "req_123"
  }
}
```

Error messages must not expose confidential infrastructure details.

---

# API Authentication

APIs may support:

- Session Authentication
- OAuth 2.0
- OpenID Connect
- Service Tokens
- API Keys for Approved Uses
- Signed Webhooks
- Mutual TLS Where Required

Authentication methods should match risk and consumer type.

---

# API Authorization

Every API request should evaluate:

- Identity
- Tenant
- Organization
- Membership
- Role
- Permission
- Resource
- Action
- Policy Conditions
- Data Classification

API access must never depend only on route secrecy.

---

# API Tenant Awareness

Tenant-aware APIs must:

- Resolve tenant explicitly
- Validate membership
- Scope all queries
- Prevent cross-tenant identifiers
- Scope rate limits where appropriate
- Scope idempotency keys
- Scope cache
- Scope logs
- Scope events
- Scope AI context

---

# API Pagination

Large collections should use approved pagination.

Possible models include:

- Page-Based Pagination
- Cursor-Based Pagination

Cursor pagination may be preferred for large or frequently changing datasets.

Pagination should define:

- Default Size
- Maximum Size
- Stable Sort
- Cursor Expiration
- Filters
- Total Count Policy

---

# API Filtering and Sorting

Filtering should:

- Use documented parameters
- Validate allowed fields
- Protect performance
- Protect unauthorized metadata
- Support indexed fields
- Remain tenant-aware

Sorting should use approved fields and stable ordering.

---

# API Idempotency

Idempotency should be supported for sensitive or retryable operations.

Examples include:

- Payment Creation
- Order Submission
- Workflow Start
- File Processing
- External Synchronization
- AI Task Submission

An idempotent operation should return the original accepted result when safely repeated.

---

# API Rate Limiting

Rate limits should consider:

- Consumer
- Tenant
- User
- API Key
- Endpoint
- Risk
- Cost
- Product Plan
- AI Usage
- Regional Requirements

Rate-limit responses should include controlled retry information.

---

# API Versioning

API versioning should protect existing consumers.

Possible approaches include:

- Path Version
- Header Version
- Media Type Version
- Schema Version

The chosen strategy should remain consistent.

---

# API Deprecation

Deprecation should include:

- Deprecated Version
- Reason
- Replacement
- Migration Guide
- Announcement Date
- Support Period
- Removal Date
- Usage Monitoring
- Owner
- Customer Communication

No important API should disappear without a controlled migration.

---

# API Compatibility

Compatibility should be validated through:

- Contract Tests
- Consumer Tests
- Schema Comparison
- SDK Tests
- Integration Tests
- Event Compatibility Tests
- Version Policies

Breaking changes require explicit approval.

---

# GraphQL Engineering

GraphQL may be used when it provides clear product value.

GraphQL engineering should address:

- Schema Ownership
- Authorization
- Query Depth
- Query Complexity
- Rate Limiting
- Pagination
- N+1 Queries
- Data Loader Patterns
- Error Handling
- Schema Version Evolution
- Introspection Policy
- Monitoring

GraphQL should not be adopted only because it is technically popular.

---

# Webhook Engineering

Webhooks should support:

- Event Identity
- Signature Verification
- Delivery Attempts
- Retry
- Backoff
- Idempotency
- Timeout
- Secret Rotation
- Tenant Scope
- Event Version
- Delivery Logs
- Suspension
- Replay Where Safe

Webhook consumers must not be trusted automatically.

---

# Webhook Payload

A webhook event should include appropriate:

- Event ID
- Event Type
- Version
- Timestamp
- Tenant
- Resource
- Data
- Correlation ID
- Signature

Sensitive data should be minimized.

---

# Event Contract Engineering

Events are also enterprise interfaces.

Event contracts should define:

- Event Name
- Version
- Producer
- Consumer Expectations
- Payload
- Security Classification
- Delivery Behavior
- Ordering
- Idempotency
- Retention
- Deprecation
- Ownership

---

# API Gateway

The API Gateway may provide:

- Routing
- Authentication
- Rate Limiting
- Request Validation
- Threat Protection
- Version Routing
- Logging
- Metrics
- Correlation IDs
- Regional Routing
- Developer Plans
- API Key Management

Business authorization should not depend only on gateway controls.

---

# API Documentation

Every API should provide:

- Purpose
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Endpoints
- Schemas
- Examples
- Error Codes
- Pagination
- Rate Limits
- Webhooks
- Versions
- Deprecation
- Support
- Changelog

OpenAPI or another approved specification should be used where appropriate.

---

# API Developer Experience

The API experience should provide:

- Quick Start
- Sandbox
- Test Credentials
- Interactive Documentation
- SDKs
- Examples
- Postman or Equivalent Collections Where Approved
- Webhook Testing
- Error Reference
- Status Information
- Changelog
- Support

---

# API Observability

API monitoring should include:

- Request Count
- Success Rate
- Error Rate
- Latency
- Rate Limit Events
- Authentication Failures
- Authorization Failures
- Consumer
- Tenant
- Version
- Endpoint
- Dependency Time
- Payload Size
- Cost Where Relevant

---

# API Security

API security should address:

- Broken Authorization
- Injection
- Excessive Data Exposure
- Rate Abuse
- Credential Leakage
- Weak Authentication
- Unsafe File Handling
- SSRF
- Replay
- Insecure Webhooks
- Schema Abuse
- Denial of Service
- Tenant Leakage

---

# API Testing

API testing should include:

- Contract Tests
- Schema Tests
- Authentication Tests
- Authorization Tests
- Tenant Isolation Tests
- Validation Tests
- Error Tests
- Pagination Tests
- Idempotency Tests
- Rate Limit Tests
- Performance Tests
- Security Tests
- Backward Compatibility Tests
- Webhook Tests

---

# API Quality Gates

Before release:

- [ ] Contract approved
- [ ] Authentication defined
- [ ] Authorization defined
- [ ] Tenant scope verified
- [ ] Error codes documented
- [ ] Pagination defined
- [ ] Rate limits defined

- [ ] SDK compatibility checked where applicable

# Cross-Discipline Collaboration

Backend, frontend, mobile, and API engineers must collaborate through shared contracts.

A standard feature flow should be:

```text
Product Requirement

↓

Architecture

↓

API Contract

↓

Backend Design

↓

Frontend and Mobile Design

↓

Security Review

↓

Parallel Implementation

↓

Contract and Integration Testing

↓

End-to-End Validation

↓

Release
```

---

# Contract-First Collaboration

Before parallel implementation begins, teams should agree on:

- Request Schema
- Response Schema
- Errors
- Permissions
- Loading Behavior
- Empty Behavior
- Pagination
- Events
- Version
- Acceptance Criteria

Mocks may be used before backend implementation is complete.

---

# Shared Definition of Done

A cross-discipline feature is complete only when:

- Backend logic is complete.
- API contract is approved and implemented.
- Frontend or mobile experience is complete where required.
- Authentication and authorization are verified.
- Tenant isolation is verified.
- Loading, empty, success, and error states exist.
- Accessibility is reviewed.
- Tests pass.
- Observability is active.
- Documentation is updated.
- Release and rollback are ready.
- Product acceptance is complete.

# Core Engineering Risk Categories

Major risks include:

- Backend Coupling
- Frontend Business Logic Duplication
- Mobile Data Leakage
- API Breaking Changes
- Tenant Isolation Failure
- Authorization Inconsistency
- Uncontrolled State
- Inaccessible Interfaces
- Poor Error Handling
- Unversioned Contracts
- Excessive Dependencies
- Weak Testing
- Incomplete Observability
- Client-Side Secret Exposure
- Offline Conflict Corruption
- Insecure Webhooks
- Performance Regression

Each risk should have an owner and mitigation.

Each discipline should maintain:

- Architecture
- Standards
- Folder Structure
- Coding Rules
- Security Rules
- Testing Rules
- Performance Targets
- Observability
- Release Process
- Runbooks
- Ownership
- Examples

- Known Limitations
- Technical Debt

---

# Core Engineering Exit Criteria

Part 12B-2 is successfully implemented when:

- Backend modules have clear boundaries and ownership.
- Business rules remain server-authoritative.
- Frontend products use one shared Design System.
- Frontend authorization supports but does not replace backend enforcement.
- Mobile products exist only for validated mobile workflows.
- Mobile data and tokens are stored securely.
- APIs follow one documented contract standard.
- Tenant and permission controls are consistent across all disciplines.
- API changes are versioned and compatibility-tested.
- All disciplines produce tests, documentation, and observability.
- Cross-discipline feature delivery follows approved contracts.
- AI-assisted engineering remains reviewed and verifiable.
- Production systems can be supported and recovered.
- New products reuse shared engineering systems instead of rebuilding them.

---

# Part 12B-2 Summary

The Core Engineering Disciplines transform approved architecture into usable enterprise products.

Their responsibilities are connected:

```text
Backend Engineering
Builds trusted enterprise behavior

API Engineering
Exposes stable enterprise contracts

Frontend Engineering
Creates accessible web experiences

Mobile Engineering
Supports validated mobile and field workflows
```

All four disciplines must remain:

- Secure
- Modular
- Contract-Driven
- Tenant-Aware
- Accessible
- Observable
- Tested
- Documented
- Reusable
- Governed
- AI-Assisted
- Human-Accountable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not to build separate backend, frontend, mobile, and API systems.

The objective is to build one coordinated engineering platform that delivers consistent enterprise capability across every supported experience.

# Part 12B-3 — Platform Engineering

Platform Engineering defines how MianX.ai builds and operates the technical foundation shared by every product, service, AI capability, industry module, customer environment, and enterprise workflow.

Platform Engineering is responsible for the systems that other engineering teams depend on.

It includes:

- Database Engineering
- Infrastructure Engineering
- AI Engineering
- Shared Platform Engineering
- Shared Runtime Capabilities
- Reliability Foundations
- Developer Enablement
- Platform Governance
- Platform Architecture

The purpose of Platform Engineering is not to centralize every technical decision.

Its purpose is to provide secure, reusable, observable, scalable, and well-governed capabilities that allow product teams to build faster without repeatedly solving foundational problems.

---

# Platform Engineering Statement

> **Build and operate one dependable engineering foundation that allows every MianX.ai product, AI agent, service, and industry platform to scale securely without rebuilding databases, infrastructure, AI services, or shared enterprise capabilities.**

---

# Platform Engineering Mission

The mission of Platform Engineering is to reduce unnecessary product complexity by providing production-ready technical capabilities as shared enterprise services.

Platform Engineering must:

- Standardize foundational architecture
- Reduce repeated engineering
- Improve security
- Improve reliability
- Improve developer productivity
- Support multiple products
- Support multiple tenants
- Support multiple environments
- Support the AI Operating System
- Support regional expansion
- Control infrastructure cost
- Preserve architectural consistency
- Maintain platform documentation
- Enable safe product autonomy

---

# Platform Engineering Objectives

Platform Engineering exists to:

- Build reliable data foundations
- Provide automated infrastructure
- Provide secure cloud environments
- Provide shared AI capabilities
- Provide reusable enterprise services
- Standardize runtime operations
- Improve developer self-service
- Reduce operational burden
- Maintain service ownership
- Improve observability
- Support disaster recovery
- Protect tenant isolation
- Enable multi-product delivery
- Prevent platform fragmentation
- Support long-term global scale

---

# Platform Engineering Principles

Every Platform Engineering capability must follow these principles:

- Platform as a Product
- Security by Default
- Reliability by Design
- Automation Before Manual Operations
- Self-Service With Governance
- Stable Interfaces
- Clear Ownership
- Multi-Tenant Awareness
- Observability Before Production
- Recovery Before Scale
- Configuration Before Forking
- Open Standards Where Practical
- Cost Visibility
- Documentation With Delivery
- Measured Adoption
- Backward Compatibility Where Required

---

# Platform as a Product

The internal platform should be treated as a product used by engineering teams, product teams, AI agents, and enterprise systems.

Platform users include:

- Backend Engineers
- Frontend Engineers
- Mobile Engineers
- AI Engineers
- Data Engineers
- DevOps Engineers
- Product Teams
- Integration Teams
- Marketplace Developers
- AI Workforce
- Operations Teams

The platform should provide:

- Clear Documentation
- Stable Interfaces
- Self-Service Workflows
- Support
- Versioning
- Reliability Targets
- Usage Metrics
- Feedback Channels
- Deprecation Policies
- Product Ownership

Internal users should not need private knowledge to use platform services safely.

---

# Platform Engineering Architecture

Platform Engineering should be organized into several connected capability groups.

```text
Platform Engineering

├── Database Engineering
├── Infrastructure Engineering
├── AI Engineering
├── Shared Platform Engineering
├── Developer Platform
├── Runtime Platform
├── Reliability Engineering
```
