# Engineering Maturity Exit Criteria

Part 12D-5 is successfully established when:

- MianX.ai has an approved L0–L5 maturity model.
- Every maturity level has clear characteristics, risks, requirements, and exit criteria.
- Critical engineering capabilities are mapped to the maturity model.
- Capability assessment uses documented evidence.
- Engineering maturity is not based on team size or technology appearance.
- Security, quality, reliability, platform reuse, AI governance, and recovery are required for advancement.
- The Engineering Excellence Framework is approved.
- Excellence is measured across customer value, architecture, security, quality, reliability, delivery, maintainability, platform reuse, developer experience, AI collaboration, knowledge, and improvement.
- Continuous Improvement follows a documented and measurable lifecycle.
- Incidents, reviews, metrics, technical debt, and feedback create improvement actions.
- Successful improvements become shared standards, tools, platform capabilities, documentation, or AI skills.
- Engineering Innovation follows a governed research-to-productization process.
- Experiments remain isolated, time-bound, measurable, and retireable.
- Maturity assessments have owners, evidence, target levels, and review dates.
- Advancement requires demonstrated sustainable capability.
- Human authority remains embedded as AI and automation mature.
- Engineering maturity directly supports the long-term MianX.ai enterprise vision.

---

# Part 12D-5 Summary

Engineering Maturity defines the controlled evolution of MianX.ai Engineering from unstructured activity into an intelligent enterprise creation capability.

The complete maturity path is:

```text
L0 — Unstructured Engineering

↓

L1 — Standardized Engineering

↓

L2 — Governed Engineering

↓

L3 — Platform-Enabled Engineering

↓

L4 — Adaptive AI-Native Engineering

↓

L5 — Autonomous Enterprise Engineering
```

The maturity system is supported by four connected foundations:

```text
Engineering Capability Model
Defines what must mature

Engineering Excellence Framework
Defines what high-quality engineering looks like

Continuous Improvement
Ensures every engineering cycle strengthens the organization

Engineering Innovation
Converts validated technical opportunities into enterprise capabilities
```

Engineering maturity must remain:

- Evidence-Based
- Capability-Driven
- Security-Governed
- Quality-Focused
- Platform-Aligned
- Customer-Outcome-Oriented
- AI-Native
- Human-Accountable
- Observable
- Recoverable
- Continuously Improving
- Financially Sustainable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not to reach the highest maturity label as quickly as possible.

The objective is to build each engineering capability deeply enough that the next level can be reached without weakening the foundations below it.

# Part 12D-6 — Long-Term Engineering Strategy

Engineering Strategy defines how MianX.ai Engineering will evolve over the next decade to become a globally scalable, AI-native, enterprise engineering organization capable of continuously building, operating, and improving Industry Operating Systems.

The purpose of this strategy is not simply to grow the engineering team.

The purpose is to build an engineering system that continuously becomes:

- Smarter
- Faster
- More Reliable
- More Secure
- More Reusable
- More Autonomous
- More Governed
- More Cost Efficient
- More Valuable to Customers
- Easier to Scale

The strategy aligns engineering evolution with the long-term MianX.ai vision of becoming an AI-powered Enterprise Creation Platform.

# Engineering Vision 2036

Engineering will no longer rebuild foundations for every product.

Instead, new products will be assembled from reusable enterprise capabilities.

The organization will combine:

- Human Leadership
- AI Workforce

- Engineering Intelligence
- Continuous Learning

into one engineering ecosystem.

The engineering organization will become:

- Platform First

- AI Native

- Security Embedded
- Continuously Improving
- Globally Scalable
- Enterprise Ready

# Part 13 — Architecture Roadmap

The Architecture Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will design, govern, evolve, secure, scale, document, and continuously improve its complete enterprise architecture.

Architecture is the structural foundation that connects:

- Company Strategy
- Product Strategy
- MianX Core Platform
- AI Operating System
- AI Workforce
- Shared Enterprise Services
- Industry Operating Systems
- Data
- Security
- Infrastructure
- Integrations
- Developer Ecosystem
- Marketplace
- Global Operations

The Architecture Roadmap is not limited to diagrams, technology choices, or system components.

It defines the long-term decision system through which MianX.ai ensures that every product, service, workflow, agent, API, database, integration, and deployment remains aligned with one enterprise vision.

---

# Architecture Roadmap Statement

> **Build one secure, modular, reusable, AI-native, multi-tenant, observable, and globally scalable enterprise architecture that supports every MianX.ai product without repeated foundational rebuilding or uncontrolled technical fragmentation.**

---

# Architecture Vision

The long-term architecture vision is to establish one permanent enterprise foundation upon which MianX.ai can repeatedly create and operate Industry Operating Systems.

The target architecture is:

```text
Enterprise Governance

↓

Enterprise Architecture

↓

MianX Core Platform

↓

Shared Enterprise Services

↓

AI Operating System

↓

Business Platform

↓

Industry Modules

↓

Customer Configuration

↓

Integrations, Plugins, and Marketplace

↓

Regional and Global Operations
```

Every new product should extend this architecture rather than create an unrelated technical foundation.

---

# Architecture Mission

The mission of Architecture is to transform enterprise strategy into stable technical structures, clear boundaries, reusable capabilities, governed interfaces, and long-term evolution paths.

Architecture must:

- Translate strategy into systems
- Define platform boundaries
- Define product boundaries
- Protect shared capabilities
- Prevent unnecessary duplication
- Maintain tenant isolation
- Standardize interfaces
- Guide technology selection
- Embed security and governance
- Support AI-native execution
- Enable independent product evolution
- Preserve compatibility
- Support reliable operations
- Prepare for regional and global scale
- Maintain ten-year-plus sustainability

---

# Architecture Objectives

The Architecture Roadmap exists to:

- Establish one enterprise reference architecture
- Define clear architecture domains
- Maintain platform-first design
- Standardize architectural decisions
- Protect modularity
- Reduce coupling
- Increase reuse
- Define service ownership
- Standardize APIs and events
- Govern data architecture
- Govern AI architecture
- Govern infrastructure architecture
- Support multi-product execution
- Support multi-project execution
- Enable marketplace and plugin expansion
- Maintain architectural documentation
- Control architecture debt
- Support continuous modernization

---

# Architecture Principles

Every architecture decision must follow these principles:

- Strategy Before Technology
- Platform Before Product Duplication
- Business Capability Before Service Boundary
- Modular Before Distributed
- Configuration Before Customization
- Reuse Before Rebuild
- Contracts Before Integration
- Security by Design
- Tenant Isolation by Design
- Data Ownership Before Data Sharing
- Observability Before Production
- Recovery Before Scale
- Versioning Before External Adoption
- Evidence Before Complexity
- Human Governance Before Autonomous Change
- Long-Term Maintainability Before Short-Term Convenience

# Architecture Non-Scope

Architecture should not become:

- Unnecessary theoretical documentation
- Technology selection without business need
- Centralized control over every small implementation detail
- Permanent approval delay
- Complex diagrams disconnected from production
- Microservices adopted for appearance
- Cloud complexity without evidence
- AI autonomy without governance
- Product-specific logic placed inside the Core Platform
- Customer customization that creates permanent forks
- Architecture decisions stored only in meetings or private chat

Architecture must guide delivery rather than block it.

# Modular Monolith Architecture

The initial platform may use a modular monolith where it provides:

- Faster delivery
- Simpler operations
- Easier transactions
- Lower cost
- Clear domain boundaries
- Controlled future extraction

A modular monolith must not become an unstructured monolith.

It must enforce:

- Module Ownership

- Dependency Rules
- Data Ownership
- Internal Contracts
- Tests
- Documentation
- Architecture Validation

# Service-Oriented Evolution

Capabilities should become separate services only when justified by evidence such as:

- Independent scaling
- Separate operational ownership
- Strong isolation requirements
- Independent release needs
- Different reliability targets
- Security boundaries
- Technology specialization
- External consumption
- Failure isolation

# Microservices Architecture

Microservices should be introduced selectively.

- The company wants to appear enterprise-grade
- The architecture diagram looks more advanced
- A technology is popular
- Team size is still small
- Service ownership is unclear
- Operational maturity is insufficient

Every service introduces:

- Network Failure

- Observability Requirements
- Versioning
- Security Boundaries
- Data Consistency Challenges
- Operational Cost

# Architecture Quality Gates

## Gate 1 — Business Alignment

Confirms:

- Business problem is clear.
- Outcome is measurable.
- Scope is approved.

## Gate 2 — Capability Classification

Confirms:

- Capability ownership is correct.
- Platform versus product boundary is clear.
- Duplication is avoided.

## Gate 3 — Architecture Design

Confirms:

- Components are defined.
- Interfaces are defined.
- Data ownership is defined.
- Dependencies are documented.

## Gate 4 — Security and Data

Confirms:

- Threats are reviewed.
- Tenant isolation is defined.
- Data classification is complete.
- Access is controlled.

## Gate 5 — Reliability and Operations

Confirms:

- Monitoring is designed.
- Recovery is defined.
- Capacity is considered.
- Operational ownership exists.

## Gate 6 — Compatibility

Confirms:

- APIs are versioned.
- Events are compatible.
- Migrations are safe.
- Product impact is understood.

## Gate 7 — Cost and Complexity

Confirms:

- Complexity is justified.
- Cost is understood.
- Operational burden is sustainable.

## Gate 8 — Documentation

Confirms:

- Architecture is documented.
- ADR is complete.
- Diagrams are current.
- Ownership is assigned.

# Architecture Debt

Architecture Debt represents structural compromises that weaken scalability, security, maintainability, or reuse.

Examples include:

- Duplicate Identity Systems
- Shared Database Without Ownership
- Tight Coupling
- Unversioned APIs
- Product Logic Inside Core
- Hidden Cross-Project Dependencies
- Direct Infrastructure Access
- Uncontrolled AI Integrations
- Missing Tenant Boundaries
- Undocumented Technology Choices

# Architecture Maturity Model

Architecture should evolve through six maturity levels.

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| AR0 | Fragmented Architecture | Systems and decisions are isolated |
| AR1 | Documented Architecture | Basic standards and diagrams exist |
| AR2 | Governed Architecture | Reviews, ownership, security, and ADRs are active |
| AR3 | Platform Architecture | Shared platform supports multiple products |
| AR4 | Adaptive Architecture | Architecture compliance and optimization use intelligence |
| AR5 | Composable Enterprise Architecture | New enterprise systems are assembled from reusable capabilities |

---

# Architecture Level AR0 — Fragmented

Characteristics:

- Product-specific foundations
- Unclear ownership
- Direct dependencies
- Limited documentation
- Manual integration
- Ad hoc technology choices
- Weak security boundaries
- High key-person dependency

Exit requires:

- Architecture inventory
- Documentation
- Basic standards
- Ownership
- Central decision records

---

# Architecture Level AR1 — Documented

Characteristics:

- Architecture diagrams exist
- Basic technology standards exist
- Initial platform boundaries are defined
- APIs and databases are documented
- Major systems have owners

Exit requires:

- Formal review process
- ADRs
- Security and data reviews
- Architecture quality gates
- Debt register

---

# Architecture Level AR2 — Governed

Characteristics:

- Architecture Review Board
- Reference architecture
- Security architecture
- Data ownership
- Tenant model
- Versioned APIs
- Infrastructure as Code
- AI architecture governance
- Architecture metrics

Exit requires:

- Shared platform services
- Multi-product support
- Developer platform
- Product isolation
- Compatibility testing

---

# Architecture Level AR3 — Platform

Characteristics:

- Shared Core Platform
- Stable service contracts
- Multi-product architecture
- Shared AI OS
- Developer Portal
- SDK and CLI
- Product-specific module isolation
- Progressive delivery
- Platform adoption metrics

Exit requires:

- Automated architecture validation
- Predictive capacity
- Dynamic routing
- Advanced knowledge architecture
- Multi-region readiness

---

# Architecture Level AR4 — Adaptive

Characteristics:

- Continuous architecture compliance
- Automated dependency analysis
- AI-assisted architecture review
- Predictive scalability analysis
- Cost-aware architecture
- Dynamic platform composition
- Policy-as-code
- Cross-product intelligence

Exit requires:

- Repeatable enterprise composition
- Dynamic product architecture
- Global platform architecture
- End-to-end enterprise creation workflows

---

# Architecture Level AR5 — Composable Enterprise Architecture

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems assembled from approved capabilities
- Dynamic platform capability selection
- Standardized industry modules
- Governed AI team composition
- Automated compatibility analysis
- Continuous security and quality
- Global deployment patterns
- Human strategic approval
- Complete auditability

---

# Architecture Roadmap Phases

The Architecture Roadmap should evolve through seven phases.

| Phase | Primary Outcome |
|---|---|
| Phase 0 | Architecture definition |
| Phase 1 | Core architecture foundation |
| Phase 2 | Governed platform architecture |
| Phase 3 | Multi-product architecture |
| Phase 4 | AI-native and ecosystem architecture |
| Phase 5 | Multi-region adaptive architecture |
| Phase 6 | Composable enterprise architecture |

---

# Phase 0 — Architecture Definition

## Objective

Document the architecture vision, principles, domains, ownership, and target state.

## Deliverables

- Architecture Vision
- Architecture Principles
- Current-State Architecture
- Target-State Architecture
- Capability Map
- Domain Map
- Technology Inventory
- Architecture Governance
- ADR Standard
- Architecture Risk Register
- Architecture Roadmap

## Exit Criteria

- Architecture scope is approved.
- Critical systems are inventoried.
- Architecture owners are assigned.
- Core principles are documented.
- Major architectural risks are visible.

---

# Phase 1 — Core Architecture Foundation

## Objective

Establish shared identity, tenancy, access, data, API, security, and infrastructure foundations.

## Deliverables

- Identity Architecture
- Tenant Architecture
- Authorization Architecture
- Core Domain Model
- Database Standards
- API Standards
- Event Standards
- Security Baseline
- Infrastructure as Code
- Observability Baseline
- Environment Strategy

## Exit Criteria

- Identity is centralized.
- Tenant isolation is designed.
- Shared architecture standards exist.
- Production systems are observable.
- Data ownership is defined.
- Critical architecture decisions are recorded.

---

# Phase 2 — Governed Platform Architecture

## Objective

Build reusable shared services and active architecture governance.

## Deliverables

- MianX Core Platform
- Shared Service Catalog
- Architecture Review Board
- Product-versus-platform boundaries
- Workflow Architecture
- Integration Architecture
- Shared Audit
- Shared Configuration
- Shared AI Gateway
- Platform Reliability Standards

## Exit Criteria

- Shared services support initial products.
- Architecture reviews are active.
- Product duplication is reduced.
- Shared platform ownership is clear.
- Compatibility is tested.

---

# Phase 3 — Multi-Product Architecture

## Objective

Support RestaurantOS, PoultryOS, and future products through one platform.

## Deliverables

- Product Module Architecture
- Product Isolation
- Product Feature Flags
- Product Configuration
- Shared Billing
- Cross-Product Analytics
- Product Release Boundaries
- Multi-Project Architecture
- Product Compatibility Matrix
- Product Architecture Templates

## Exit Criteria

- At least two products operate on one Core.
- Product-specific logic remains modular.
- Shared changes do not destabilize all products.
- Product data and configuration remain isolated.
- Product architecture is documented.

---

# Phase 4 — AI-Native and Ecosystem Architecture

## Objective

Integrate the AI Operating System, developer ecosystem, plugins, and marketplace.

## Deliverables

- AI OS Architecture
- Agent Architecture
- Memory Architecture
- Knowledge Architecture
- Model and Tool Registries
- Developer Platform
- SDK
- CLI
- Plugin Framework
- Marketplace Architecture
- Partner Integration Architecture

## Exit Criteria

- Products use shared AI architecture.
- AI context is tenant-aware.
- Plugins operate through explicit boundaries.
- Marketplace assets are versioned and governed.
- Developers can extend the platform safely.

---

# Phase 5 — Multi-Region Adaptive Architecture

## Objective

Support regional operations, predictive architecture, and intelligent optimization.

## Deliverables

- Multi-Region Architecture
- Regional Data Architecture
- Data Residency Controls
- Regional Failover
- Global Observability
- Automated Architecture Compliance
- Predictive Capacity
- Dynamic AI Routing
- Advanced Policy Automation
- Cross-Product Intelligence

## Exit Criteria

- Regional operations remain reliable.
- Data residency requirements are supported.
- Architecture risks are detected earlier.
- Adaptive systems improve measurable outcomes.
- Human approval remains active for high-risk changes.

---

# Phase 6 — Composable Enterprise Architecture

## Objective

Enable repeatable creation of Industry Operating Systems from reusable capabilities.

## Deliverables

- Enterprise Capability Composition
- Industry Architecture Templates
- Dynamic Product Composition
- Dynamic AI Workforce Composition
- Automated Dependency Validation
- Continuous Security and Quality
- Enterprise Creation Workflows
- Global Deployment Blueprints
- Portfolio Architecture Intelligence
- Enterprise Learning Architecture

## Exit Criteria

- New products can be composed without rebuilding foundations.
- Architecture remains governed and explainable.
- Industry modules are reusable.
- Global operations remain secure and observable.
- Human strategic authority remains embedded.
- Every enterprise creation cycle strengthens the architecture.

- Platform Fragmentation
- Product Forking
- Tenant Data Leakage
- Excessive Coupling
- Unclear Ownership
- Unversioned APIs
- Shared Service Failure
- Database Scaling Failure
- Infrastructure Lock-In
- AI Context Leakage
- Insecure Plugins
- Uncontrolled Marketplace Extensions
- Architecture Debt
- Overengineering
- Premature Microservices
- Weak Observability
- Untested Recovery
- Regional Architecture Inconsistency
- Technology Obsolescence

Each risk must have an owner and mitigation plan.

# Architecture Completion Standard

An architecture capability is complete only when:

- Business purpose is documented.
- Scope is clear.
- Ownership is assigned.
- Boundaries are defined.
- Interfaces are documented.
- Data ownership is defined.
- Security is reviewed.
- Tenant impact is understood.
- Reliability is designed.
- Observability is designed.
- Recovery is documented.
- Cost is understood.
- Risks are documented.
- ADRs are complete.
- Implementation follows the design.
- Production behavior is validated.
- Documentation reflects reality.
- Future evolution is considered.

---

# Architecture Exit Criteria

The Architecture Roadmap is successfully established when:

- MianX.ai has one approved enterprise architecture vision.
- Architecture domains and owners are documented.
- Business, product, platform, application, data, AI, security, and infrastructure architectures are aligned.
- The MianX Core Platform owns reusable enterprise capabilities.
- Product-specific logic remains outside the Core where appropriate.
- Shared services expose stable and versioned contracts.
- Tenant, project, product, and regional isolation are defined and tested.
- Data ownership and systems of record are clear.
- AI agents, models, tools, memory, and knowledge operate through governed architecture.
- Security is embedded across every architecture layer.
- Production systems are observable and recoverable.
- Architecture decisions are recorded through ADRs.
- Architecture exceptions are controlled.
- Architecture debt is visible and governed.
- Multi-product and multi-project operations do not fragment the platform.
- Marketplace and plugin extensions operate through explicit boundaries.
- Regional expansion does not require rebuilding the platform.
- Architecture metrics provide measurable evidence.
- New Industry Operating Systems can be composed from shared capabilities.
- Human strategic authority remains permanent as architecture becomes increasingly automated.

# Part 14A — Infrastructure Strategy & Foundation

Infrastructure is the technical foundation upon which every MianX.ai product, platform service, AI capability, workflow, integration, database, environment, and enterprise operation depends.

It provides the compute, storage, networking, runtime, security, automation, observability, resilience, and recovery capabilities required to operate the complete MianX.ai ecosystem.

Infrastructure is not only a cloud account, server, container, or deployment environment.

It is a governed enterprise capability responsible for ensuring that every technical system can operate:

- Securely
- Reliably
- Predictably
- Efficiently
- Observably
- Recoverably
- Cost-Effectively
- At Enterprise Scale

The Infrastructure Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will design, build, automate, secure, govern, operate, scale, and continuously improve its infrastructure over the next decade and beyond.

---

# Infrastructure Roadmap Statement

> **Build one secure, automated, observable, resilient, cost-aware, multi-product, multi-tenant, and globally scalable infrastructure foundation capable of supporting every MianX.ai platform, Industry Operating System, AI agent, enterprise service, and customer environment.**

# Infrastructure Mission Outcomes

The Infrastructure organization must ensure that:

- Engineering teams can obtain environments predictably.
- Products can deploy through standardized pipelines.
- Production systems remain observable.
- Security controls are embedded by default.
- Infrastructure changes are versioned and auditable.
- Critical systems can recover from failure.
- Capacity can scale before customer impact occurs.
- Costs remain measurable and controlled.
- Tenant and product isolation remain intact.
- Infrastructure knowledge is documented and reusable.
- AI agents operate only through authorized infrastructure interfaces.
- Global expansion does not require complete infrastructure replacement.

---

# Infrastructure Philosophy

MianX.ai Infrastructure should follow a platform-oriented philosophy.

Infrastructure should be built as a reusable internal product rather than a collection of manually managed resources.

The Infrastructure Philosophy is based on the following beliefs:

- Infrastructure should be defined as code.
- Automation should replace repetitive administration.
- Security should be enabled by default.
- Environments should be reproducible.
- Production should not depend on private operator knowledge.
- Infrastructure changes should be reviewed like application changes.
- Observability should exist before production traffic.
- Recovery should be designed before failure.
- Capacity should be planned before exhaustion.
- Shared infrastructure should not weaken tenant isolation.
- Complexity should be introduced only when justified.
- Infrastructure cost is an engineering concern.
- Provider flexibility should be considered strategically.
- AI may assist operations but must remain governed.
- Every infrastructure decision should support long-term enterprise sustainability.

---

# Infrastructure Principles

Every infrastructure decision must follow the principles defined below.

---

## 1. Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure should be defined through version-controlled code wherever practical.

This includes:

- Networks
- Compute
- Storage
- Databases
- Load Balancers
- DNS
- Queues
- Monitoring
- Access Policies
- Environments
- Backup
- Regional Resources

Manual undocumented infrastructure changes should be prohibited.

---

## 2. Automation Before Manual Operations

Repeated infrastructure tasks should become automated workflows.

Examples include:

- Environment Provisioning
- Deployment
- Certificate Renewal
- Secret Rotation
- Backup
- Restore Validation
- Scaling
- Patching
- Monitoring Configuration
- Policy Validation

Manual execution should remain limited to exceptional or high-risk operations.

---

## 3. Security by Default

Infrastructure should begin in a secure state.

Default security should include:

- Private Networking Where Appropriate
- Least-Privilege Access
- Encryption
- Secret Management
- Restricted Administrative Access
- Audit Logging
- Secure Base Images
- Vulnerability Scanning
- Environment Isolation
- Backup Protection

Security should not depend on every team remembering to enable it independently.

---

## 4. Reliability by Design

Critical infrastructure must be designed for failure.

Reliability design should include:

- Redundancy
- Health Checks
- Failover
- Retry
- Backup
- Recovery
- Capacity Planning
- Graceful Degradation
- Incident Response
- Dependency Awareness

---

## 5. Observability Before Production

No production workload should operate as a black box.

Every production system should expose appropriate:

- Logs
- Metrics
- Traces
- Health Checks
- Audit Events
- Security Signals
- Capacity Signals
- Cost Signals
- Business Signals

---

## 6. Recovery Before Scale

Infrastructure must have a documented recovery model before business dependence increases.

Recovery should define:

- Recovery Time Objective
- Recovery Point Objective
- Restore Procedure
- Failover Procedure
- Credential Recovery
- Validation
- Communication
- Ownership

---

## 7. Environment Separation

Development, testing, staging, and production environments must remain clearly separated.

Separation should cover:

- Data
- Credentials
- Access
- Networking
- Configuration
- Integrations
- Monitoring
- Deployment Authority
- Retention

---

## 8. Least Privilege

Every human, service, agent, application, pipeline, and integration should receive only the access required for its approved purpose.

Access must be:

- Role-Based
- Time-Bound Where Appropriate
- Revocable
- Audited
- Regularly Reviewed

---

## 9. Immutable and Reproducible Delivery

Production workloads should use verified, versioned, and reproducible artifacts.

The preferred model is:

```text
Source

↓

Verified Build

↓

Immutable Artifact

↓

Controlled Promotion

↓

Production Runtime
```

---

## 10. Multi-Tenant Awareness

Infrastructure supporting multiple customers must preserve tenant boundaries across:

- Databases
- Storage
- Caches
- Search
- Logs
- Events
- AI Workloads
- Networks Where Required
- Backup
- Export
- Recovery

---

## 11. Product and Project Isolation

Shared infrastructure should allow reuse without causing uncontrolled impact between products and projects.

Isolation may include:

- Separate Configurations
- Namespaces
- Accounts
- Networks
- Databases
- Queues
- Storage Locations
- Credentials
- Resource Quotas
- Monitoring Boundaries

---

## 12. Standardization Before Exception

The organization should maintain approved infrastructure patterns.

Teams should use standard patterns for:

- Services
- Databases
- Queues
- Storage
- Deployments
- Networking
- Monitoring
- Backup
- Secrets

Exceptions require documented justification and approval.

---

## 13. Simplicity Before Complexity

Infrastructure complexity must solve a validated business or technical problem.

MianX.ai should avoid adopting:

- Kubernetes without operational need
- Multi-cloud without strategic justification
- Microservice infrastructure before service maturity
- Complex networking without security or scale requirements
- Multiple observability platforms without benefit
- Several database technologies without operational justification

---

## 14. Provider Flexibility

The organization should avoid unnecessary dependence on one provider where portability has strategic value.

Provider flexibility may be supported through:

- Open Standards
- Containers
- Infrastructure as Code
- Portable Data Formats
- Abstracted Interfaces
- Documented Exit Plans
- Backup Outside One Failure Boundary

Portability should not create needless abstraction or cost.

---

## 15. Cost-Aware Infrastructure

Infrastructure cost should be measurable and attributable.

Cost should be reviewed by:

- Product
- Tenant
- Environment
- Region
- Service
- Workload
- Team
- AI Workflow

Infrastructure should not scale without financial visibility.

---

## 16. Policy-Governed Infrastructure

Infrastructure policies should increasingly be enforced through automated controls.

Policies may cover:

- Encryption
- Network Exposure
- Approved Regions
- Resource Tags
- Backup
- Retention
- Logging
- Image Sources
- Privileged Access
- Resource Limits
- Data Residency
- Production Change Approval

---

## 17. Human-Governed Automation

Automation should reduce operational effort without removing human authority over high-risk actions.

Human approval may remain required for:

- Production Destruction
- Regional Failover
- Data Restore
- Major Network Change
- Privileged Access
- Critical Security Policy Change
- Large Cost Expansion
- Irreversible Migration
- Customer Data Movement

---

## 18. Documentation With Infrastructure

Infrastructure documentation must change with infrastructure code.

Documentation should cover:

- Purpose
- Ownership
- Architecture
- Configuration
- Access
- Security
- Deployment
- Monitoring
- Backup
- Recovery
- Cost
- Risks
- Runbooks
- Version History

- Major Observability Changes
- AI Infrastructure Changes

# Infrastructure Change Governance

```text

↓

↓

↓

Change Plan

↓

↓

Approval

↓

↓

Validation

↓

Evidence

↓

Operational Review
```

# Infrastructure Change Categories

## Standard Change

A tested and pre-approved low-risk change.

## Normal Change

A planned change requiring review and approval.

## Emergency Change

An urgent change required to protect security, availability, data, or continuity.

## Major Change

A high-impact change affecting architecture, regions, production, or several products.

---

# Infrastructure Risk Classification

Infrastructure changes may use:

| Risk | Description |
|---|---|
| I0 | No meaningful runtime impact |
| I1 | Low-risk and easily reversible |
| I2 | Standard environment or service impact |
| I3 | Elevated production, networking, database, or security impact |
| I4 | Critical regional, data, identity, or recovery impact |
| I5 | Enterprise-wide or potentially irreversible impact |

Risk should determine:

- Required Reviewers
- Approval Level
- Change Window
- Testing
- Rollback
- Monitoring
- Communication
- Evidence
- Post-Change Review

# Infrastructure Success Criteria

- Manual production drift is reduced.
- Environments are clearly separated.
- Security defaults are centrally enforced.
- Secrets are managed securely.
- Production systems are observable.
- Critical data is backed up.
- Restore procedures are verified.
- Infrastructure cost is measurable.
- Capacity is planned.
- Product and tenant isolation are preserved.
- AI agents operate through governed infrastructure permissions.
- Infrastructure documentation reflects production reality.
- Global growth can occur without replacing the complete foundation.

# Part 14B-1 — Cloud & Compute Architecture

Cloud and Compute Architecture defines how MianX.ai will select, organize, secure, automate, operate, scale, and govern the cloud foundations and computing resources used by every product, platform service, AI workload, development environment, customer deployment, and enterprise operation.

Cloud infrastructure is not only a collection of virtual machines or managed services.

It is the governed execution foundation upon which MianX.ai will operate:

- MianX Core Platform
- AI Operating System
- AI Workforce
- Shared Enterprise Services
- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- Future Industry Operating Systems
- API Platform
- Developer Portal
- SDK and CLI Services
- Marketplace
- Plugin Framework
- Enterprise Integrations
- Data Platform
- Security Platform
- Observability Platform
- Internal Engineering Systems
- Customer-Dedicated Environments
- Regional and Global Deployments

Cloud and compute decisions directly influence:

- Security
- Availability
- Performance
- Scalability
- Cost
- Compliance
- Recovery
- Portability
- Developer Experience
- Operational Complexity
- Customer Trust

The objective is not to adopt every available cloud technology.

The objective is to establish the smallest dependable cloud foundation capable of supporting current delivery while providing a controlled path toward multi-product, multi-region, hybrid, and global enterprise operations.

---

# Cloud & Compute Architecture Statement

> **Build a secure, automated, resilient, observable, cost-aware, and provider-portable cloud and compute foundation that supports every MianX.ai workload without uncontrolled complexity, weak isolation, or repeated infrastructure rebuilding.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai should begin with a practical cloud architecture and evolve according to verified business, product, security, performance, and regional requirements.

The initial architecture should favor:

- Managed Services
- Simple Operational Models
- Infrastructure as Code
- Strong Environment Isolation
- Central Identity
- Secure Networking
- Automated Deployment
- Built-In Monitoring
- Verified Backup and Recovery
- Measurable Cost

Advanced infrastructure patterns should be introduced only when current architecture can no longer satisfy documented requirements.

Examples include:

- Multiple Availability Zones
- Multiple Cloud Regions
- Kubernetes
- Dedicated Customer Infrastructure
- Hybrid Cloud
- Private Cloud
- Multi-Cloud
- Specialized AI Compute
- Global Traffic Management

The preferred evolution path is:

```text
Single Cloud Provider

↓

Secure Cloud Foundation

↓

Managed Application Runtime

↓

Multi-Environment Architecture

↓

Multi-Availability-Zone Reliability

↓

Multi-Product Infrastructure

↓

Regional Expansion

↓

Hybrid or Multi-Cloud Where Justified

↓

Global Adaptive Infrastructure
```

This approach reduces unnecessary infrastructure complexity while preserving strategic flexibility.

---

# Cloud Architecture

Cloud Architecture defines how cloud providers, accounts, subscriptions, projects, regions, networks, identities, services, data, monitoring, security, and billing boundaries are organized.

The architecture should provide one governed foundation for all cloud-hosted resources.

# Cloud Architecture Objectives

Cloud Architecture should:

- Establish secure cloud foundations
- Separate environments
- Separate products and projects where required
- Protect production resources
- Centralize identity and access
- Standardize resource creation
- Enable infrastructure automation
- Support reliable deployment
- Provide cost visibility
- Support backup and recovery
- Enable regional expansion
- Reduce manual infrastructure administration
- Maintain architecture consistency
- Support public, private, and hybrid models where required
- Prevent uncontrolled cloud resource creation

# Cloud Architecture Principles

Cloud architecture must follow:

- Secure Foundations First
- Managed Services Before Self-Managed Infrastructure
- One Primary Cloud Before Multi-Cloud
- Environment Isolation
- Infrastructure as Code
- Least Privilege
- Private Connectivity Where Practical
- Immutable Workloads
- Multi-Zone Reliability for Critical Services
- Backup and Recovery by Default

- Standard Resource Naming

- Central Logging

- Provider Portability Where Strategically Valuable
- Human Approval for High-Risk Changes

# Cloud Strategy

Cloud Strategy defines why MianX.ai uses cloud infrastructure, how providers are selected, which services are preferred, and how the cloud footprint should evolve.

---

# Cloud Strategy Vision

The Cloud Strategy should provide enough capability to support rapid product delivery while avoiding premature operational complexity.

MianX.ai should use cloud infrastructure to achieve:

- Faster Environment Provisioning
- Managed Reliability
- Elastic Capacity
- Global Reach
- Strong Security Services
- Automation
- Built-In Observability
- Managed Databases
- Managed Storage
- Rapid Experimentation
- Disaster Recovery
- Customer-Specific Deployment Options

---

# Primary Cloud Strategy

MianX.ai should initially select one primary cloud platform for most production workloads.

A primary cloud approach provides:

- Lower Operational Complexity
- Simpler Identity Management
- Simpler Billing
- Faster Team Learning
- Consistent Security Controls
- Easier Monitoring
- Easier Automation
- Reduced Integration Burden
- Faster Product Delivery

The primary cloud should be selected through a documented architecture decision.

---

# Primary Cloud Selection Criteria

The selected provider should be evaluated against:

- Security
- Reliability
- Regional Availability
- Managed Services
- Database Services
- AI Services
- Container Support
- Networking
- Identity Integration
- Compliance
- Pricing
- Vendor Support
- Developer Experience
- Infrastructure as Code Support
- Portability
- Customer Requirements
- Long-Term Stability

---

# Managed-Service-First Strategy

MianX.ai should prefer managed services when they provide:

- Lower Operational Burden
- Stronger Reliability
- Built-In Backup
- Automated Patching
- Easier Scaling
- Security Integration
- Monitoring
- Faster Delivery
- Reduced Staffing Requirements

Examples may include:

- Managed PostgreSQL
- Managed Redis
- Managed Object Storage
- Managed Message Queues
- Managed Application Runtime
- Managed Container Registry
- Managed Logging
- Managed Secrets
- Managed DNS
- Managed Load Balancing

Managed services should still be evaluated for:

- Cost
- Lock-In
- Portability
- Recovery
- Data Export
- Regional Availability
- Service Limits
- Operational Control

---

# Cloud-Native Strategy

Cloud-native architecture should use cloud capabilities intentionally rather than making every workload provider-specific.

Cloud-native capabilities may include:

- Managed Scaling
- Managed Identity
- Event-Driven Services
- Managed Queues
- Managed Databases
- Managed Observability
- Managed Secrets
- Infrastructure Automation
- Regional Deployment
- Automated Recovery

Provider-specific services should be adopted when the benefits outweigh portability concerns.

---

# Portability Strategy

MianX.ai should maintain reasonable workload portability through:

- Containers
- Open Protocols
- Standard Databases
- Infrastructure as Code
- Portable Application Configuration
- Standard Monitoring Interfaces
- Exportable Data
- Documented Provider Dependencies
- Versioned Service Contracts
- Provider Exit Plans

The goal is strategic portability, not artificial provider independence at every layer.

|---|---|
| Strategic | Preferred for long-term enterprise use |
| Approved | Allowed for standard use |
| Limited | Allowed for specific cases |
| Experimental | Restricted evaluation only |
| Contained | Existing usage only |
| Deprecated | Migration required |
| Prohibited | Not allowed |

Before adopting a new cloud service, document:

- Business Need
- Technical Need
- Owner
- Security Review
- Data Classification
- Region
- Reliability
- Backup
- Recovery
- Cost
- Provider Lock-In
- Portability
- Monitoring
- Skills Required
- Exit Strategy

---

# Multi-Cloud Strategy

Multi-cloud means operating meaningful workloads or capabilities across more than one public cloud provider.

MianX.ai should not adopt multi-cloud architecture only for appearance or theoretical resilience.

Multi-cloud significantly increases:

- Identity Complexity
- Security Complexity
- Network Complexity
- Operational Cost
- Monitoring Complexity
- Skills Requirements
- Vendor Management
- Data Governance
- Incident Coordination
- Recovery Complexity

---

# Multi-Cloud Strategy Statement

> **Use one primary cloud by default and introduce additional cloud providers only when a validated business, customer, regulatory, resilience, or technical requirement justifies the added complexity.**

---

# Multi-Cloud Adoption Triggers

Multi-cloud may be justified when:

- An enterprise customer requires a specific provider
- A country or region requires a specific deployment platform
- A critical service exists only on another provider
- Provider concentration risk becomes unacceptable
- A regulated customer requires provider separation
- Strategic AI models or services require another provider
- Acquisition introduces another cloud
- Commercial terms justify controlled workload placement
- Disaster recovery requirements cannot be met in one provider
- Marketplace or partner integration requires it

---

# Multi-Cloud Non-Triggers

Multi-cloud should not be adopted only because:

- It sounds enterprise-grade
- Vendor lock-in exists in theory
- The architecture team wants more technologies
- The company has not yet mastered one cloud
- Current workloads are small
- Operations and monitoring are immature
- Recovery is not yet tested in the primary cloud

---

# Multi-Cloud Operating Models

## Model 1 — Primary Cloud With Specialized Secondary Services

The primary cloud hosts most workloads.

A secondary provider supports a specific capability, such as:

- AI Models
- Data Processing
- Customer Integration
- Regional Service

This is the preferred initial multi-cloud model where required.

---

## Model 2 — Customer-Selected Cloud

MianX.ai may deploy customer-dedicated environments to the provider required by the customer.

Shared product architecture remains consistent.

Infrastructure implementation may vary through provider-specific modules.

---

## Model 3 — Regional Cloud Allocation

Different regions may use different providers where business, legal, or service availability requires it.

Global governance and observability remain centralized.

---

## Model 4 — Active-Passive Cross-Cloud Recovery

A secondary cloud may maintain recovery capability for selected critical systems.

This model is complex and should be adopted only after strong single-cloud recovery maturity.

---

## Model 5 — Active-Active Multi-Cloud

Workloads run actively across several providers.

This should be considered only for highly mature and critical global services because it introduces major consistency, networking, observability, and operational complexity.

---

Any multi-cloud architecture must define:

- Primary Provider

# Initial Cloud Account Model


The structure should be simple enough to operate but strong enough to preserve production isolation.

---

# Environment Account Separation

Where practical, production should use a separate account, subscription, or project from non-production.

Benefits include:

- Reduced Production Access
- Separate Billing
- Stronger Policy
- Better Incident Containment
- Reduced Accidental Changes
- Clearer Audit
- Separate Service Limits
- Easier Recovery

---

# Product Account Separation

Separate product accounts may be justified when:

- Products require strong isolation
- Products have different owners
- Products have different regulatory requirements
- Customer contracts require isolation
- Cost allocation requires clear boundaries
- Failure domains should be separated
- Independent deployment is required

Small products should not automatically receive separate cloud organizations.

---

# Shared Services Account

A shared services account may host:

- DNS
- Container Registry
- Artifact Registry
- Monitoring
- Logging
- CI/CD Runners
- Secrets Control Plane
- Network Hub
- Identity Integrations
- Security Tooling

Shared services must have stronger operational and security controls because several products may depend on them.

---

# Security and Audit Account

A dedicated security or audit account should store:

- Central Audit Logs
- Security Findings
- Cloud Activity Logs
- Threat Detection
- Compliance Evidence
- Configuration History
- Security Alerts

Application teams should not be able to modify or delete critical audit evidence.

# Cloud Account Provisioning

# Resource Naming

Cloud resources should use consistent naming.

A naming model may include:

```text
<company>-<environment>-<region>-<product>-<service>-<resource>
```

Example:

```text
mianx-prod-pk-core-auth-api
```

The final format should account for provider naming limits.

---

Mandatory tags may include:

- Organization
- Environment
- Product
- Service
- Owner
- Cost Center
- Data Classification
- Criticality
- Managed By
- Project
- Region
- Expiration Where Applicable

Resource creation should fail or alert when mandatory tags are missing.

---

# Account Access Controls

Account access should enforce:

- Central Identity Federation
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Named Human Accounts
- Role-Based Access
- Temporary Privilege
- Service Identities
- Audit
- Regular Review
- Emergency Access
- Rapid Revocation

Root or owner-level credentials should be protected and rarely used.

# Cloud Regions

A cloud region is a geographic location containing cloud infrastructure.

Region selection directly affects:

- Latency
- Data Residency
- Availability
- Service Access
- Cost
- Recovery
- Customer Requirements
- Compliance
- Support

---

# Primary Region Strategy

MianX.ai should begin with one primary region selected according to:

- Customer Location
- Data Residency
- Network Latency
- Service Availability
- Provider Reliability
- Pricing
- Support
- Backup Options
- Disaster Recovery Options
- Future Expansion

---

# Region Selection Criteria

Every region should be evaluated against:

- Business Demand
- Customer Location
- Legal Requirements
- Data Residency
- Service Availability
- Availability Zones
- Network Connectivity
- Operational Support
- Cost
- Backup and Recovery
- Vendor Roadmap
- AI Service Availability
- Database Service Availability

---

# Regional Deployment Model

A mature regional architecture may follow:

```text
Global Governance

↓

Primary Global Platform Control

↓

Regional Runtime

├── Regional Application Services
├── Regional Database or Data Partition
├── Regional Storage
├── Regional Cache
├── Regional Queues
└── Regional Monitoring

↓

Global Reporting and Governance
```

---

# Single-Region Architecture

A single-region architecture may be appropriate initially when:

- User volume is limited
- Customer location is concentrated
- Data residency permits it
- Recovery requirements can be met
- Operational maturity is early
- Cost control is important

A single region should still use multiple availability zones for critical workloads where supported.

---

# Multi-Region Adoption Triggers

A second region may be justified when:

- Customer latency becomes unacceptable
- Data residency requires regional storage
- Business continuity requires regional recovery
- Enterprise contracts require it
- User volume becomes geographically distributed
- A market launch requires local infrastructure
- Provider regional risk becomes material
- Regional integrations require local deployment

---

# Multi-Region Architecture Models

## Active-Passive

The primary region serves traffic.

A secondary region remains ready for recovery.

Benefits:

- Simpler Data Model
- Lower Cost
- Easier Operations

Challenges:

- Recovery Time
- Data Replication
- Failover Testing

---

## Active-Active

Several regions serve traffic simultaneously.

Benefits:

- Lower Latency
- Regional Resilience
- Better Global Availability

Challenges:

- Data Consistency
- Conflict Resolution
- Operational Complexity
- Higher Cost
- More Difficult Testing

---

## Regional Product Deployment

Some products may operate in selected regions while the Core Platform remains global.

This may support:

- Industry-Specific Markets
- Enterprise Contracts
- Regional Regulations
- Product Demand

---

# Regional Data Strategy

Regional data models may include:

- Global Shared Data
- Region-Owned Data
- Tenant-Owned Regional Data
- Replicated Read Data
- Centralized Metadata
- Regional Transactional Data

Data classification must determine where data may be stored or replicated.

---

# Regional Failure Planning

Every region should define:

- Failure Detection
- Traffic Handling
- Data Recovery
- Dependency Behavior
- DNS Behavior
- Customer Communication
- Recovery Authority
- Validation
- Return to Primary
- Evidence

---

# Region Governance

Adding a region should require:

- Business Approval
- Architecture Review
- Security Review
- Data Governance
- Cost Review
- Capacity Forecast
- Operations Plan
- Recovery Plan
- Monitoring
- Support Readiness
- Vendor Review

---

# Availability Zones

Availability Zones are isolated infrastructure locations within a cloud region.

They reduce the risk that one facility-level failure affects the complete service.

---

# Availability Zone Strategy

Critical production services should use multiple availability zones where:

- Provider support exists
- Application architecture supports it
- Database architecture supports it
- Cost is justified
- Reliability requirements demand it

---

# Multi-Zone Architecture

A multi-zone architecture may follow:

```text
Regional Load Balancer

↓

Availability Zone A
Application Instances

+

Availability Zone B
Application Instances

+

Availability Zone C
Application Instances

↓

Multi-Zone Database

↓

Regional Storage and Messaging
```

---

# Multi-Zone Workload Requirements

Applications using multiple zones should support:

- Stateless Runtime Where Practical
- Distributed Health Checks
- Load Balancing
- Zone-Aware Scheduling
- Shared or Replicated Data
- Graceful Failure
- Session Strategy
- Queue Resilience
- Deployment Coordination
- Capacity Across Remaining Zones

---

# Zone Failure Planning

The architecture should define behavior when:

- One compute zone fails
- One network zone fails
- One database replica fails
- One storage service degrades
- Capacity becomes unavailable in one zone

The remaining zones should have enough capacity to maintain critical operation or controlled degradation.

---

# Zone Affinity

Zone affinity may be used to:

- Reduce Latency
- Reduce Data Transfer Cost
- Keep Related Services Together
- Optimize Stateful Workloads

However, strict zone affinity can reduce resilience.

---

# Zone Redundancy Requirements

Every critical workload should define:

- Minimum Number of Zones
- Capacity Per Zone
- Database Placement
- Storage Placement
- Queue Placement
- Failure Threshold
- Recovery Behavior
- Testing Cadence

---

# Availability Zone Testing

Resilience tests may include:

- Terminating Instances in One Zone
- Blocking Zone Traffic
- Removing a Node Pool
- Simulating Database Replica Failure
- Testing Capacity After Zone Loss
- Verifying Alerting
- Verifying Customer Impact
- Verifying Recovery

---

Compute Infrastructure provides processing resources for application services, APIs, workers, AI workloads, integration services, CI/CD pipelines, and internal tools.

Compute should be selected according to workload characteristics.

- Reduce idle resources
- Preserve portability where practical

- Embedding Generation

- Internal Tools

- Monitoring Services

# Compute Decision Matrix

| Workload | Preferred Starting Model |
|---|---|
| Standard Web Application | Managed Application Platform |
| API Service | Managed Runtime or Container Platform |
| Background Worker | Managed Worker or Container |
| Scheduled Task | Managed Scheduler or Serverless Job |
| Short Event Function | Serverless |
| Stateful Legacy Service | Virtual Machine or Managed Service |
| Complex Multi-Service Platform | Container Platform |
| Large Orchestrated Workloads | Kubernetes Where Justified |
| AI Inference | Managed AI Service or Specialized Compute |
| CI Build | Managed Runner or Isolated Build Worker |

# CPU and Memory Sizing

Sizing should use measured demand.

The process should include:

```text
Initial Estimate

↓

Load Test

↓

Production Baseline

↓

Monitoring

↓

Right-Sizing

↓

Continuous Review
```

Overprovisioning increases cost.

Underprovisioning increases reliability risk.

---

# Resource Requests and Limits

Containerized workloads should define appropriate:

- CPU Requests
- CPU Limits
- Memory Requests
- Memory Limits
- Temporary Storage
- Concurrency
- Process Limits

Incorrect resource limits may cause:

- Performance Degradation
- Unstable Scheduling
- Out-of-Memory Termination
- Resource Starvation
- Increased Cost

---

# Compute Scaling

Scaling may be:

- Vertical
- Horizontal
- Scheduled
- Metric-Based
- Queue-Based
- Event-Based
- Predictive
- Manual

---

# Vertical Scaling

Vertical scaling increases the resources of one compute instance.

It may be appropriate for:

- Databases
- Legacy Services
- Low-Complexity Workloads
- Short-Term Capacity Needs

Its limitations include:

- Upper Resource Limits
- Restart Requirements
- Larger Failure Impact
- Reduced Flexibility

---

# Horizontal Scaling

Horizontal scaling adds more instances.

It is preferred for stateless and parallel workloads.

Requirements include:

- Shared State Strategy
- Load Balancing
- Health Checks
- Idempotency
- Distributed Session Handling
- Coordinated Deployment
- Consistent Configuration

---

# Autoscaling

Autoscaling may use:

- CPU
- Memory
- Request Count
- Queue Depth
- Latency
- Concurrent Sessions
- Custom Business Metrics
- AI Task Queue
- Scheduled Demand
- Predictive Demand

Every autoscaling policy should define:

- Minimum Capacity
- Maximum Capacity
- Scale-Up Threshold
- Scale-Down Threshold
- Cooldown
- Cost Limit
- Failure Behavior
- Monitoring

---

# Compute Availability

Critical compute workloads should support:

- Multiple Instances
- Multiple Zones
- Health-Based Replacement
- Automated Restart
- Load Balancing
- Graceful Shutdown
- Deployment Redundancy
- Capacity Headroom

- Process Health

- Startup

- Database Connectivity
- Disk Capacity

Health checks should not create false positives or unnecessary dependency cascades.

# Virtual Machines

Virtual Machines provide dedicated operating-system environments for workloads requiring greater runtime control.

Virtual machines should not be the default for every application.

They should be used when their benefits justify the operational responsibility.

---

# Virtual Machine Use Cases

Virtual machines may be appropriate for:

- Legacy Applications
- Specialized Operating Systems
- Vendor Software
- Stateful Services Without Managed Alternatives
- Dedicated Enterprise Deployments
- Security Appliances
- Build Runners
- Specialized Network Services
- Temporary Migration Workloads
- Customer-Specific Requirements

---

# Virtual Machine Non-Use Cases

Virtual machines should generally not be selected for:

- Standard Stateless Web Services
- Small APIs
- Short Event Tasks
- Simple Background Jobs
- Workloads Supported by Reliable Managed Platforms
- Applications Requiring Frequent Scaling

---

# Virtual Machine Architecture

A production virtual machine architecture may include:

```text
Load Balancer

↓

Auto-Scaling or Managed Instance Group

↓

Virtual Machines Across Zones

↓

Managed Database and Shared Storage

↓

Central Logs, Metrics, Backup, and Security
```

---

```text
↓
```

```text

Yes
Use approved managed service.

No

↓

Can a managed application or container runtime meet the need?

Yes
Use managed runtime.

No

↓

Does the workload require specialized orchestration?

Yes
Consider Kubernetes.

No

↓

Does the workload require operating-system control?

Yes
Use governed virtual machines.

No

↓

Reassess architecture and requirements.
```

# Cloud & Compute Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| CC0 | Uncontrolled Compute | Manual resources, weak ownership, unclear cost |
| CC1 | Standardized Cloud | Basic accounts, environments, naming, and monitoring |
| CC2 | Governed Compute | Infrastructure as Code, security controls, cost and capacity governance |
| CC3 | Multi-Product Cloud Platform | Shared cloud foundation supporting several products |
| CC4 | Regional Adaptive Compute | Multi-region scaling, predictive capacity, policy automation |
| CC5 | Global Composable Cloud | Workloads placed dynamically across approved global infrastructure |

---

# CC0 — Uncontrolled Compute

Characteristics:

- Manual server creation
- Shared credentials
- Mixed environments
- Unknown owners
- Missing monitoring
- No cost allocation
- Weak backup
- Direct production changes

Exit requirements:

- Resource inventory
- Environment separation
- Account ownership
- Basic identity controls
- Basic monitoring
- Basic backup
- Initial Infrastructure as Code

---

# CC1 — Standardized Cloud

Characteristics:

- Primary cloud selected
- Development and production separated
- Resource naming standardized
- Basic tags
- Managed compute preferred
- Basic monitoring
- Basic cost reporting
- Protected administrative access

Exit requirements:

- Stronger Infrastructure as Code
- Security policies
- Multi-zone reliability
- Capacity planning
- Restore testing
- Compute catalog
- Workload placement policy

---

# CC2 — Governed Compute

Characteristics:

- Infrastructure as Code enforced
- Compute platforms approved
- Resource quotas active
- Cost allocation active
- Security review active
- Patching governed
- Recovery documented
- Critical workloads multi-zone

Exit requirements:

- Shared multi-product foundation
- Product cost allocation
- Self-service environments
- Standard runtime platform
- Central observability
- Compatibility and release governance

---

# CC3 — Multi-Product Cloud Platform

Characteristics:

- Several products share cloud foundations
- Product environments remain isolated
- Shared services are standardized
- Managed compute and containers are widely used
- Cloud cost is visible by product
- Platform provisioning is automated

Exit requirements:

- Regional architecture
- Global DNS
- Regional data policy
- Predictive capacity
- Automated policy enforcement
- Advanced recovery

---

# CC4 — Regional Adaptive Compute

Characteristics:

- Several regions supported
- Workloads scale based on demand
- Capacity risks predicted
- Regional recovery tested
- Policy-as-code mature
- Cloud cost optimization increasingly automated
- Selected customer-dedicated environments supported

Exit requirements:

- Dynamic workload placement
- Global capacity intelligence
- Strong hybrid and multi-cloud support where required
- Automated global compliance validation
- Enterprise composition workflows

---

# CC5 — Global Composable Cloud

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems consume approved global infrastructure blueprints
- Workloads are placed according to policy, region, cost, security, and capacity
- Human approval remains active for major risk
- Global observability and recovery are integrated
- Infrastructure knowledge improves future deployments
- Public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud models are supported where justified

---

# Part 14B-1 Exit Criteria

Part 14B-1 is complete when:

- Cloud Architecture is documented.
- One primary cloud strategy is approved.
- Multi-cloud adoption rules are defined.
- Cloud accounts, subscriptions, or projects have a governed structure.
- Production is separated from non-production.
- Cloud regions are selected through documented criteria.
- Availability-zone requirements are defined for critical systems.
- Compute workload categories are documented.
- Workload placement rules are approved.
- Virtual machine use is limited to justified workloads.
- Managed compute is preferred for suitable applications.
- Compute ownership is assigned.
- Resource sizing, scaling, monitoring, security, cost, and recovery requirements are defined.
- Cloud resource naming and tagging are standardized.
- Compute access and privileged operations are governed.
- Infrastructure as Code is required for production resources.
- Cloud and compute risks are recorded.
- Cloud and compute maturity levels are defined.
- The architecture is ready to progress into containers, Kubernetes, and serverless runtime design.

# Part 14B-2 — Runtime Architecture

Runtime Architecture defines how MianX.ai packages, deploys, isolates, schedules, scales, secures, observes, and governs application workloads across container platforms, Kubernetes clusters, serverless environments, background workers, AI workloads, and shared enterprise services.

The runtime layer sits between infrastructure resources and application software.

It determines how approved application artifacts become active production workloads.

Runtime Architecture must support:

- MianX Core Platform
- AI Operating System
- AI Workforce
- Shared Enterprise Services
- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- Future Industry Operating Systems
- APIs
- Background Workers
- Workflow Engines
- Integration Services
- Data Processing
- AI Model and Agent Workloads
- Developer Platform Services
- Marketplace and Plugin Services
- Internal Engineering Systems
- Customer-Dedicated Deployments
- Regional Runtime Environments

The objective is not to place every workload inside containers, Kubernetes, or serverless functions.

The objective is to select the simplest approved runtime that meets each workload’s security, scaling, availability, performance, portability, operational, and cost requirements.

---

# Runtime Architecture Statement

> **Provide secure, portable, observable, scalable, and governed runtime platforms that allow every MianX.ai workload to execute reliably without unnecessary infrastructure complexity or uncontrolled operational variation.**

---

# Runtime Architecture Vision

The long-term Runtime Architecture should provide a unified execution model across:

- Managed Application Platforms
- Managed Container Platforms
- Kubernetes
- Serverless Functions
- Serverless Jobs
- Queue Workers
- Scheduled Workloads
- AI Compute
- Customer-Dedicated Environments
- Regional Deployments

The preferred evolution path is:

```text
Managed Runtime

↓

Standardized Containers

↓

Managed Container Platform

↓

Kubernetes Where Justified

↓

Serverless for Suitable Event Workloads

↓

Multi-Product Runtime Platform

↓

Regional Runtime Architecture

↓

Policy-Governed Adaptive Runtime
```

---

# Runtime Architecture Mission

The mission of Runtime Architecture is to provide approved workload execution environments that:

- Protect application isolation
- Standardize deployments
- Reduce environment drift
- Support automatic scaling
- Maintain production availability
- Protect secrets and identities
- Enforce resource limits
- Enable observability
- Support rollback and recovery
- Control runtime cost
- Support multiple products and tenants
- Provide workload portability
- Support human and AI engineering teams
- Reduce manual runtime administration

---

# Runtime Architecture Objectives

Runtime Architecture exists to:

- Standardize application packaging
- Establish approved runtime options
- Define workload placement rules
- Provide secure container execution
- Govern container registries
- Define Kubernetes adoption criteria
- Standardize clusters and namespaces
- Govern node pools and scheduling
- Define service-mesh adoption
- Support serverless workloads
- Enforce runtime security
- Enable horizontal scaling
- Improve deployment reliability
- Maintain runtime observability
- Reduce operational fragmentation
- Control runtime cost
- Support multi-region growth
- Maintain recoverability

---

# Runtime Architecture Principles

Every runtime decision should follow these principles:

- Managed Runtime Before Self-Managed Runtime
- Containers Before Environment-Specific Packaging
- Kubernetes Only When Justified
- Serverless Only for Suitable Workloads
- Immutable Artifacts
- One Workload, One Clear Owner
- Least Privilege
- Non-Root Execution by Default
- Resource Requests and Limits
- Health Checks Before Production
- Logs and Metrics Before Production
- Stateless Execution Where Practical
- Externalized Configuration
- Secrets Outside Images
- Automated Scaling With Boundaries
- Workload Isolation
- Runtime Portability Where Valuable
- Cost Visibility
- Versioned Deployment
- Human Approval for High-Risk Runtime Changes

---

# Runtime Scope

Runtime Architecture covers:

- Container Images
- Container Registries
- Container Runtime
- Managed Container Services
- Kubernetes
- Kubernetes Clusters
- Namespaces
- Node Pools
- Workload Scheduling
- Service Discovery
- Ingress
- Egress
- Service Mesh
- Serverless Functions
- Serverless Jobs
- Background Workers
- Scheduled Tasks
- AI Workloads
- Runtime Identities
- Runtime Secrets
- Runtime Configuration
- Runtime Security
- Runtime Observability
- Runtime Scaling
- Runtime Recovery
- Runtime Cost
- Runtime Governance

---

# Runtime Non-Scope

Runtime Architecture does not directly own:

- Product Business Logic
- Domain Rules
- User Experience
- Database Domain Design
- Product Requirements
- AI Agent Role Design
- Business Process Ownership
- Customer Support Procedures
- Product Analytics Interpretation

Runtime Architecture provides the execution foundation for these capabilities.

---

# Runtime Reference Model

```text
Source Code

↓

Build Pipeline

↓

Immutable Artifact or Container Image

↓

Artifact and Container Registry

↓

Runtime Policy Validation

↓

Deployment Configuration

↓

Runtime Platform

├── Managed Application Runtime
├── Managed Container Runtime
├── Kubernetes
├── Serverless Functions
├── Serverless Jobs
└── Dedicated Compute

↓

Networking, Identity, Secrets, and Storage

↓

Logs, Metrics, Traces, and Audit

↓

Scaling, Recovery, and Governance
```

---

# Runtime Selection Model

Every workload should pass through a documented placement decision.

```text
Workload Requirement

↓

Can an approved managed service provide the capability?

Yes
Use the managed service.

No

↓

Can an approved managed application runtime host it?

Yes
Use the managed application runtime.

No

↓

Can an approved managed container platform host it?

Yes
Use the managed container platform.

No

↓

Is the workload event-driven, short-lived, and stateless?

Yes
Consider serverless.

No

↓

Does it require advanced orchestration, scheduling, networking, or isolation?

Yes
Consider Kubernetes.

No

↓

Does it require operating-system-level control?

Yes
Use governed virtual machines.

No

↓

Reassess the architecture.
```

---

# Runtime Workload Classification

Every workload should be classified.

| Workload Type | Typical Runtime |
|---|---|
| Web Application | Managed Application or Container Runtime |
| API Service | Managed Runtime or Container |
| Background Worker | Container Worker or Managed Worker |
| Queue Consumer | Container Worker or Serverless Consumer |
| Scheduled Job | Serverless Job or Managed Scheduler |
| Short Event Function | Serverless Function |
| Long-Running Workflow | Container or Workflow Runtime |
| Stateful Legacy Application | Virtual Machine or Managed Service |
| High-Scale Multi-Service Platform | Kubernetes Where Justified |
| AI Inference | Managed AI Runtime or Specialized Container |
| Batch Data Processing | Managed Batch or Container Job |
| CI/CD Build | Managed Runner or Isolated Build Container |
