The Public Edge Domain handles internet-facing traffic.

It may include:

- Public DNS
- CDN
- DDoS Protection
- Web Application Firewall
- Public Load Balancers
- Public API Gateway
- Edge Functions

Trust Level:

```text
Untrusted
```

Required controls include:

- TLS
- Traffic Filtering
- Rate Limiting
- Abuse Protection
- Logging
- Health Checks
- Minimal Backend Exposure
- Security Monitoring

---

# Domain 2 — Application Ingress Domain

The Application Ingress Domain routes approved traffic from the edge into product and platform workloads.

It may include:

- Ingress Controllers
- Reverse Proxies
- Internal Gateways
- Product Routers
- API Routing

Trust Level:

```text
Restricted
```

---

# Domain 3 — Core Platform Domain

The Core Platform Domain contains:

- Identity
- Organizations
- Permissions
- Audit
- Notifications
- Files
- Search
- Billing
- Workflow
- AI Gateway

This is a high-value shared domain.

It requires:

- Strong Availability
- Strict Access
- Central Monitoring
- Controlled Product Connectivity
- Strong Change Governance

---

# Domain 4 — Product Domains

Each product may have its own domain.

Examples:

- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- HospitalOS
- SchoolOS
- Marketplace

Each product domain should define:

- Product Services
- Product Data Access
- Product Ingress
- Shared Platform Dependencies
- External Integrations
- Product Monitoring
- Product Cost

---

# Domain 5 — Data Domain

The Data Domain contains:

- Databases
- Caches
- Search
- Queues
- Vector Stores
- Data Pipelines
- Analytics Storage
- Backup Interfaces

Trust Level:

```text
Highly Restricted
```

General internet access should not be available.

---

# Domain 6 — AI Platform Domain

The AI Platform Domain may contain:

- AI Gateway
- Agent Runtime
- Model Router
- Tool Gateway
- Memory Services
- Knowledge Retrieval
- Vector Storage
- Evaluation Systems

It requires controls for:

- Tenant Scope
- Project Scope
- Tool Access
- External Model Egress
- Data Classification
- Cost
- Audit
- Human Approval

---

# Domain 7 — Management Domain

The Management Domain contains:

- Administrative Interfaces
- Infrastructure Management
- Runtime Management
- Deployment Systems
- Monitoring Administration
- Backup Administration
- Security Administration

This domain requires the strongest human-access controls.

---

# Domain 8 — Observability Domain

The Observability Domain contains:

- Log Collection
- Metrics
- Tracing
- Dashboards
- Alerting
- Flow Logs
- Audit Events
- Network Analytics

Write access should be limited.

Critical audit evidence should resist deletion or alteration by normal application teams.

---

# Domain 9 — Security Domain

The Security Domain may contain:

- Threat Detection
- Security Monitoring
- Vulnerability Systems
- WAF Management
- Firewall Management
- Security Analytics
- Incident Tooling
- Audit Archive

---

# Domain 10 — Integration Domain

The Integration Domain manages connectivity with external systems.

It may contain:

- Integration Gateway
- Webhook Receivers
- Partner API Adapters
- Customer Connectors
- Message Bridges
- Data Exchange Services

External systems should not connect directly to internal databases.

---

# Domain 11 — Developer Domain

The Developer Domain may contain:

- Development Services
- CI/CD Runners
- Preview Environments
- Test Services
- Package Mirrors
- Developer Portal
- Sandbox Integrations

It should not receive broad production connectivity.

---

# Domain 12 — Customer Connectivity Domain

This domain terminates:

- Customer VPNs
- Private Links
- Dedicated Connections
- Customer Allowlist Rules
- Enterprise Private APIs

Each customer connection should remain isolated from unrelated customer connections.

---

# Domain 13 — Disaster Recovery Domain

The Disaster Recovery Domain supports:

- Backup Access
- Recovery Infrastructure
- Standby Services
- Recovery DNS
- Regional Failover
- Emergency Administration

---

# Network Domain Trust Levels

Domains may be classified as:

| Trust Level | Description |
|---|---|
| T0 | Public and untrusted |
| T1 | Externally connected and restricted |
| T2 | Internal standard workload |
| T3 | Sensitive platform or product |
| T4 | Highly restricted data or management |
| T5 | Critical security, identity, or recovery |

A higher trust classification should require stronger controls.

Trust levels should not create automatic communication rights.

---

# Network Segmentation

Network Segmentation divides the enterprise network into controlled zones to reduce unauthorized access, failure impact, attack movement, and operational interference.

Segmentation should be based on meaningful risk and ownership boundaries.

It should not create complexity without control value.

---

# Network Segmentation Objectives

Segmentation should:

- Protect Production
- Protect Data
- Protect Identity
- Protect Management Systems
- Separate Environments
- Separate Products
- Separate Customers
- Restrict Lateral Movement
- Reduce Blast Radius
- Improve Monitoring
- Improve Cost Attribution
- Support Compliance
- Support Incident Containment
- Support Regional Independence

---

# Segmentation Dimensions

Segmentation may occur by:

- Environment
- Region
- Product
- Platform
- Project
- Tenant
- Customer
- Workload Type
- Data Classification
- Security Level
- Operational Owner
- Compliance Requirement
- Runtime Platform

---

# Environment Segmentation

Environment segmentation should separate:

- Local
- Development
- Test
- Integration
- Staging
- Production
- Disaster Recovery
- Sandbox
- Security Testing

Production should not trust non-production networks.

---

# Product Segmentation

Product segmentation should ensure that:

- Product traffic is identifiable.
- Product dependencies are documented.
- Product failures can be isolated.
- Product network cost is measurable.
- Product access to shared services is controlled.
- Products do not access each other's data directly.

---

# Platform Segmentation

Shared platform services should be separated from product workloads where needed.

This allows:

- Stronger Security
- Central Ownership
- Independent Scaling
- Failure Isolation
- Controlled Product Access
- Better Monitoring

---

# Data Segmentation

Data services should be segmented according to:

- Data Domain
- Tenant
- Product
- Sensitivity
- Regulatory Requirement
- Region
- System of Record
- Operational Ownership

---

# Management Segmentation

Administrative interfaces should not share unrestricted paths with normal application traffic.

Management access should use:

- Separate Network
- Private Endpoint
- Bastion
- VPN
- Zero Trust Access Proxy
- Strong Identity
- Session Audit

---

# Security Segmentation

Security systems should have protected communication paths.

Application teams should not have unrestricted control over:

- Audit Logs
- Security Alerts
- Firewall Evidence
- Threat Detection
- Incident Evidence
- Security Configuration

---

# Customer Segmentation

Customer-dedicated connectivity should prevent:

- Customer-to-Customer Routing
- Shared Credential Use
- Shared VPN Identity
- Uncontrolled Route Propagation
- Customer Access to Shared Management Systems
- Customer Access to Other Tenant Data

---

# Kubernetes Segmentation

Kubernetes segmentation may use:

- Cluster Boundaries
- Namespaces
- Network Policies
- Service Accounts
- Node Pools
- Ingress Policies
- Egress Policies
- Pod Security
- Resource Quotas

Namespaces alone do not provide complete isolation.

---

# Serverless Segmentation

Serverless workloads should be segmented through:

- Dedicated Identities
- Private Connectors
- Restricted Network Access
- Function-Level Permissions
- Separate Environments
- Egress Controls
- Tenant Context
- Logging

---

# AI Workload Segmentation

AI workloads may require segmentation by:

- Product
- Tenant
- Project
- Agent Role
- Tool Risk
- Data Classification
- Model Provider
- Cost Center
- Human Approval Level

High-risk AI tools may require isolated execution environments.

---

# Micro-Segmentation

Micro-segmentation applies policies between individual services or workload groups.

It may use:

- Security Groups
- Network Policies
- Service Mesh Policies
- Identity-Aware Proxies
- Host Firewalls
- Workload Identity

Micro-segmentation should be introduced progressively where risk and scale justify it.

---

# North-South Segmentation

North-south traffic moves between external networks and internal workloads.

Controls may include:

- Edge Security
- WAF
- Load Balancers
- API Gateway
- Firewall
- Rate Limiting
- TLS
- Ingress Policy
- DDoS Protection

---

# East-West Segmentation

East-west traffic moves between internal services.

Controls may include:

- Service Identity
- Network Policy
- Security Groups
- Private DNS
- Mutual TLS
- Service Mesh
- Application Authorization
- Flow Monitoring

---

# Segmentation Policy Model

A segmentation rule should define:

- Rule ID
- Source Domain
- Destination Domain
- Protocol
- Port
- Purpose
- Environment
- Product
- Identity
- Data Classification
- Owner
- Approval
- Monitoring
- Expiration
- Review Date

---

# Default Segmentation Rules

Recommended default rules include:

- Public Internet cannot access databases directly.
- Non-production cannot access production data by default.
- Product networks cannot access unrelated product databases.
- Customer networks cannot route to other customer networks.
- Application workloads cannot access management systems.
- AI agent runtimes cannot access unrestricted internal systems.
- Build systems cannot receive permanent production administration rights.
- Databases accept traffic only from approved services.
- Administrative interfaces remain private.
- External integrations terminate in approved integration components.
- Egress is restricted where practical.
- Audit systems cannot be modified by normal application workloads.

---

# Segmentation Exceptions

A segmentation exception should include:

- Source
- Destination
- Business Need
- Technical Need
- Data
- Protocol
- Port
- Duration
- Risk
- Compensating Controls
- Owner
- Security Approval
- Review Date
- Removal Plan

---

# Segmentation Validation

Segmentation should be validated through:

- Automated Policy Tests
- Connectivity Tests
- Denied-Path Tests
- Security Scans
- Flow Log Analysis
- Penetration Testing
- Cross-Tenant Tests
- Cross-Environment Tests
- Route Validation
- Firewall Validation
- Kubernetes Policy Tests

---

# Segmentation Monitoring

Monitor:

- Unexpected Cross-Domain Traffic
- Denied Connections
- New Communication Paths
- Broad Firewall Rules
- Public Exposure
- Cross-Environment Traffic
- Cross-Product Traffic
- Cross-Customer Traffic
- Administrative Access
- Unapproved Egress
- Network Policy Violations

---

# Segmentation Maturity

## Level S0 — Flat Network

Characteristics:

- Shared network
- Broad connectivity
- Weak environment separation
- Limited traffic visibility

## Level S1 — Environment Segmentation

Characteristics:

- Development and production separated
- Databases private
- Basic security groups
- Basic ingress control

## Level S2 — Product and Data Segmentation

Characteristics:

- Product domains
- Data domains
- Controlled cross-service communication
- Central monitoring
- Controlled egress

## Level S3 — Identity-Aware Micro-Segmentation

Characteristics:

- Workload identity
- Network policies
- Default deny in sensitive zones
- Automated policy validation
- Strong management isolation

## Level S4 — Regional Zero Trust Segmentation

Characteristics:

- Regional policy
- Identity-aware routing
- Continuous verification
- Automated risk analysis
- Regional failure containment

## Level S5 — Global Adaptive Segmentation

Characteristics:

- Policy-driven global communication
- Dynamic access based on identity, risk, region, and workload
- Continuous automated validation
- Human approval for elevated-risk exceptions

# Enterprise Network Foundation Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| NF0 | Flat and Uncontrolled | Broad connectivity, weak ownership, limited visibility |
| NF1 | Basic Secure Network | Environment separation, private data services, controlled ingress |
| NF2 | Governed Segmented Network | Product, data, management, and integration domains |
| NF3 | Multi-Product Enterprise Network | Shared hub, isolated spokes, centralized security and DNS |
| NF4 | Regional Zero Trust Network | Identity-aware access, multi-region policy, advanced monitoring |
| NF5 | Global Adaptive Network | Dynamic policy-driven connectivity across products, regions, and providers |

---

# NF0 — Flat and Uncontrolled

Characteristics:

- Shared network
- Broad routing
- Public services
- Shared administrator access
- Limited monitoring
- No formal segmentation
- Unknown dependencies

Exit requirements:

- Network inventory
- Production separation
- Private database access
- Controlled ingress
- Basic firewall
- Ownership
- Flow logging
- Infrastructure as Code

---

# NF1 — Basic Secure Network

Characteristics:

- Development and production separated
- Public and private subnets
- Databases private
- Approved load balancer
- Basic DNS
- Restricted administrative access
- Initial security groups

Exit requirements:

- Product segmentation
- Data-domain segmentation
- Controlled egress
- Central DNS
- Shared connectivity model
- Network policy standards
- Route governance

---

# NF2 — Governed Segmented Network

Characteristics:

- Clear network domains
- Product separation
- Data separation
- Management separation
- Integration gateway
- Network monitoring
- Segmentation testing
- Formal exceptions

Exit requirements:

- Hub-and-spoke or equivalent architecture
- Multi-product operations
- Centralized firewall and egress
- Private endpoints
- Customer connectivity patterns
- Stronger Zero Trust controls

---

# NF3 — Multi-Product Enterprise Network

Characteristics:

- Shared network hub
- Isolated product spokes
- Shared security
- Shared DNS
- Controlled product-to-platform access
- Dedicated customer connectivity
- Network cost allocation
- Central visibility

Exit requirements:

- Multi-region architecture
- Regional routing
- Global DNS
- Regional recovery
- Identity-aware service communication
- Advanced policy automation

---

# NF4 — Regional Zero Trust Network

Characteristics:

- Several regions
- Strong workload identity
- Regional segmentation
- Automated policy validation
- Private service connectivity
- Controlled hybrid access
- Advanced threat detection
- Regional failure isolation

Exit requirements:

- Global policy intelligence
- Dynamic access decisions
- Mature multi-cloud where required
- Global recovery coordination
- Adaptive cost and traffic routing

---

# NF5 — Global Adaptive Network

Characteristics:

- Global network domains operate through approved blueprints
- Connectivity decisions consider identity, product, tenant, region, risk, cost, and capacity
- Policies are continuously validated
- Low-risk network operations are automated
- High-risk network changes remain human-approved
- Global traffic, security, and recovery remain observable
- New Industry Operating Systems consume established network patterns

---

# Enterprise Network Foundation Roadmap

## Phase 1 — Basic Secure Foundation

- Inventory networks
- Separate production and non-production
- Create private application and data networks
- Establish approved ingress
- Establish basic DNS
- Restrict administrative access
- Enable network logs
- Define ownership
- Move network configuration into code

---

## Phase 2 — Segmentation and Governance

- Define network domains
- Define trust levels
- Segment products
- Segment data
- Segment management systems
- Control egress
- Create network rule standards
- Establish exception process
- Add automated validation

---

## Phase 3 — Multi-Product Enterprise Network

- Introduce hub-and-spoke or equivalent model
- Centralize shared DNS
- Centralize firewall and inspection
- Establish shared-services network
- Establish product spokes
- Establish customer connectivity patterns
- Allocate network cost by product
- Improve dependency mapping

---

## Phase 4 — Identity-Aware Networking

- Introduce workload identity
- Strengthen service-to-service authentication
- Add micro-segmentation
- Expand default-deny controls
- Strengthen administrative access
- Improve AI network isolation
- Add policy as code
- Improve automated compliance

---

## Phase 5 — Regional Networking

- Add second-region addressing
- Add regional ingress
- Add regional routing
- Add global DNS
- Add cross-region private connectivity
- Add regional monitoring
- Test regional failure
- Establish data-residency network controls

---

## Phase 6 — Global Adaptive Networking

- Integrate global traffic intelligence
- Automate low-risk route and capacity actions
- Add dynamic policy decisions
- Optimize cross-region transfer
- Support controlled hybrid and multi-cloud connectivity
- Strengthen predictive failure detection
- Provide reusable network blueprints for new products and regions

---

# Part 14B-3A Exit Criteria

Part 14B-3A is complete when:

- The Enterprise Network Architecture is documented.
- Network Philosophy and Principles are approved.
- Network objectives align with security, reliability, product, tenant, AI, operational, and global requirements.
- Network layers are clearly defined.
- The Enterprise Network Model is selected for the current maturity stage.
- Production and non-production boundaries are defined.
- Public, private, application, platform, data, management, integration, observability, security, customer, and recovery domains are defined.
- Trust classifications are assigned.
- Product, project, customer, and tenant isolation requirements are documented.
- Network Segmentation standards are approved.
- North-south and east-west traffic controls are defined.
- Administrative access is separated from normal application traffic.
- Public exposure requires explicit approval.
- Private services remain private by default.
- Network addressing avoids overlap.
- Network communication paths require ownership.
- Network policy and infrastructure are version-controlled.
- Network logging and monitoring requirements are defined.
- Network quality gates, metrics, risks, maturity levels, and roadmap are documented.
- The foundation is ready for detailed virtual network, subnet, routing, peering, private connectivity, VPN, and dedicated connectivity architecture.

---

Enterprise Network Foundation establishes the communication model for every MianX.ai product, platform, service, customer, agent, integration, and region.

The foundation follows:

```text
Network Philosophy and Principles

↓

Network Layers

↓

Enterprise Network Model

↓

Network Domains

↓

Segmentation and Trust Boundaries

↓

Controlled Communication

↓

Monitoring, Governance, and Recovery
```

```text
Executive Summary
Defines the enterprise networking requirement

Network Architecture
Defines the structural communication model

Network Philosophy
Defines the operating beliefs

Network Principles
Defines mandatory design rules

Network Objectives
Defines expected outcomes

Network Layers
Separates communication responsibilities

Enterprise Network Model

Network Domains
Defines trust and ownership boundaries

Network Segmentation
Restricts communication and failure impact
```

MianX.ai Enterprise Network Foundation must remain:

- Private by Default
- Deny by Default
- Identity-Aware
- Segmented
- Environment-Isolated
- Product-Aware
- Tenant-Protective
- AI-Governed
- Multi-Zone
- Region-Ready
- Observable
- Encrypted
- Recoverable
- Cost-Aware
- Policy-Governed
- Human-Accountable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to connect systems.

The objective is to ensure that every system communicates only with the approved identities, services, environments, products, customers, and destinations required to perform its enterprise responsibility.

# Part 14B-3B — Core Network Infrastructure

Core Network Infrastructure defines how MianX.ai creates, organizes, connects, isolates, routes, secures, monitors, and governs the private network foundations used by every product, platform, runtime, database, AI system, integration, customer environment, and regional deployment.

This section converts the Enterprise Network Foundation into implementable infrastructure.

It defines the architecture for:

- Virtual Networks
- Subnets
- IP Address Management
- Routing
- Route Tables
- Transit Networks
- Network Peering
- Private Connectivity
- Private Endpoints
- VPN
- Dedicated Connectivity
- Hybrid Connectivity

Core Network Infrastructure must provide reliable communication without creating uncontrolled trust.

The network should allow approved systems to communicate while protecting:

- Production
- Customer Data
- Tenant Boundaries
- Product Boundaries
- Shared Platform Services
- Administrative Systems
- Databases
- AI Workloads
- Customer Environments
- Regional Infrastructure
- Disaster Recovery Systems

---

# Core Network Infrastructure Statement

> **Build a private, segmented, non-overlapping, explicitly routed, highly available, observable, and policy-governed network foundation that securely connects approved MianX.ai environments, products, services, customers, and regions.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai should begin with a simple network model and expand only when justified by scale, security, customer, or regional requirements.

The preferred progression is:

```text
Single Virtual Network

↓

Separated Production and Non-Production Networks

↓

Public, Application, Data, and Management Subnets

↓

Private Service Connectivity

↓

Product and Platform Network Segmentation

↓

Central Transit Architecture

↓

Customer VPN and Private Connectivity

↓

Dedicated Enterprise Connectivity

↓

Multi-Region and Hybrid Network
```

The objective is not to create excessive networks or routes.

The objective is to ensure that every important communication path is:

- Explicit
- Necessary
- Authorized
- Encrypted
- Monitored
- Owned
- Revocable
- Recoverable
- Cost-Aware
- Documented

---

# Core Network Objectives

Core Network Infrastructure should:

- Establish non-overlapping address spaces
- Separate environments
- Separate trust zones
- Keep internal services private
- Protect databases and administrative services
- Standardize subnet design
- Centralize critical routing
- Reduce unnecessary network peering
- Support private platform-service access
- Support customer and partner connectivity
- Support hybrid infrastructure
- Support multi-region expansion
- Maintain network visibility
- Support disaster recovery
- Automate network provisioning
- Prevent manual configuration drift
- Control network cost
- Maintain long-term scalability

---

# Core Network Principles

Every core network decision should follow these principles:

- Non-Overlapping Addressing
- Private by Default
- Explicit Routing
- Least Connectivity
- Environment Separation
- Product and Platform Awareness
- Central Governance
- High Availability for Critical Gateways
- Encryption Across Untrusted Boundaries
- Infrastructure as Code
- Policy-Based Validation
- Observable Traffic
- Documented Ownership
- Revocable Connectivity
- Cost-Aware Data Transfer
- Recovery-Aware Design
- Human Approval for High-Risk Changes

---

# Core Network Reference Architecture

A mature Core Network Architecture may follow:

```text
Global or Regional Edge

↓

Central Network Hub or Transit Layer

├── Firewall
├── DNS
├── Egress
├── VPN
├── Dedicated Connectivity
├── Security Inspection
└── Regional Transit

↓

Spoke Networks

├── Core Platform
├── Product Networks
├── AI Platform
├── Data Platform
├── Developer Platform
├── Non-Production
├── Customer-Dedicated Networks
└── Disaster Recovery

↓

Private Application and Data Subnets

↓

Managed Services Through Private Endpoints
```

---

# Virtual Networks

Virtual Networks provide isolated private address spaces for cloud-hosted workloads and services.

Depending on the cloud provider, equivalent constructs may be called:

- Virtual Private Cloud
- Virtual Network
- Network Project
- Private Cloud Network

Virtual Networks are foundational security and operational boundaries.

They should not be created without a documented purpose and owner.

---

# Virtual Network Objectives

Virtual Networks should:

- Isolate environments
- Isolate products where required
- Isolate customers where required
- Contain failures
- Control routing
- Enable private communication
- Support private service endpoints
- Support regional deployment
- Support cost allocation
- Support centralized security
- Support repeatable automation

---

# Virtual Network Classification

Virtual Networks may be classified as:

- Shared Services Network
- Production Platform Network
- Production Product Network
- Non-Production Network
- Data Platform Network
- AI Platform Network
- Management Network
- Security Network
- Customer-Dedicated Network
- Integration Network
- Disaster Recovery Network
- Transit Network

---

# Initial Virtual Network Model

During the early stage, MianX.ai may use:

```text
Development Virtual Network

Staging Virtual Network

Production Virtual Network

Shared Security and Operations Network
```

This provides essential environment separation without excessive complexity.

---

# Mature Virtual Network Model

At greater scale:

```text
Regional Network Hub

├── Shared Services Spoke
├── Core Platform Spoke
├── RestaurantOS Spoke
├── PoultryOS Spoke
├── AI Platform Spoke
├── Data Platform Spoke
├── Developer Platform Spoke
├── Customer Spokes
└── Disaster Recovery Spoke
```

---

# Virtual Network Boundaries

A separate Virtual Network may be justified by:

- Environment Separation
- Product Isolation
- Customer Contract
- Security Classification
- Compliance Requirement
- Regional Requirement
- Different Routing Policy
- Different Operational Ownership
- Dedicated Connectivity
- Blast-Radius Reduction
- Independent Cost Allocation

---

# Virtual Network Non-Justifications

Separate networks should not be created merely because:

- Every application wants its own network
- A team prefers independent control
- Subnets and policies would provide sufficient isolation
- A network name appears more organized
- The architecture lacks central ownership

Excessive network count creates:

- Routing Complexity
- Peering Complexity
- DNS Complexity
- Security Policy Drift
- Higher Cost
- Operational Burden

---

# Virtual Network Metadata

Every Virtual Network should define:

- Network ID
- Name
- Purpose
- Environment
- Product
- Region
- Address Range
- Owner
- Security Owner
- Cost Owner
- Criticality
- Connected Networks
- Routing Model
- DNS Model
- Logging Status
- Lifecycle Status
- Review Date

# Virtual Network Naming

A naming convention may follow:

```text
<company>-<environment>-<region>-<purpose>-vnet
```

Example:

```text
mianx-prod-pk-core-vnet
```

The final format should respect provider naming limitations.

Each network should receive a non-overlapping address range from a centrally governed address plan.

- Service Networks

- Disaster Recovery
- Regional Expansion
- Reserved Growth Capacity

Network size should reflect:

- Expected Workload Count
- Subnet Count

- Container Addressing
- Serverless Connectors
- Private Endpoints
- Customer Connections
- Future Growth

Very small ranges create expansion risk.

Unnecessarily large ranges may create conflicts with customer or hybrid networks.

- Egress Policy

# Subnets

Subnets divide Virtual Networks into smaller address ranges based on workload type, trust, routing, availability, and operational requirements.

Subnets should represent meaningful boundaries.

They should not be created only for visual organization.

---

# Subnet Objectives

Subnets should:

- Separate public and private workloads
- Separate application and data workloads
- Support routing policies
- Support firewall policies
- Support availability zones
- Support private endpoints
- Support management access
- Support runtime platforms
- Improve failure containment
- Improve address management
- Improve observability

---

# Standard Subnet Categories

Potential subnet categories include:

- Public Ingress Subnet
- Private Application Subnet
- Private Worker Subnet
- Data Subnet
- Management Subnet
- Integration Subnet
- Private Endpoint Subnet
- Kubernetes Node Subnet
- Kubernetes Pod Subnet
- Serverless Connector Subnet
- Firewall Subnet
- Gateway Subnet
- Load Balancer Subnet
- Observability Subnet
- Backup Subnet
- Disaster Recovery Subnet

---

# Public Subnet

A public subnet may contain approved internet-facing infrastructure such as:

- Public Load Balancers
- NAT Gateways Where Provider Architecture Requires
- Edge Gateways
- Bastion Hosts Where Approved
- Public API Gateways

Application and database workloads should generally not run directly in public subnets.

---

# Private Application Subnet

Private Application Subnets may contain:

- APIs
- Backend Services
- Web Application Runtimes
- Workflow Services
- Product Services
- Shared Platform Services

These workloads may receive inbound traffic only from approved ingress layers.

---

# Worker Subnet

Worker subnets may host:

- Queue Workers
- Scheduled Jobs
- Data Processors
- File Processing
- Notification Workers
- Integration Workers
- AI Task Workers

Workers may require controlled egress but generally should not receive public inbound traffic.

---

# Data Subnet

Data subnets may contain:

- Managed Database Interfaces
- Cache
- Search
- Queues
- Data Services
- Self-Managed Data Systems Where Approved

Data subnets should be highly restricted.

---

# Management Subnet

Management subnets may host:

- Bastion
- Administrative Tools
- Patch Systems
- Monitoring Collectors
- Infrastructure Management
- Recovery Tools

Access should require stronger controls.

---

# Private Endpoint Subnet

Dedicated subnets may be used for private endpoints to:

- Managed Databases
- Object Storage
- Secrets Services
- Messaging Services
- AI Services
- Container Registries
- Monitoring Services

---

# Gateway Subnet

Some cloud platforms require dedicated subnets for:

- VPN Gateway
- Transit Gateway
- Network Virtual Appliance
- Firewall
- Dedicated Connectivity Gateway

These subnets should follow provider-specific standards.

---

# Kubernetes Subnets

Kubernetes may require subnet allocations for:

- Nodes
- Pods
- Services
- Internal Load Balancers
- Ingress
- Egress

Kubernetes addressing should be planned before cluster creation.

---

# Serverless Connector Subnet

Serverless workloads requiring private network access may use dedicated connectors or subnet integrations.

These should define:

- Address Capacity
- Scaling Capacity
- Route Policy
- Egress
- Security
- Service Access
- Cost

---

# Subnet Sizing

Subnet size should consider:

- Current Resources
- Expected Growth
- Scaling
- Availability Zones
- Private Endpoints
- Runtime Requirements
- Provider-Reserved Addresses
- Kubernetes Workloads
- Serverless Connectors
- Recovery Capacity

---

# Zone-Aware Subnet Design

Where the cloud architecture uses availability zones, subnets may be created per zone.

Example:

```text
application-zone-a

application-zone-b

application-zone-c

data-zone-a

data-zone-b

data-zone-c
```

Zone-based subnets can improve:

- Resilience
- Scheduling
- Routing Control
- Failure Analysis
- Capacity Planning

Every subnet should define:

- Transit Routes

- Customer Routes
- Inspection Routes
- Blackhole or Deny Routes Where Supported

Subnet security should include:

- Security Groups
- Network ACLs Where Appropriate
- Route Restrictions
- Flow Logging
- Private DNS
- Controlled Egress
- Approved Service Endpoints
- Ownership
- Monitoring

# IP Address Management

IP Address Management coordinates private and public address allocation across:

- Regions
- Environments
- Virtual Networks
- Subnets
- Kubernetes
- Customer Networks

- Disaster Recovery
- Multi-Cloud Networks

Without central IP management, future connectivity becomes difficult and expensive.

---

# IP Address Management Objectives

IPAM should:

- Prevent address overlap
- Reserve future capacity
- Support customer connectivity
- Support regional expansion
- Support hybrid deployment
- Support Kubernetes addressing
- Maintain ownership
- Record usage
- Support automation
- Support decommissioning
- Improve troubleshooting

---

# IP Address Hierarchy

A structured model may allocate ranges by:

```text
Enterprise Address Space

↓

Region

↓

Environment

↓

Network Domain

↓

Virtual Network

↓

Subnet

↓

Workload
```

---

# Address Allocation Record

Every allocation should record:

- Allocation ID
- CIDR
- Region
- Environment
- Product
- Network
- Subnet
- Purpose
- Owner
- Status
- Creation Date
- Expiration Where Temporary
- Connected Customer Networks
- Notes

---

# Reserved Address Capacity

Address plans should reserve capacity for:

- New Products
- New Regions
- Disaster Recovery
- Kubernetes
- Customer Connectivity
- Acquisitions
- Hybrid Environments
- Multi-Cloud
- Security Services
- Private Endpoints

---

# Overlapping Address Detection

Automated checks should detect overlap before:

- Network Creation
- Customer VPN Approval
- Peering
- Regional Expansion
- Hybrid Connection
- Multi-Cloud Connection
- Kubernetes Cluster Creation

---

# Customer Address Conflicts

Customer networks may use address ranges that overlap with MianX.ai networks.

Conflict strategies may include:

- Network Address Translation
- Proxy-Based Integration
- Application-Level Connectivity
- Dedicated Customer Network
- Alternate Address Allocation
- Private Endpoint Architecture
- Customer Renumbering Where Possible

---

# Public IP Governance

Public IP addresses should be:

- Minimized
- Owned
- Tagged
- Monitored
- Protected
- Associated With Approved Services
- Reviewed
- Released When Unused

Unattached public IPs should be detected and removed.

---

# Routing

Routing determines how network traffic moves between sources and destinations.

Routing must remain explicit, minimal, documented, and testable.

A route can create connectivity across security boundaries.

Therefore, routing changes should be treated as security-sensitive infrastructure changes.

---

# Routing Objectives

Routing should:

- Deliver approved traffic reliably
- Prevent unauthorized paths
- Support environment isolation
- Support product isolation
- Support transit architecture
- Support private endpoints
- Support customer connectivity
- Support regional connectivity
- Support disaster recovery
- Maintain predictable traffic flow
- Enable monitoring and troubleshooting

---

# Routing Principles

Routing should follow:

- Least Route Privilege
- No Implicit Cross-Environment Routing
- No Uncontrolled Route Propagation
- Central Governance for Shared Routes
- Explicit Default Routes
- Symmetric Routing Where Required
- Inspection-Aware Routing
- Failure-Aware Routing
- Cost-Aware Routing
- Version-Controlled Changes
- Documented Ownership

---

# Route Categories

Routes may include:

- Local Network Routes
- Default Internet Route
- NAT or Egress Route
- Firewall Inspection Route
- Transit Route
- Peering Route
- Private Endpoint Route
- VPN Route
- Dedicated Connection Route
- Customer Route
- Regional Route
- Disaster Recovery Route
- Blackhole Route
- Service Endpoint Route

---

# Local Routing

Local routing supports communication within one Virtual Network.

Local access should still be restricted through:

- Security Groups
- Firewall Policies
- Network ACLs
- Kubernetes Network Policies
- Application Authorization

---

# Internet Routing

Internet access may be:

- Public Inbound
- Controlled Outbound
- Fully Private
- Proxy-Based
- NAT-Based
- Firewall-Inspected

Private application and data workloads should not receive direct public inbound routes.

---

# Egress Routing

Outbound traffic should pass through approved components such as:

- NAT Gateway
- Central Firewall
- Secure Web Proxy
- Egress Gateway
- API Gateway
- Service-Specific Private Endpoint

Egress routing should support:

- Destination Control
- Logging
- Threat Detection
- Cost Visibility
- IP Allowlisting
- Incident Response

---

# Inspection Routing

Sensitive traffic may be routed through:

- Network Firewall
- Intrusion Detection
- Intrusion Prevention
- Secure Proxy
- Data Loss Prevention
- Malware Inspection

Inspection must not create an unplanned single point of failure.

---

# Regional Routing

Regional routes should define:

- Which networks may communicate
- Which traffic remains regional
- Which traffic may cross regions
- Which data may move
- Which paths support failover
- Which traffic uses global services
- Which cost boundaries apply

---

# Disaster Recovery Routing

Disaster recovery routing should define:

- Normal State
- Standby State
- Failover Trigger
- Route Activation
- DNS Changes
- Customer Connectivity
- Return-to-Primary Process
- Validation
- Rollback

---

# Routing Ownership

Every important route should define:

- Route ID
- Source
- Destination
- Prefix
- Next Hop
- Purpose
- Environment
- Product
- Owner
- Security Approval
- Monitoring
- Review Date
- Expiration Where Temporary

---

# Routing Validation

Routing should be validated through:

- Reachability Analysis
- Connectivity Tests
- Denied-Path Tests
- Route Simulation
- Flow Logs
- Packet Analysis
- Failover Testing
- Customer Connectivity Testing
- Regional Recovery Testing

---

# Route Tables

Route Tables contain rules that determine where traffic should be sent.

They should remain:

- Minimal
- Purpose-Specific
- Version-Controlled
- Documented
- Reviewed
- Observable
- Reversible

---

# Route Table Types

Potential route-table types include:

- Public Ingress Route Table
- Private Application Route Table
- Data Route Table
- Management Route Table
- Integration Route Table
- Transit Route Table
- VPN Route Table
- Customer Route Table
- Regional Route Table
- Disaster Recovery Route Table
- Kubernetes Route Table

---

# Public Route Table

A public route table may provide:

- Internet Gateway Route
- Edge Service Access
- Public Load Balancer Connectivity

Only approved public subnets should use it.

---

# Private Application Route Table

Private application routes may provide access to:

- Shared Platform Services
- Data Services
- Controlled Internet Egress
- Internal Load Balancers
- Private Endpoints
- Monitoring
- DNS

---

# Data Route Table

Data route tables should be highly restricted.

They should generally permit:

- Approved Application Sources
- Backup Systems
- Monitoring
- Replication
- Administrative Recovery Paths

They should not normally contain direct internet routes.

---

# Management Route Table

Management routes may connect:

- Administrative Access Gateway
- Bastion
- Monitoring
- Patch Systems
- Recovery Systems
- Infrastructure Management

---

# Transit Route Table

Transit route tables coordinate communication between:

- Spokes
- Regions
- VPN Connections
- Dedicated Connections
- Shared Services
- Firewalls

They should avoid unintended route propagation.

---

# Route Propagation

Automatic route propagation should be used carefully.

It may simplify connectivity but can introduce:

- Unintended Routes
- Cross-Environment Access
- Customer Route Leakage
- Difficult Troubleshooting
- Excessive Blast Radius

Propagation policies should define:

- Allowed Sources
- Allowed Destinations
- Route Filters
- Priorities
- Ownership
- Monitoring

---

# Route Priority

When several routes match, route priority must be understood.

The architecture should document:

- Longest Prefix Match
- Static Route Priority
- Dynamic Route Preference
- Failover Route Priority
- Blackhole Behavior
- Provider-Specific Resolution

---

# Route Table Change Control

Changes should require:

- Proposed Rule
- Business Purpose
- Security Review
- Impact Analysis
- Conflict Check
- Connectivity Test
- Rollback
- Approval
- Monitoring
- Evidence

---

# Route Table Quality Gates

- [ ] Route owner is assigned
- [ ] Source and destination are documented
- [ ] Purpose is justified
- [ ] No environment boundary is bypassed
- [ ] No customer route conflict exists
- [ ] Security review is complete
- [ ] Failover impact is understood
- [ ] Cost impact is reviewed
- [ ] Route is defined as code
- [ ] Connectivity is tested
- [ ] Denied paths remain denied
- [ ] Monitoring is active
- [ ] Rollback is available

---

# Transit Network

A Transit Network provides centralized connectivity between several Virtual Networks, regions, customer connections, hybrid environments, and shared services.

It reduces the need for full-mesh peering.

---

# Transit Network Statement

> **Use centralized transit to simplify governed connectivity, not to create unrestricted communication between every connected network.**

---

# Transit Network Objectives

Transit should:

- Centralize routing
- Reduce peering complexity
- Support shared security
- Support VPN
- Support dedicated connectivity
- Support regional connections
- Support customer connections
- Improve visibility
- Improve route governance
- Improve failure containment
- Support scalable expansion

---

# Transit Architecture Model

```text
Spoke Network A

Spoke Network B

Spoke Network C

Customer VPN

Dedicated Connection

Regional Network

↓

Transit Hub

├── Route Domains
├── Firewall
├── DNS
├── Inspection
├── Egress
└── Monitoring
```

---

# Transit Adoption Criteria

Transit may be justified when:

- Several Virtual Networks exist
- Several products require controlled connectivity
- Customer private connections are growing
- Hybrid connectivity exists
- Multi-region connectivity exists
- Central inspection is required
- Peering complexity is increasing
- Shared routing governance is required

---

# Transit Non-Adoption Criteria

Transit may be unnecessary when:

- Only one or two networks exist
- Managed platform services satisfy connectivity needs
- Peering remains simple
- Operational ownership is immature
- The cost exceeds current benefit

---

# Transit Route Domains

Transit networks may separate route domains for:

- Production
- Non-Production
- Shared Services
- Customer Connectivity
- Management
- Security
- Data
- Regional Traffic
- Disaster Recovery

Connecting to the same transit does not mean all domains may communicate.

---

# Transit Security

Transit security should include:

- Route Segmentation
- Firewall Inspection
- Access Control
- Flow Logging
- Route Filtering
- Customer Isolation
- Environment Isolation
- High Availability
- Change Governance
- Threat Detection

---

# Transit High Availability

Critical transit infrastructure should support:

- Multi-Zone Deployment
- Redundant Gateways
- Redundant Links
- Redundant Firewall Instances
- Health Monitoring
- Failover
- Capacity Headroom
- Recovery Testing

---

# Transit Capacity Planning

Transit capacity should consider:

- Total Throughput
- Connection Count
- Route Count
- Customer Connections
- Cross-Region Traffic
- Inspection Capacity
- VPN Capacity
- Dedicated Link Capacity
- Failover Capacity
- Growth

---

# Transit Monitoring

Monitor:

- Route Status
- Connection Status
- Throughput
- Packet Loss
- Latency
- Firewall Health
- VPN Health
- Customer Link Health
- Route Changes
- Rejected Traffic
- Cost
- Capacity

---

# Transit Risks

Risks include:

- Central Failure
- Route Leakage
- Incorrect Propagation
- Cross-Environment Connectivity
- Customer Route Exposure
- Inspection Bottleneck
- Capacity Exhaustion
- Cost Growth
- Configuration Complexity

---

# Network Peering

Network Peering creates direct private connectivity between two Virtual Networks.

Peering can be simple and efficient, but excessive peering creates an unmanageable full-mesh architecture.

---

# Peering Objectives

Peering should:

- Support approved private communication
- Reduce internet exposure
- Provide low-latency connectivity
- Support shared services
- Support controlled product dependencies
- Remain observable
- Remain owned
- Remain revocable

---

# Peering Use Cases

Peering may be appropriate for:

- Product-to-Shared-Platform Connectivity
- Production-to-Shared-Services Connectivity
- Closely Related Network Domains
- Low-Latency Regional Communication
- Small-Scale Architecture Before Transit

---

# Peering Non-Use Cases

Peering should not be used for:

- Uncontrolled Any-to-Any Connectivity
- Customer-to-Customer Connectivity
- Cross-Environment Trust
- Large-Scale Full-Mesh Networking
- Hidden Product Dependencies
- Temporary Connections Without Expiration

---

# Peering Properties

Architecture should account for whether peering is:

- Transitive
- Non-Transitive
- Regional
- Global
- Bidirectional
- Route-Propagated
- DNS-Integrated
- Costed by Traffic Direction

---

# Peering Request

A peering request should include:

- Source Network
- Destination Network
- Business Purpose
- Technical Purpose
- Required Services
- Address Ranges
- Routing
- DNS
- Security Rules
- Data Classification
- Owner
- Duration
- Monitoring
- Approval

---

# Peering Governance

Peering should require:

- Network Architecture Review
- Security Review
- Address Conflict Check
- Route Review
- Cost Review
- Dependency Documentation
- Infrastructure-as-Code Deployment
- Connectivity Validation
- Periodic Review

---

# Peering Alternatives

Before creating peering, consider:

- Private Endpoint
- API Gateway
- Shared Service Interface
- Transit Network
- Message Queue
- Event Integration
- Application-Level Integration
- Secure Proxy

A private endpoint is often safer than broad network connectivity.

---

# Peering Monitoring

Monitor:

- Peering Status
- Traffic Volume
- Denied Connections
- Route Changes
- DNS Resolution
- Cost
- Unused Peerings
- Unexpected Service Access
- Dependency Growth

---

```text
Requested

↓

Reviewed

↓

Approved

↓

Created

↓

Validated

↓

Monitored

↓

Reviewed

↓

Removed
```

# Private Connectivity

Private Connectivity allows systems to access services without sending traffic across the public internet.

Private connectivity may include:

- Private Endpoints
- Private Service Connect
- Private Links
- Service Endpoints
- Internal Load Balancers
- Transit
- Peering
- VPN
- Dedicated Connections

# Private Connectivity Objectives

Private Connectivity should:

- Reduce public exposure
- Protect sensitive services
- Improve policy control
- Support customer requirements
- Support regulated workloads
- Improve auditability
- Support stable source addressing
- Protect data services
- Reduce attack surface

# Private Connectivity Use Cases

Private connectivity should be considered for:

- Databases
- Object Storage
- Secrets Services
- Container Registries
- AI Services
- Message Queues
- Internal APIs
- Customer Enterprise APIs
- Management Interfaces
- Data Platforms
- Backup Systems

```text
Application Workload

↓

Private DNS

↓

↓
```

- No Public Service Exposure
- Private Routing
- Stronger Firewall Control
- Stable Network Boundary
- Better Compliance Support
- Reduced Internet Dependency

# Private Endpoint Risks

- DNS Complexity

- Cost
- Regional Constraints
- Route Confusion
- Service Limitations
- Operational Ownership Gaps

# Private DNS Integration

Private endpoints usually require private DNS.

# Private Service Publishing

# VPN

Virtual Private Networks provide encrypted connectivity across untrusted networks.

VPNs may connect:

- Engineers
- Administrators
- Offices
- Customer Networks
- Partner Networks
- Cloud Regions
- Hybrid Infrastructure
- Disaster Recovery Environments

# VPN Types

# Remote-Access VPN

Remote-access VPN may provide controlled access for:

- Infrastructure Administrators
- Security Engineers
- Database Administrators
- Support Engineers
- Approved Vendors

Remote access should increasingly integrate with Zero Trust access models rather than granting broad network access.

---

# Remote-Access VPN Requirements

Remote VPN should require:

- Named User Identity
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Device Validation Where Possible
- Role-Based Access
- Restricted Routes
- Session Logging
- Timeouts
- Rapid Revocation
- Access Review
- No Shared Credentials

---

# Site-to-Site VPN

Site-to-site VPN may connect:

- Office to Cloud
- Customer Network to MianX.ai
- Customer Data Center to Dedicated Environment
- Cloud to Cloud
- Primary Region to Recovery Region
- Partner Network to Integration Gateway

# Site-to-Site VPN Architecture

```text
Customer or Remote Gateway

↓

Encrypted Tunnels

↓

MianX.ai VPN Gateway

↓

Customer-Specific Route Domain

↓

Approved Integration or Product Services
```

# VPN High Availability

Critical VPNs should use:

- Redundant Tunnels
- Redundant Gateways
- Multiple Provider Endpoints
- Dynamic Routing Where Appropriate
- Health Monitoring
- Automatic Failover Where Safe
- Documented Recovery

# VPN Routing

VPN routing should define:

- Local Prefixes
- Remote Prefixes

- Static or Dynamic Routing
- Route Filtering
- Priorities
- Failover
- Customer Isolation
- Overlap Handling

---

# VPN Encryption

VPN standards should define:

- Approved Protocols
- Approved Algorithms
- Key Exchange
- Certificate or Pre-Shared-Key Policy
- Rotation
- Perfect Forward Secrecy Where Supported
- Expiration
- Revocation

---

# VPN Customer Isolation

Each customer VPN should use:

- Separate Connection
- Separate Route Policy
- Separate Authentication Material
- Separate Monitoring
- Separate Ownership
- Separate Incident Handling
- Separate Cost Allocation Where Practical

Customer networks must not route to one another.

# Dedicated Connectivity

Dedicated Connectivity provides private or carrier-managed network links between MianX.ai cloud environments and:

- Enterprise Customers
- Data Centers
- Private Clouds
- Major Partners
- Secondary Cloud Providers
- Regional Facilities

Equivalent services may include:

- Dedicated Interconnect
- Express Connection
- Direct Connect
- Private Circuit
- Carrier Ethernet
- MPLS Integration

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Objectives

Dedicated Connectivity may provide:

- Predictable Bandwidth
- Lower Latency
- Greater Stability
- Private Routing
- Enterprise Integration
- Reduced Internet Dependency
- Regulatory Support
- Large Data Transfer
- Improved Hybrid Operations

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Adoption Criteria

Dedicated connectivity may be justified when:

- A major enterprise customer requires it
- Large data volumes move regularly
- Internet VPN performance is insufficient
- Low latency is critical
- Compliance requires private connectivity
- Hybrid applications require stable connectivity
- Multi-cloud workloads require predictable transfer
- Business continuity requires independent network paths

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Non-Justifications

Dedicated links should not be created when:

- VPN meets requirements
- Traffic volume is low
- Business demand is temporary
- Customer architecture is unstable
- Cost exceeds value
- Operational ownership is unclear
- Redundancy cannot be provided
- Contractual responsibility is undefined

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Architecture

```text
Customer or Data Center Network

↓

Primary Dedicated Circuit

+

Secondary Circuit or VPN Backup

↓

Provider Edge

↓

MianX.ai Connectivity Gateway

↓

Transit Network

↓

Customer Route Domain

↓

Approved Private Services
```

---

# Dedicated Link Redundancy

Critical dedicated connectivity should consider:

- Two Circuits
- Two Physical Paths
- Two Provider Locations
- Two Customer Routers
- Two Cloud Gateways
- VPN Backup
- Automatic or Controlled Failover
- Regular Failover Testing

Two circuits sharing one physical path do not provide true redundancy.

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Routing

Routing may use:

- Border Gateway Protocol
- Static Routing
- Provider-Managed Routing

Dynamic routing policy should define:

- Accepted Prefixes
- Advertised Prefixes
- Route Filters
- Route Priority
- Failover
- Default Route Policy
- Customer Isolation
- Monitoring

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Security

Security should include:

- Private Routing
- Route Filtering
- Encryption Where Required
- Firewall Inspection
- Customer-Specific Segmentation
- Strong Ownership
- Monitoring
- Contractual Security Responsibilities
- Incident Coordination
- Access Review

Private connectivity does not replace authentication or encryption requirements.

---

# Dedicated Connectivity Capacity

Capacity planning should define:

- Committed Bandwidth
- Peak Bandwidth
- Burst Capability
- Data Growth
- Product Growth
- Customer Growth
- Failover Capacity
- Backup Link Capacity
- Regional Demand
- Cost

# Hybrid Connectivity

Hybrid Connectivity joins cloud infrastructure with:

- On-Premises Systems
- Customer Data Centers
- Private Clouds
- Branch Locations
- Legacy Systems
- Specialized Industry Systems

Hybrid connectivity should remain application-aware and security-controlled.

---

# Hybrid Connectivity Principles

Hybrid architecture should follow:

- No Implicit Trust
- Minimal Routes
- Strong Identity
- Encryption
- Customer Isolation
- Application-Level Authorization
- Monitoring
- Failure Containment
- Data Governance
- Clear Ownership
- Documented Exit Strategy

---

# Hybrid Connectivity Models

## Application Integration Model

Cloud and on-premises systems communicate through controlled APIs or events.

This is generally preferred.

## Private Network Extension Model

Cloud and on-premises networks are connected through VPN or dedicated connectivity.

Use only when network-level integration is required.

## Data Replication Model

Approved data is synchronized between environments.

This requires strong data governance.

## Managed Gateway Model

A controlled integration gateway mediates communication.

This reduces direct exposure.

---

# Hybrid Risks

Major hybrid risks include:

- Flat Network Extension
- Shared Credentials
- Route Leakage
- Overlapping Addresses
- Weak Customer Security
- Legacy Protocols
- Unencrypted Traffic
- Slow Failure Detection
- Unclear Ownership
- Vendor Dependency
- Complex Recovery
- Data Residency Violations

- Incorrect Default Routes
- Public Data-Service Exposure

- Transit Hub Failure

- Private DNS Failure
- Unmonitored Private Endpoints
- Manual Configuration Drift
- Cross-Environment Routing

# Core Network Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| CN0 | Unstructured Connectivity | Shared networks, manual routes, weak ownership |
| CN1 | Standardized Private Network | Environment separation, standard subnets, basic routing |
| CN2 | Governed Core Network | Central IPAM, route governance, private connectivity, VPN controls |
| CN3 | Enterprise Transit Network | Hub-and-spoke, shared security, product and customer connectivity |
| CN4 | Regional Hybrid Network | Multi-region routing, dedicated connectivity, advanced automation |
| CN5 | Global Adaptive Core Network | Dynamic policy-driven connectivity across regions and providers |

---

# CN0 — Unstructured Connectivity

Characteristics:

- Flat networks
- Manual routes
- Shared administrator access
- Public services
- Unknown dependencies
- No central IP management
- Limited monitoring

Exit requirements:

- Network inventory
- Environment separation
- Private data services
- Standard subnet model
- Route ownership
- Flow logging
- Infrastructure as Code

---

# CN1 — Standardized Private Network

Characteristics:

- Production and non-production separated
- Standard subnet types
- Private applications and databases
- Approved ingress
- Basic VPN
- Standard route tables
- Initial IP plan

Exit requirements:

- Central IPAM
- Product segmentation
- Route governance
- Private endpoints
- Peering standards
- Customer VPN isolation
- Strong monitoring

---

# CN2 — Governed Core Network

Characteristics:

- Central IPAM
- Route control
- Private endpoints
- Controlled egress
- Formal VPN process
- Peering governance
- Network policies as code
- Customer connectivity standards

Exit requirements:

- Transit network
- Shared inspection
- Product spokes
- Dedicated connectivity
- Multi-product cost allocation
- Stronger recovery

---

# CN3 — Enterprise Transit Network

Characteristics:

- Hub-and-spoke or equivalent model
- Central routing
- Shared security
- Customer connectivity domains
- Dedicated enterprise links
- Shared DNS and monitoring
- Product isolation
- Transit route segmentation

Exit requirements:

- Multi-region connectivity
- Regional route policy
- Global network monitoring
- Regional recovery
- Hybrid and multi-cloud governance

---

# CN4 — Regional Hybrid Network

Characteristics:

- Several regions
- Regional transit
- Global connectivity
- Hybrid customer connections
- Dedicated links
- Regional failure testing
- Automated route validation
- Predictive capacity

Exit requirements:

- Dynamic global policy
- Automated low-risk routing
- Global cost optimization
- Adaptive customer connectivity
- Composable network blueprints

---

# CN5 — Global Adaptive Core Network

Characteristics:

- Global connectivity follows approved policy
- Routes consider region, identity, product, customer, risk, cost, and capacity
- Low-risk changes are automated
- High-risk changes remain human-approved
- New products consume reusable network blueprints
- Global connectivity remains observable and recoverable

# Part 14B-3B Exit Criteria

Part 14B-3B is complete when:

- Virtual Network standards are documented.
- Production and non-production networks are separated.
- Product, platform, customer, and regional network criteria are defined.
- Subnet categories and sizing rules are standardized.
- Availability-zone subnet patterns are defined.
- Central IP Address Management exists.
- Address overlap is automatically detected.
- Public IP usage is governed.
- Routing principles and route categories are documented.
- Route tables are version-controlled and reviewed.
- Route propagation is restricted and monitored.
- Transit Network adoption criteria are defined.
- Transit route domains and security requirements are documented.
- Network Peering has a controlled request and lifecycle process.
- Private Connectivity and Private Endpoint standards are defined.
- Private DNS requirements are documented.
- VPN types, encryption, routing, redundancy, and customer isolation are standardized.
- Dedicated Connectivity adoption, redundancy, monitoring, and vendor requirements are documented.
- Hybrid Connectivity follows minimal-trust patterns.
- Core network inventory, monitoring, ownership, risks, KPIs, and maturity levels are defined.
- Core network quality gates and recovery requirements are approved.
- The architecture is ready to progress into DNS, service discovery, load balancing, global traffic management, CDN, and edge architecture.

Core Network Infrastructure converts enterprise network principles into implementable connectivity foundations.

```text
Peering or Central Transit
```

```text
Virtual Networks

Subnets

Routing
Controls approved traffic movement

Route Tables
Define explicit network paths

Transit Network
Scales centralized enterprise connectivity

Network Peering
Provides direct private connectivity where justified

Private Connectivity
Keeps managed and internal services off the public internet

VPN
Provides encrypted remote and site connectivity

Dedicated Connectivity
Supports high-value enterprise and hybrid connections
```

MianX.ai Core Network Infrastructure must remain:

- Private by Default
- Non-Overlapping
- Explicitly Routed
- Segmented
- Highly Available
- Customer-Isolated
- Product-Aware
- Environment-Aware
- Region-Ready
- Encrypted
- Observable
- Recoverable
- Cost-Aware

- Policy-Governed
- Human-Accountable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to create connectivity.

The objective is to create the minimum approved connectivity required for each product, service, customer, environment, and region while preventing unnecessary trust and uncontrolled network expansion.

# Part 14B-3C-1 — DNS Architecture

DNS Architecture defines how MianX.ai names, discovers, resolves, routes, secures, monitors, governs, and manages domains and service records across public, internal, private, regional, product, tenant, customer, runtime, and disaster-recovery environments.

DNS is a foundational enterprise dependency.

Every major MianX.ai capability depends on reliable name resolution, including:

- Public Websites
- Web Applications
- APIs
- Mobile Applications
- MianX Core Platform
- AI Operating System
- AI Workforce
- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- Future Industry Operating Systems
- Internal Services
- Databases
- Caches
- Message Queues
- Container Platforms
- Kubernetes
- Serverless Workloads
- Developer Environments
- Customer Integrations
- Partner Integrations
- Private Endpoints
- Regional Infrastructure
- Disaster Recovery
- Monitoring and Security Systems

DNS converts human-readable and service-readable names into network destinations.

A DNS failure can make a healthy application appear completely unavailable.

A DNS misconfiguration can cause:

- Service Outages
- Incorrect Traffic Routing
- Customer Downtime
- Regional Failover Failure
- Certificate Failure
- Security Exposure
- Domain Hijacking
- Email Delivery Failure
- API Unavailability
- Private Endpoint Failure
- Customer Integration Failure
- Deployment Failure
- Disaster-Recovery Failure
- Internal Service Discovery Failure

DNS must therefore be treated as critical enterprise infrastructure rather than a simple domain-management task.

---

# DNS Architecture Statement

> **Build a secure, resilient, automated, observable, environment-aware, product-aware, region-aware, and policy-governed DNS architecture that reliably directs every approved MianX.ai name to the correct service while preventing unauthorized domain, zone, and record changes.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai DNS Architecture must support both public and private resolution.

Public DNS must support:

- Corporate Domains
- Product Domains
- Public Websites
- Public APIs
- Customer-Facing Applications
- Global Traffic Routing
- CDN
- Edge Security
- Email Security Records
- Certificate Validation
- Regional Failover
- Marketplace and Developer Services

Internal and Private DNS must support:

- Private Services
- Databases
- Caches
- Message Queues
- Internal APIs
- Kubernetes Services
- Private Endpoints
- Infrastructure Management
- Monitoring Systems
- Customer-Dedicated Environments
- Regional Private Networks
- Disaster-Recovery Systems

The preferred DNS evolution path is:

```text
Central Domain Ownership

↓

Managed Authoritative DNS

↓

Standard Public DNS Zones

↓

Environment and Product Subdomains

↓

Private DNS Zones

↓

Automated Record Management

↓

Global DNS and Health-Based Routing

↓

Regional DNS and Failover

↓

Policy-Governed Enterprise DNS
```

The objective is not to create an excessive number of domains and DNS zones.

The objective is to ensure that every DNS name is:

- Necessary
- Owned
- Secure
- Version-Controlled Where Practical
- Monitored
- Documented
- Environment-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Region-Aware
- Recoverable
- Revocable
- Lifecycle-Governed

---

# DNS Architecture Mission

The mission of DNS Architecture is to provide reliable and secure name resolution for every approved MianX.ai service, application, platform, environment, product, customer connection, and regional deployment.

DNS Architecture must ensure that:

- Public domains remain centrally governed.
- Production domains are protected.
- Internal services use private resolution.
- Private endpoints resolve correctly.
- DNS changes are auditable.
- DNS records are owned.
- DNS dependencies are visible.
- Expired and unused records are removed.
- Global traffic can fail over safely.
- DNS supports multiple regions.
- DNS supports multiple products.
- DNS supports customer-dedicated environments.
- DNS supports disaster recovery.
- DNS security controls are active.
- DNS is monitored as a critical service.
