# Part 14B-3C-3A — CDN & Edge Infrastructure

CDN and Edge Infrastructure define how MianX.ai distributes digital content, accelerates user requests, reduces origin load, improves global performance, manages cache behavior, routes traffic through geographically distributed edge locations, and supports reliable delivery across products, regions, customers, applications, APIs, and enterprise environments.

The edge is the first infrastructure layer that many users and external systems interact with.

It may serve:

- Corporate Websites
- Product Websites
- Web Applications
- Mobile Application Assets
- Public APIs
- Developer Documentation
- Marketplace Content
- Images
- Videos
- Fonts
- JavaScript Bundles
- Stylesheets
- Downloadable Files
- Software Packages
- Public Reports
- Product Documentation
- Customer Portals
- Regional Product Experiences
- Static Industry Content
- Selected Dynamic Responses

The edge should improve performance without weakening:

- Security
- Privacy
- Authorization
- Data Residency
- Cache Correctness
- Tenant Isolation
- Product Boundaries
- Content Integrity
- Operational Control
- Customer Trust

CDN and Edge Infrastructure are not merely mechanisms for caching files.

They form a globally distributed delivery layer that can influence:

- Traffic Routing
- Availability
- Latency
- Origin Capacity
- Release Safety
- Regional Operations
- Customer Experience
- Infrastructure Cost
- Security Exposure
- Incident Response

---

# CDN & Edge Infrastructure Statement

> **Build a secure, globally distributed, cache-aware, observable, resilient, and policy-governed edge delivery platform that accelerates approved MianX.ai content and traffic while preserving correctness, privacy, tenant boundaries, and origin control.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai should use CDN and edge infrastructure to reduce the distance between users and approved content.

The edge should handle appropriate workloads before traffic reaches the origin infrastructure.

Suitable edge capabilities may include:

- Static Asset Caching
- Image Delivery
- Document Delivery
- Frontend Bundle Delivery
- DNS Integration
- TLS Termination
- Global Traffic Entry
- Cache-Control Enforcement
- Origin Shielding
- Compression
- Protocol Optimization
- Limited Request Transformation
- Regional Routing
- Health-Based Origin Selection
- Controlled Edge Storage

The edge should not become an uncontrolled location for:

- Sensitive Business Logic
- Permanent Application State
- Unbounded Customer Data
- Private Secrets
- Unsupported Authorization Decisions
- Unreviewed AI Processing
- Irreversible Transactions
- Hidden Product Logic
- Untraceable Customer-Specific Behavior

The preferred evolution path is:

```text
Direct Origin Delivery

↓

Managed CDN for Static Assets

↓

Standard Cache Policies

↓

Origin Protection and Shielding

↓

Multi-Product Edge Delivery

↓

Regional Edge Routing

↓

Controlled Dynamic Acceleration

↓

Governed Edge Computing and Storage

↓

Global Adaptive Edge Platform
```

The initial objective should be simple:

- Deliver static assets quickly
- Reduce origin traffic
- Improve availability
- Centralize TLS
- Provide clear cache behavior
- Maintain easy invalidation
- Preserve content correctness
- Prevent sensitive data caching

Advanced edge behavior should be added only when measurable requirements justify the complexity.

---

The mission of the Content Delivery Network is to deliver approved MianX.ai content through geographically distributed infrastructure with lower latency, higher availability, reduced origin demand, and controlled caching behavior.

The CDN must:

- Serve public static content

- Reduce repeated origin requests
- Improve global delivery speed
- Support high traffic
- Protect origin capacity
- Support versioned assets

- Support regional delivery
- Integrate with DNS
- Integrate with load balancing
- Integrate with edge security
- Maintain cache correctness
- Support rapid invalidation
- Provide traffic visibility
- Support cost governance
- Maintain reliable fallback to origin

# CDN Objectives

The CDN should:

- Reduce content latency

- Reduce origin request volume
- Improve static asset availability
- Support global users
- Support regional users
- Support product-specific content
- Support customer-facing applications
- Improve release performance

- Session Tokens

# CDN Architecture

CDN Architecture defines how users, edge locations, cache layers, origin systems, storage services, applications, and regional infrastructure interact.

---

# CDN Reference Architecture

```text
User or External Client

↓

Global DNS

↓

Nearest or Policy-Selected Edge Location

↓

Edge Request Processing

↓

Cache Lookup

├── Cache Hit
│   ↓
│   Response Served From Edge
│
└── Cache Miss
    ↓
    Regional Edge or Origin Shield
    ↓
    Origin Load Balancer
    ↓
    Application or Storage Origin
    ↓
    Response Returned and Cached Where Allowed
```

---

# CDN Architecture Layers

## Layer 1 — DNS and Global Entry

This layer selects the approved CDN or edge endpoint.

Responsibilities include:

- Domain Resolution
- CDN Endpoint Selection
- Regional Entry
- Failover
- Custom Domain Mapping
- Certificate Alignment

---

## Layer 2 — Edge Point of Presence

The nearest or policy-selected edge location receives the request.

Responsibilities may include:

- TLS Termination
- Protocol Negotiation
- Cache Lookup
- Compression
- Basic Request Normalization
- Static Response Delivery
- Edge Security Integration
- Logging

---

## Layer 3 — Regional Cache

A regional cache may aggregate requests from several edge locations.

Responsibilities include:

- Increased Cache Efficiency
- Reduced Origin Requests
- Regional Content Retention
- Large Asset Distribution
- Origin Protection

---

## Layer 4 — Origin Shield

An Origin Shield provides an additional centralized caching layer before the origin.

Responsibilities include:

- Request Collapsing
- Reduced Origin Load
- Better Cache Hit Ratio
- Controlled Origin Access
- Reduced Multi-Edge Origin Duplication

---

## Layer 5 — Origin

The origin may be:

- Object Storage
- Web Application
- API
- Managed Application Runtime
- Kubernetes Ingress
- Load Balancer
- Static Site Platform
- Media Service
- Package Registry
- Document Service

---

## Layer 6 — Management and Governance

This layer provides:

- Configuration
- Cache Policies
- Invalidation
- Logging
- Metrics
- Access Control
- Cost
- Security
- Audit
- Incident Response
- Lifecycle Management

---

# CDN Origin Types

CDN origins may include:

- Public Object Storage
- Private Object Storage
- Static Site Hosting
- Regional Load Balancer
- Application Gateway
- API Gateway
- Managed Application Platform
- Kubernetes Ingress
- Media Platform
- Document Service
- Software Package Repository

Private origins should be preferred where supported.

---

# Private Origin Architecture

A private origin should accept traffic only from approved CDN or edge infrastructure.

The model should follow:

```text
Public User

↓

CDN Edge

↓

Authenticated or Restricted Origin Connection

↓

Private Origin
```

The origin should not accept unrestricted public bypass traffic.

---

# Origin Authentication

The edge may authenticate to the origin using:

- Signed Requests
- Origin Access Identity
- Workload Identity
- Mutual TLS
- Private Connectivity
- Restricted Source Network
- Secret Header Where Stronger Methods Are Unavailable

Static shared headers should not be treated as the strongest security control.

---

# Multiple Origins

A CDN distribution may use multiple origins for:

- Static Assets
- Web Application
- API
- Media
- Downloads
- Product-Specific Content
- Regional Content
- Error Pages

Routing should define:

- Path
- Host
- Origin
- Cache Policy
- Security Policy
- Failure Behavior
- Owner

---

# Multi-Product CDN Architecture

A multi-product architecture may use:

```text
Corporate CDN Distribution

RestaurantOS CDN Distribution

PoultryOS CDN Distribution

Marketplace CDN Distribution

Developer Platform CDN Distribution
```

or a shared edge platform with product-aware routing.

The decision should consider:

- Product Isolation
- Ownership
- Certificates
- Release Independence
- Traffic Volume
- Cache Policy
- Customer Contracts
- Cost

---

# Shared CDN Distribution

A shared CDN may reduce:

- Configuration Duplication
- Certificate Management
- Provider Cost
- Operational Burden

However, it may increase:

- Blast Radius
- Routing Complexity
- Policy Coupling
- Product Dependency
- Change Risk

---

# Dedicated CDN Distribution

Dedicated distributions may provide:

- Stronger Product Isolation
- Separate Ownership
- Separate Metrics
- Separate Release Control
- Separate Security Policies
- Separate Cost Allocation

They may also increase operational overhead.

---

# Regional CDN Architecture

Regional content delivery may be used when:

- Data Residency Requires It
- Product Availability Differs by Region
- Regional Origin Performance Is Important
- Customer Contracts Require Local Delivery
- Content Rights Differ by Region
- Regulatory Requirements Apply

Regional CDN behavior should not violate central governance.

---

# CDN High Availability

The CDN should use provider-managed global infrastructure where practical.

High availability should consider:

- Distributed Edge Locations
- Regional Cache Redundancy
- Multiple Origin Instances
- Origin Failover
- DNS Resilience
- Certificate Availability
- Configuration Recovery
- Provider Incident Response

---

# CDN Failover

CDN failover may occur between:

- Primary and Secondary Origin
- Region A and Region B
- Static Storage and Application Origin
- Current and Previous Release
- Primary CDN and Secondary Delivery Path

Failover should define:

- Trigger
- Health Signal
- Secondary Readiness
- Cache Behavior
- Data Currency
- Customer Impact
- Monitoring
- Return to Primary
- Human Approval Where Required

---

# CDN Provider Strategy

A CDN provider should be evaluated against:

- Global Coverage
- Edge Locations
- Reliability
- Security
- Caching Features
- Invalidation
- Origin Shielding
- Protocol Support
- Image Optimization
- Logging
- Real-Time Metrics
- API
- Infrastructure as Code
- Regional Controls
- Private Origin Support
- Cost
- Support
- Vendor Stability
- Exit Strategy

---

# Multi-CDN Strategy

A Multi-CDN strategy uses more than one CDN provider.

It may be justified when:

- Traffic Volume Is Extremely High
- Global Availability Requirements Are Exceptional
- Provider Concentration Risk Is Unacceptable
- Regional Coverage Differs Significantly
- Customer Contracts Require It
- Media Delivery Requires Provider Diversity

Multi-CDN adds:

- Configuration Synchronization
- Cache Policy Differences
- DNS Complexity
- Log Aggregation Complexity
- Security Policy Duplication
- Cost
- Operational Burden
- Failover Testing Requirements

It should not be adopted prematurely.

---

# CDN Philosophy

CDN Philosophy defines the beliefs guiding how MianX.ai uses distributed content delivery.

---

# CDN Philosophy Statement

> **Cache only what is safe, serve only what is valid, keep origins protected, and make every edge response traceable to an approved source and policy.**

---

# Cache Correctness Before Cache Hit Ratio

A high cache-hit ratio is valuable only when responses are correct.

Incorrect caching may cause:

- User Data Leakage
- Tenant Data Leakage
- Stale Application Behavior
- Incorrect Pricing
- Outdated Permissions
- Old Releases
- Broken Authentication
- Customer Trust Damage

Correctness must remain more important than maximizing caching.

---

# Public Content by Default, Private Content by Exception

The CDN should primarily serve public or safely cacheable content.

Private content should require:

- Clear Authentication
- Authorization
- Cache-Key Design
- Privacy Review
- Tenant Isolation
- Expiration
- Purge Capability
- Logging
- Incident Response

---

# Versioned Assets Over Mutable Assets

Static assets should use versioned names or content hashes.

Example:

```text
app.8f31d2.js

logo.v3.svg

styles.1.4.0.css
```

This allows:

- Long Cache Lifetimes
- Safe Releases
- Simple Rollback
- Reduced Invalidation
- Better Cache Efficiency

---

# Origin Protection

The CDN should shield origins from:

- Repeated Requests
- Traffic Spikes
- Unnecessary Global Connections
- Large Asset Delivery
- Basic Abuse
- Redundant Cache Misses

Origin protection should not depend only on caching.

---

# Explicit Cacheability

Applications should explicitly define whether responses are cacheable.

Cache behavior should not rely on accidental defaults.

---

# Minimum Edge Logic

Edge logic should remain minimal, deterministic, observable, and reversible.

Complex business logic should normally remain in governed application services.

---

# Consistent Policies Across Products

Products may have different content, but they should consume shared edge standards for:

- TLS
- Cache Headers
- Asset Versioning
- Invalidation
- Origin Access
- Logging
- Error Handling
- Security
- Cost Allocation

---

# Edge Resilience

The edge should continue serving safe cached content during temporary origin degradation where appropriate.

It must not hide severe origin failures indefinitely.

---

# CDN Principles

The following principles are mandatory.

---

## 1. Managed CDN by Default

Use an approved managed CDN rather than self-hosting global delivery infrastructure.

---

## 2. Private Origins Where Practical

Origins should avoid unrestricted public access.

---

## 3. Cache Only Explicitly Approved Content

Cache behavior should be defined through policy.

---

## 4. Never Cache Sensitive Responses by Default

Sensitive responses should use restrictive cache directives.

---

## 5. Version Static Assets

Use immutable asset names or content hashes.

---

## 6. Long TTL for Immutable Assets

Versioned immutable content may use long cache lifetimes.

---

## 7. Shorter TTL for Mutable Content

Content that changes without a new URL should use controlled shorter lifetimes.

---

## 8. Use Cache-Control Headers

Applications should communicate cache intent explicitly.

---

## 9. Minimize Cache-Key Variation

Cache keys should vary only on fields that materially change the response.

---

## 10. Protect Tenant Boundaries

Tenant-specific responses must never share an unsafe cache entry.

---

## 11. Separate Environments

Development, staging, and production edge configurations must remain separated.

---

## 12. Separate Public and Private Content

Public delivery and restricted delivery should use clearly governed patterns.

---

## 13. Use Compression

Eligible content should use approved compression.

---

## 14. Prefer Modern Protocols

The edge should support modern secure delivery protocols where available.

---

## 15. Automate Configuration

CDN distributions and policies should be managed through code where practical.

---

## 16. Monitor Cache Behavior

Cache hits, misses, bypasses, errors, and invalidations must be observable.

---

## 17. Control Invalidation

Invalidation must be authorized, scoped, logged, and cost-aware.

---

## 18. Preserve Origin Traceability

Every edge route should identify its approved origin.

---

## 19. Do Not Trust Client Cache Headers Blindly

Cache decisions must follow controlled server and edge policies.

---

## 20. Human Approval for High-Risk Global Changes

Global distribution, origin replacement, apex routing, broad invalidation, and emergency edge changes should require authorized approval.

---

# Edge Infrastructure

Edge Infrastructure is the geographically distributed runtime and delivery layer between external consumers and central or regional origin infrastructure.

It may provide:

- CDN
- TLS
- Global Entry
- Static Caching
- Dynamic Acceleration
- Request Routing
- Edge Security
- Edge Functions
- Regional Content Delivery
- Limited Edge Storage
- Request and Response Transformation
- Traffic Observability

---

# Edge Infrastructure Objectives

Edge Infrastructure should:

- Reduce latency
- Reduce origin load
- Improve availability
- Support global traffic
- Support product routing
- Support regional routing
- Support edge security
- Support cache control
- Support controlled edge processing
- Improve user experience
- Reduce bandwidth cost
- Support traffic spikes
- Maintain observability
- Support emergency controls
- Preserve content integrity

---

# Edge Infrastructure Model

```text
Global User

↓

Nearest Approved Edge Location

↓

TLS and Request Processing

↓

Security and Routing Policy

↓

Cache or Edge Logic

↓

Regional or Central Origin

↓

Response Processing

↓

User
```

---

# Edge Infrastructure Components

Potential components include:

- Edge DNS
- CDN Cache
- Edge Proxy
- Edge Load Balancer
- WAF
- DDoS Protection
- Bot Management
- Rate Limiting
- Edge Function Runtime
- Edge Storage
- Image Optimization
- Certificate Service
- Traffic Logs
- Edge Analytics
- Origin Shield

---

# Edge Control Plane

The control plane manages:

- Distributions
- Domains
- Origins
- Cache Policies
- Edge Functions
- Certificates
- Security Policies
- Routing Rules
- Invalidations
- Logging
- Access
- Releases

The control plane is a high-risk administrative surface.

---

# Edge Data Plane

The data plane handles live traffic.

It performs:

- TLS
- Request Receipt
- Cache Lookup
- Routing
- Security Enforcement
- Response Delivery
- Metrics
- Logging

---

# Edge Provider Access

Administrative access should use:

- Enterprise Identity
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Named Accounts
- Least Privilege
- Service Identities
- Audit
- Access Review
- Emergency Access
- Rapid Revocation

---

# Edge Configuration Management

Edge configuration should be:

- Version-Controlled
- Reviewed
- Tested
- Environment-Specific
- Product-Aware
- Reversible
- Audited
- Documented

---

# Edge Deployment

Edge configuration deployment should support:

- Preview
- Validation
- Staging
- Controlled Production Release
- Global Propagation Monitoring
- Rollback
- Evidence

---

# Edge Configuration Propagation

Global configuration may take time to propagate.

The deployment process should define:

- Expected Propagation Time
- Partial Propagation Behavior
- Validation Regions
- Rollback Behavior
- Monitoring
- Incident Threshold

---

# Edge Network

The Edge Network is the distributed network of provider infrastructure used to receive and serve traffic near users.

It may include:

- Points of Presence
- Regional Edge Caches
- Backbone Connections
- Anycast Networks
- Peering
- Internet Exchange Connectivity
- Private Origin Connectivity
- Global Control Systems

---

# Edge Network Objectives

The Edge Network should:

- Reduce network distance
- Reduce latency
- Improve throughput
- Avoid congested routes where possible
- Protect origin networks
- Support global availability
- Support region-aware delivery
- Support edge security
- Provide stable public entry
- Maintain global monitoring

---

# Edge Network Routing

Edge selection may consider:

- DNS
- Anycast
- User Location
- Network Topology
- Latency
- Edge Health
- Product Availability
- Regional Policy
- Data Residency
- Provider Capacity

---

# Anycast Edge

Anycast allows several edge locations to advertise the same network address.

Benefits may include:

- Nearest-Path Routing
- Global Resilience
- Simplified Entry
- Faster Failover

Risks include:

- Route Instability
- Provider Dependency
- Difficult Troubleshooting
- Internet Routing Variation

---

# Edge Backbone

Some providers route traffic across private global backbones after entry.

This may improve:

- Latency
- Reliability
- Cross-Region Performance
- Congestion Avoidance

Architecture should understand where traffic leaves the public internet and where data travels.

---

# Origin Connectivity

The edge may connect to origins through:

- Public TLS
- Private Backbone
- Private Link
- Restricted Source Addresses
- Mutual TLS
- Provider-Origin Authentication
- Regional Gateway

---

# Edge Network Availability

Availability should consider:

- Edge POP Failure
- Regional Edge Failure
- Provider Backbone Failure
- DNS Failure
- Certificate Failure
- Origin Failure
- Routing Failure
- Control-Plane Failure

---

# Edge POPs

A Point of Presence is a geographic edge location where user traffic can enter the provider network and cached content may be served.

---

# POP Responsibilities

A POP may perform:

- TLS Termination
- Cache Lookup
- Static Delivery
- Compression
- Request Filtering
- Basic Routing
- Edge Function Execution
- Rate Limiting
- Logging
- Security Checks

---

# POP Selection

POP selection may depend on:

- Network Proximity
- Provider Routing
- Geographic Location
- POP Health
- Capacity
- Product Policy
- Data Policy
- Customer Network

---

# POP Cache Behavior

A POP may:

- Serve Local Cache
- Forward to Regional Cache
- Forward to Origin Shield
- Forward to Origin
- Bypass Cache
- Store Response
- Revalidate Cached Response

---

# POP Failure

If one POP fails, traffic should move to another suitable location.

The architecture should define:

- Detection
- Provider Behavior
- User Impact
- Monitoring
- Regional Fallback
- Incident Escalation

---

# POP Monitoring

Monitor where available:

- POP Request Volume
- Cache Hit Ratio
- Latency
- Error Rate
- Origin Fetch Rate
- Security Events
- Capacity
- Geographic Distribution
- Provider Incident

---

# Edge Regions

Edge Regions group edge locations or regional cache infrastructure serving larger geographic areas.

They may provide:

- Regional Cache
- Origin Shield
- Regional Security Processing
- Regional Logs
- Regional Edge Functions
- Regional Content Controls

---

# Edge Region Selection

Edge regions should align with:

- Customer Distribution
- Product Markets
- Data Residency
- Origin Regions
- Provider Coverage
- Latency
- Cost
- Regional Regulations
- Disaster Recovery

---

# Edge Region and Origin Alignment

An edge region may prefer a matching origin region.

Example:

```text
European Edge Traffic

↓

European Regional Cache

↓

European Origin
```

This may reduce latency and support data controls.

---

# Regional Edge Isolation

Regional edge policies may differ for:

- Data Residency
- Content Availability
- Legal Restrictions
- Product Availability
- Customer Contracts
- Security Policy
- Language
- Localization

Differences should remain centrally governed.

---

# Edge Routing

Edge Routing determines which origin, region, product, release, or cache behavior applies to an incoming request.

---

# Edge Routing Inputs

Routing may use:

- Host
- Path
- Method
- Header
- Cookie
- Geography
- Region
- Product
- Tenant
- Customer Domain
- Release Cohort
- Origin Health
- Capacity
- Security Policy

---

# Host-Based Edge Routing

Examples:

```text
www.mianx.ai
Corporate Website

app.mianx.ai
Platform Application

restaurant.mianx.ai
RestaurantOS

poultry.mianx.ai
PoultryOS

cdn.mianx.ai
Shared Assets
```

---

# Path-Based Edge Routing

Examples:

```text
/assets/*
Static Assets

/docs/*
Documentation

/api/*
API Gateway

/downloads/*
File Distribution
```

---

# Product-Aware Edge Routing

Product routes should identify:

- Product Owner
- Origin
- Cache Policy
- Security Policy
- Certificate
- Region
- Logging
- Cost

---

# Tenant-Aware Edge Routing

Tenant-aware routing may be used for:

- Custom Domains
- Dedicated Origins
- Home Regions
- Enterprise Contracts
- Branded Portals

Trusted tenant identity must be established safely.

---

# Region-Aware Edge Routing

Regional routing may consider:

- User Location
- Tenant Region
- Data Residency
- Product Availability
- Origin Health
- Capacity
- Maintenance
- Cost

---

# Release-Aware Edge Routing

Edge routing may support:

- Blue-Green Release
- Canary Release
- Weighted Release
- Regional Release
- Customer Pilot
- Internal Preview

Release routing must remain reversible.

---

# Edge Route Record

Every significant route should define:

- Route ID
- Domain
- Path
- Product
- Environment
- Origin
- Cache Policy
- Security Policy
- Region
- Owner
- Priority
- Version
- Monitoring
- Rollback
- Review Date

---

# Caching Strategy

Caching Strategy defines which responses may be stored, where they may be stored, how long they may remain valid, how they are revalidated, and how they are invalidated.

---

# Caching Strategy Statement

> **Cache content only when response reuse is safe, correct, measurable, and governed.**

---

# Cache Categories

Content may be classified as:

- Immutable Public Content
- Mutable Public Content
- Public Dynamic Content
- Authenticated Cacheable Content
- Tenant-Specific Content
- Private Non-Cacheable Content
- Sensitive Non-Cacheable Content
- Temporary Content
- Regional Content

---

# Immutable Public Content

Examples:

- Versioned JavaScript
- Versioned CSS
- Versioned Images
- Fonts
- Product Assets
- Versioned Downloads

Recommended behavior:

- Long TTL
- Immutable Directive
- Content-Hash Naming
- No Routine Invalidation

---

# Mutable Public Content

Examples:

- Corporate Home Page
- Product Landing Pages
- Documentation Index
- Public Announcements

Recommended behavior:

- Controlled Moderate TTL
- Revalidation
- Targeted Invalidation
- Version Awareness

---

# Public Dynamic Content

Examples:

- Public Catalog
- Public Pricing Summary
- Public Product Metadata

Caching may be allowed if:

- Data Is Public
- Freshness Rules Are Clear
- Cache Key Is Safe
- Invalidation Is Reliable
- Incorrect Staleness Has Low Risk

---

# Authenticated Content

Authenticated content should not be cached by shared edge infrastructure unless explicitly designed.

Required review includes:

- Cache Key
- Authorization
- User Scope
- Tenant Scope
- Privacy
- Token Handling
- Response Headers
- Purge
- Incident Response

---

# Tenant-Specific Content

Tenant-specific edge caching may use:

- Dedicated Domain
- Trusted Tenant Key
- Separate Cache Namespace
- Private CDN
- Signed URL
- Signed Cookie

The cache key must prevent cross-tenant reuse.

---

# Non-Cacheable Content

Responses should generally remain non-cacheable when they contain:

- Authentication State
- Authorization Results
- Personal Data
- Tenant-Confidential Data
- Financial Transactions
- Payment Data
- Administrative Information
- Security Events
- Private Reports
- Dynamic User-Specific Data
- Sensitive AI Output

---

# Cache-Control Headers

Applications should use suitable directives such as:

- `public`
- `private`
- `no-store`
- `no-cache`
- `max-age`
- `s-maxage`
- `must-revalidate`
- `immutable`
- `stale-while-revalidate`
- `stale-if-error`

Headers should follow approved standards.

---

# Browser Cache Versus Shared Cache

Caching policy should distinguish:

- Browser Cache
- CDN Shared Cache
- Regional Cache
- Origin Shield

A response may be private to a browser but unsuitable for a shared CDN.

---

# Cache TTL

TTL should reflect:

- Content Mutability
- Business Freshness
- Release Frequency
- Security Risk
- Invalidation Reliability
- Origin Capacity
- User Experience
- Cost

---

# Suggested Cache Classes

| Cache Class | Typical Use | TTL Direction |
|---|---|---|
| C0 | Sensitive or private | No shared caching |
| C1 | Highly dynamic public | Very short |
| C2 | Mutable public content | Short to moderate |
| C3 | Stable public content | Moderate to long |
| C4 | Versioned immutable asset | Very long |
| C5 | Archive or fixed release | Very long |

Exact values should be defined by product policy.

---

# Cache Key

The cache key determines which requests share one cached response.

It may include:

- Host
- Path
- Query Parameters
- Selected Headers
- Selected Cookies
- Language
- Region
- Product
- Tenant Where Safe
- Device Category Where Necessary
- Content Version

---

# Cache-Key Principles

The cache key should:

- Include every value that materially changes the response.
- Exclude irrelevant variation.
- Avoid secret values.
- Avoid full authorization tokens.
- Avoid unnecessary cookies.
- Protect tenant boundaries.
- Remain documented.
- Be tested.

---

# Query Parameter Caching

Query parameters should be classified as:

- Cache-Relevant
- Ignored
- Tracking-Only
- Security-Sensitive
- Unsupported

Uncontrolled query variation can destroy cache efficiency.

---

# Header-Based Caching

Headers may vary cache content by:

- Language
- Content Type
- API Version
- Compression
- Region

Headers should not be included without need because they increase cache fragmentation.

---

# Cookie-Based Caching

Cookies should normally disable shared caching unless a controlled design exists.

Analytics or irrelevant cookies should be excluded from cache-key decisions where safe.

---

# Cache Revalidation

Revalidation may use:

- ETag
- Last-Modified
- Conditional Requests
- Origin Validation
- Background Refresh

Revalidation reduces full content transfer while preserving freshness.

---

# ETag Strategy

ETags should:

- Represent Content Version
- Remain Stable for Identical Content
- Support Conditional Requests
- Avoid Leaking Sensitive Internal Information

---

# Stale-While-Revalidate

This policy may serve slightly stale content while refreshing in the background.

Suitable for:

- Public Documentation
- Product Pages
- Non-Critical Public Data

It should not be used when freshness is essential.

---

# Stale-If-Error

This policy may serve stale content during temporary origin failure.

Suitable for:

- Static Public Pages
- Documentation
- Non-Sensitive Product Content
- Public Assets

It should define:

- Maximum Stale Duration
- Origin Failure Conditions
- Customer Impact
- Monitoring

---

# Cache Hierarchy

A cache hierarchy may include:

```text
Browser Cache

↓

Edge POP Cache

↓

Regional Cache

↓

Origin Shield

↓

Origin
```

Each layer should have a clear policy.

---

# Cache Warming

Cache warming may preload:

- Critical Assets
- Product Home Pages
- Major Documentation
- Release Bundles
- Regional Content

Cache warming should not create uncontrolled origin load.

---

# Request Collapsing

When several edge requests miss the cache simultaneously, the CDN may combine them into one origin request.

This protects against:

- Traffic Spikes
- Cache Stampede
- Large Release Demand
- Popular File Demand

---

# Cache Stampede Protection

Controls may include:

- Request Collapsing
- Locking
- Stale Serving
- Background Refresh
- Origin Shield
- Randomized TTL
- Pre-Warming

---

# Negative Caching

Negative responses such as `404` may be cached briefly.

Risks include:

- Hiding Newly Created Content
- Delaying Recovery
- Incorrect Long-Lived Error Responses

Negative-cache TTL should remain controlled.

---

# Error Caching

Selected error pages may be cached to reduce origin pressure.

Do not cache sensitive or transient errors too aggressively.

---

# Cache Bypass

Cache bypass may be required for:

- Authenticated Requests
- Administrative Paths
- Debugging
- Security Events
- Real-Time Data
- Payment Flows
- Webhooks
- Dynamic Writes
- Personalized Content

Bypass rules should be explicit.

---

# Caching Strategy Quality Gates

- [ ] Content classification is defined
- [ ] Cacheability is explicit
- [ ] Sensitive content is excluded
- [ ] Tenant isolation is tested
- [ ] Cache key is documented
- [ ] TTL is approved
- [ ] Revalidation is defined
- [ ] Invalidation is available
- [ ] Origin failure behavior is defined
- [ ] Cache metrics are active
- [ ] Cost impact is understood
- [ ] Security review is complete
- [ ] Rollback is available

---

# Cache Invalidation

Cache Invalidation removes or refreshes cached content before its normal expiration.

Invalidation is operationally powerful and potentially disruptive.

---

# Cache Invalidation Statement

> **Use versioned content to avoid broad invalidation, and invalidate only the smallest necessary scope when content must change immediately.**

---

# Invalidation Use Cases

Invalidation may be required for:

- Security Fix
- Incorrect Content
- Legal Removal
- Broken Asset
- Product Release
- Emergency Update
- Customer Branding Change
- Documentation Correction
- Revoked Download
- Incorrect Redirect

---

# Invalidation Types

## URL Invalidation

Removes one exact object.

## Path Invalidation

Removes a path or prefix.

## Tag-Based Invalidation

Removes objects associated with a cache tag.

## Product Invalidation

Removes product-specific cache entries.

## Regional Invalidation

Removes entries in selected regions where supported.

## Full Distribution Invalidation

Removes all cached content.

This should remain exceptional.

---

# Targeted Invalidation

Targeted invalidation should be preferred because it reduces:

- Origin Load
- Cost
- Customer Disruption
- Cache Refill Time
- Global Risk

---

# Full Purge Risk

A global purge may cause:

- Origin Traffic Spike
- Higher Latency
- Increased Cost
- Availability Risk
- Cache Stampede
- Product-Wide Impact

It should require elevated approval.

---

# Versioning as Invalidation Avoidance

Versioned assets should use a new URL instead of purging the old one.

Example:

```text
/app.1.0.0.js

/app.1.0.1.js
```

---

# Invalidation Workflow

```text
Invalidation Need

↓

Content and Impact Classification

↓

Scope Selection

↓

Origin Capacity Review

↓

Security and Product Approval

↓

Invalidation Execution

↓

Global Propagation Monitoring

↓

Content Validation

↓

Origin Load Monitoring

↓

Closure
```

---

# Invalidation Record

Every significant invalidation should define:

- Invalidation ID
- Reason
- Product
- Environment
- Distribution
- Paths or Tags
- Owner
- Approver
- Execution Time
- Expected Propagation
- Origin Capacity Impact
- Result
- Related Incident
- Evidence

---

# Emergency Invalidation

Emergency invalidation may be used for:

- Leaked Sensitive Content
- Malicious File
- Security Vulnerability
- Legal Requirement
- Incorrect Critical Product Behavior

The emergency process should preserve auditability.

---

# Invalidation Permissions

Permissions should distinguish:

- View Cache
- Purge Non-Production
- Purge Specific Production Object
- Purge Product Scope
- Purge Global Distribution
- Emergency Purge

---

# Automated Invalidation

Automation may invalidate:

- Changed Mutable Pages
- Updated Product Metadata
- Removed Documents
- Changed Redirects
- Customer Branding Assets

Automation should remain bounded and testable.

---

# Invalidation Monitoring

Monitor:

- Invalidation Status
- Propagation Time
- Failure
- Origin Request Spike
- Cache Hit Reduction
- Customer Errors
- Cost
- Unauthorized Requests

---

# Static Asset Delivery

Static Asset Delivery defines how immutable or infrequently changing files are built, stored, versioned, published, cached, secured, and retired.

---

# Static Asset Types

Static assets may include:

- JavaScript
- CSS
- Images
- Icons
- Fonts
- Documents
- Videos
- Audio
- Product Screenshots
- Illustration Files
- Public Downloads
- Application Manifests
- Source Maps Where Approved
- Localization Files

---

# Static Asset Delivery Model

```text
Source Repository

↓

Build Pipeline

↓

Asset Validation

↓

Versioning or Content Hashing

↓

Object Storage or Static Origin

↓

CDN Distribution

↓

Browser Cache

↓

User
```

---

# Asset Naming

Assets should use:

- Content Hash
- Semantic Version
- Release Version
- Stable Logical Name Plus Version

Example:

```text
main.8f91c7.js

brand-logo.v4.svg

guide.2.3.0.pdf
```

---

# Asset Immutability

An immutable asset URL should always return the same content.

Do not replace the content behind a versioned or hashed URL.

---

# Asset Storage

Static assets should be stored in:

- Approved Object Storage
- Static Site Platform
- Media Platform
- Package Repository
- Document Platform

Storage should define:

- Owner
- Region
- Access
- Encryption
- Retention
- Versioning
- Backup
- Lifecycle
- Cost

---

# Public Asset Access

Public assets may be directly readable through the CDN.

The origin should preferably remain restricted to the CDN.

---

# Private Asset Delivery

Private assets may require:

- Signed URL
- Signed Cookie
- Temporary Token
- Authenticated CDN
- Private Distribution
- Access Gateway

Private asset URLs should be:

- Time-Bound
- Scope-Bound
- Revocable Where Possible
- Logged
- Tenant-Aware

---

# Signed URLs

Signed URLs may grant temporary access to:

- Private File
- Customer Document
- Paid Download
- Export
- Restricted Media

They should define:

- Resource
- Expiration
- Consumer
- Tenant
- Permissions
- Signature
- Logging

---

# Asset Compression

Text-based assets should use suitable compression such as:

- Brotli
- Gzip

Compression should be selected based on client support and performance.

---

# Image Optimization

Image delivery may support:

- Resizing
- Format Conversion
- Quality Optimization
- Responsive Variants
- Lazy Loading
- Device-Aware Selection

Image processing should preserve:

- Brand Quality
- Accessibility
- Metadata Policy
- Privacy
- Cost Control

---

# Font Delivery

Fonts should define:

- License
- Format
- CORS
- Cache Policy
- Version
- Subset Strategy
- Performance
- Fallback

---

# Source Maps

Source maps may aid debugging but can expose source details.

Production source-map access should be:

- Restricted
- Uploaded to Approved Error Monitoring
- Excluded From Public Delivery Where Appropriate
- Versioned
- Retention-Controlled

---

# Static Error Pages

The edge should support static error pages for:

- Origin Unavailable
- Maintenance
- Regional Failure
- Access Denied
- Rate Limit
- Service Temporarily Unavailable

Error pages should:

- Avoid Sensitive Details
- Preserve Brand
- Provide Useful Guidance
- Include Correlation Information Where Safe
- Support Localization

```text
Build

↓

Validation

↓

↓

↓

CDN Availability

↓

Application Reference Update

↓

Traffic Validation

↓
```

# Asset Rollback

Rollback should restore application references to a previous approved asset set.

Old immutable assets should remain available for the supported rollback period.

- Deprecated Assets
- Temporary Preview Assets
- Customer Assets
- Legal Hold
- Deletion

# Dynamic Content Acceleration

Dynamic Content Acceleration improves delivery of responses that cannot be fully cached.

It may optimize:

- Network Path
- Connection Reuse
- TLS
- Protocol
- Regional Entry
- Origin Selection
- Request Routing
- Compression
- Partial Caching
- Edge Revalidation

---

# Dynamic Acceleration Objectives

Dynamic acceleration should:

- Reduce round-trip latency
- Improve connection performance
- Improve global API access
- Reuse edge-to-origin connections
- Route through optimized networks
- Reduce TLS overhead
- Support regional origins
- Protect origin capacity
- Maintain security
- Preserve response correctness

---

# Dynamic Content Examples

Examples may include:

- Authenticated Web Application HTML
- Public APIs
- Search Results
- Product Catalog
- Personalized Pages
- Real-Time Dashboards
- AI Interaction Requests
- Customer Portal Requests

Not all are cacheable.

---

# Dynamic Acceleration Model

```text
User

↓

Nearby Edge

↓

Optimized Provider Network

↓

Regional Origin or Application Gateway

↓

Dynamic Application Response

↓

Optimized Return Path

↓

User
```

---

# Connection Reuse

The edge may reuse connections to the origin.

Benefits include:

- Lower Latency
- Reduced TLS Handshake
- Reduced Origin Connection Load
- Better Throughput

---

# Protocol Optimization

The edge may support:

- HTTP/2
- HTTP/3
- QUIC
- Connection Multiplexing
- Header Compression
- TLS Session Reuse

Origin protocol may differ from client protocol.

---

# Dynamic Route Optimization

The edge may select an origin based on:

- Health
- Region
- Latency
- Tenant Home Region
- Data Policy
- Product Availability
- Capacity
- Maintenance

---

# API Acceleration

Public APIs may use edge infrastructure for:

- TLS
- Network Optimization
- WAF
- Rate Limiting
- Request Size Controls
- Routing
- Limited Safe Caching
- Regional Entry
- Observability

Application authorization must remain enforced.

---

# Dynamic Cache Fragments

Selected public response fragments may be cached while the complete response remains dynamic.

This should be introduced only with clear application support.

---

# Personalized Content

Personalized content should not be shared across users or tenants through unsafe caching.

Acceleration may still use:

- Network Optimization
- Compression
- Connection Reuse
- Edge Routing
- Private Cache Where Supported

---

# Dynamic Acceleration Risks

Risks include:

- Incorrect Caching
- Header Loss
- Cookie Mismanagement
- Authorization Failure
- Tenant Leakage
- Protocol Compatibility
- Hidden Retry
- Duplicate Write
- Increased Cost
- Edge Provider Dependency
- Difficult Troubleshooting

---

- [ ] Content is classified
- [ ] Shared caching is disabled where unsafe
- [ ] Authentication is preserved
- [ ] Authorization is enforced at origin
- [ ] Tenant context is trusted
- [ ] Request and response headers are validated
- [ ] Retry behavior is safe
- [ ] Write requests are not duplicated
- [ ] Regional routing respects data policy
- [ ] Latency improvement is measured

- Feature Configuration
- Security Lists
- Public Metadata

Edge Storage should not automatically become a primary enterprise database.

# Edge Storage Statement

# CDN & Edge Infrastructure Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| CE0 | Direct Origin Delivery | Users connect directly to origin with limited caching |
| CE1 | Standard CDN | Static assets use managed CDN and basic cache policies |
| CE2 | Governed Edge Delivery | Private origins, cache governance, invalidation, observability |
| CE3 | Multi-Product Edge Platform | Shared standards across products, regions, and customer experiences |
| CE4 | Adaptive Regional Edge | Dynamic regional routing, controlled edge processing, advanced caching |
| CE5 | Global Composable Edge | Reusable global edge blueprints with policy-driven delivery |

---

# CE0 — Direct Origin Delivery

Characteristics:

- Direct origin access
- Limited caching
- High origin load
- Weak global performance
- Manual asset release
- Limited edge visibility

Exit requirements:

- Managed CDN
- Static asset versioning
- Basic cache policy
- TLS
- Origin monitoring
- Asset ownership

---

# CE1 — Standard CDN

Characteristics:

- Static assets served through CDN
- Basic compression
- Versioned assets
- Basic invalidation
- Managed certificates
- Basic metrics

Exit requirements:

- Private origins
- Cache classification
- Cache-key governance
- Invalidation workflow
- Origin shielding
- Stronger logging
- Infrastructure as Code

---

# CE2 — Governed Edge Delivery

Characteristics:

- Public and private delivery patterns
- Cache policies by content class
- Origin protection
- Targeted invalidation
- Edge logs
- Product ownership
- Security review
- Edge storage restrictions

Exit requirements:

- Multi-product edge architecture
- Regional origins
- Customer domains
- Product cost allocation
- Dynamic acceleration
- Edge routing governance

---

# CE3 — Multi-Product Edge Platform

Characteristics:

- Several products consume shared edge standards
- Product-specific distributions or routes
- Regional content delivery
- Static and selected dynamic acceleration
- Central observability
- Cost allocation
- Automated release integration

Exit requirements:

- Regional edge intelligence
- Advanced origin selection
- Controlled edge computing
- Policy-driven caching
- Predictive origin protection
- Global consistency

---

# CE4 — Adaptive Regional Edge

Characteristics:

- Region-aware edge routing
- Dynamic origin selection
- Advanced cache behavior
- Controlled edge functions
- Regional storage where justified
- Automated low-risk invalidation
- Predictive performance and capacity signals

Exit requirements:

- Global edge composition
- Reusable product blueprints
- Automated policy validation
- Multi-provider readiness where required
- Enterprise edge intelligence

---

# CE5 — Global Composable Edge

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems inherit approved edge architecture.
- Edge routes consider product, tenant, region, content, security, health, latency, and cost.
- Static and dynamic delivery remain policy-controlled.
- Low-risk edge operations are automated.
- High-risk global changes remain human-approved.
- Edge behavior remains explainable, observable, reversible, and auditable.

---

# CDN & Edge Infrastructure Roadmap

## Phase 1 — Static CDN Foundation

- Select approved CDN provider
- Serve public static assets
- Enable TLS
- Version assets
- Configure basic caching
- Enable compression
- Add basic metrics
- Assign distribution ownership

---

## Phase 2 — Cache Governance

- Define cache classes
- Standardize Cache-Control
- Define cache keys
- Protect sensitive responses
- Define invalidation workflow
- Add asset lifecycle
- Add origin monitoring
- Move configuration into code

---

## Phase 3 — Origin Protection

- Restrict public origin access
- Add origin authentication
- Add origin shield
- Add request collapsing
- Add stale-if-error where appropriate
- Add origin capacity monitoring
- Test origin failure

---

## Phase 4 — Multi-Product Edge

- Add product-specific routes or distributions
- Add product cost allocation
- Add customer custom-domain support
- Add shared asset standards
- Add product observability
- Add regional content policy
- Add automated release integration

---

## Phase 5 — Regional and Dynamic Acceleration

- Add regional origins
- Add region-aware routing
- Add dynamic content acceleration
- Add advanced protocol support
- Add private asset delivery
- Add regional edge storage where justified
- Test regional failure

---

## Phase 6 — Adaptive Global Edge

- Add policy-driven edge routing
- Add predictive origin protection
- Automate low-risk cache operations
- Add global performance intelligence
- Add reusable edge blueprints
- Evaluate Multi-CDN where justified
- Maintain human approval for critical global changes

# Part 14B-3C-3A Exit Criteria

Part 14B-3C-3A is complete when:

- CDN Architecture is documented.
- CDN Philosophy and Principles are approved.
- Approved CDN providers and origin patterns are defined.
- Public and private origin models are documented.
- Multi-product and regional CDN patterns are defined.
- Edge Infrastructure components and responsibilities are documented.
- Edge Network, POP, and regional behavior are understood.
- Edge Routing supports product, region, release, and approved tenant patterns.
- Caching Strategy classifies public, private, immutable, mutable, dynamic, and tenant-specific content.
- Sensitive content is excluded from shared caching by default.
- Cache keys, TTLs, headers, revalidation, stale behavior, and bypass rules are standardized.
- Cache Invalidation supports targeted, authorized, auditable, and reversible operations.
- Full-distribution purge requires elevated approval.
- Static Asset Delivery uses versioned or content-hashed files.
- Asset storage, compression, image optimization, private access, retention, and rollback are governed.
- Dynamic Content Acceleration preserves authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, and data policy.
- Edge Storage is limited to bounded, low-risk, non-authoritative data.
- CDN distributions, routes, origins, and policies have assigned owners.
- CDN configuration is version-controlled where practical.
- CDN metrics, risks, KPIs, maturity levels, quality gates, and roadmap are documented.
- The architecture is ready to progress into Edge Computing, Edge Security, WAF, DDoS protection, API protection, rate limiting, bot protection, edge authentication, edge authorization, TLS, certificate management, and Zero Trust Edge.

# Part 14B-3C-3A Summary

CDN & Edge Infrastructure establishes the globally distributed content-delivery foundation for MianX.ai.

The complete delivery model is:

```text
Approved Content or Request

↓

Global DNS

↓

Nearest or Policy-Selected Edge Location

↓

TLS, Routing, and Cache Evaluation

↓

Cache Hit or Approved Edge Processing

↓

Regional Cache, Origin Shield, or Origin

↓

Secure Response Delivery

↓

Monitoring, Invalidation, and Governance
```

The architecture is built around fifteen connected capabilities:

```text
Executive Summary
Defines the enterprise edge requirement

CDN
Provides globally distributed content delivery

CDN Architecture
Defines edge-to-origin communication

CDN Philosophy
Prioritizes correctness, protection, and traceability

CDN Principles
Establish mandatory delivery and caching rules

Edge Infrastructure
Provides the globally distributed delivery platform

Edge Network
Connects users to approved edge locations

Edge POPs
Serve and process traffic near users

Edge Regions
Provide regional caching and policy control

Edge Routing
Selects product, origin, region, and release

Caching Strategy
Defines safe content reuse

Cache Invalidation
Removes or refreshes outdated content

Static Asset Delivery
Publishes immutable files efficiently

Dynamic Content Acceleration
Improves non-cacheable request delivery

Edge Storage
Stores limited low-risk data near edge execution
```

MianX.ai CDN & Edge Infrastructure must remain:

- Globally Distributed
- Secure
- Cache-Correct
- Origin-Protective
- Product-Aware
- Tenant-Safe
- Region-Aware
- Versioned
- Observable
- Resilient
- Reversible
- Cost-Aware
- Policy-Governed
- AI-Compatible
- Human-Accountable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to place files closer to users.

The objective is to create a controlled global delivery layer that improves performance and availability while preserving content correctness, privacy, tenant isolation, origin security, and enterprise governance.

# Part 14B-3C-3B — Edge Security Platform

The Edge Security Platform defines how MianX.ai protects public applications, APIs, digital assets, customer portals, product interfaces, AI endpoints, marketplace services, partner integrations, and enterprise access points before traffic reaches internal infrastructure.

The edge is the first enforceable security boundary between external consumers and MianX.ai systems.

It must protect:

- Corporate Websites
- Product Applications
- Public APIs
- Customer Portals
- Mobile Application APIs
- Developer Platform
- Marketplace
- Plugin Services
- Public Files
- Authentication Endpoints
- Webhooks
- Partner Integrations
- AI Gateway
- AI Agent APIs
- Customer-Dedicated Applications
- Regional Applications
- Administrative Entry Points
- Zero Trust Access Services

The Edge Security Platform combines:

- Edge Computing
- Edge Functions
- Edge Security
- Web Application Firewall
- DDoS Protection
- API Protection
- Rate Limiting
- Bot Protection
- Edge Authentication
- Edge Authorization
- Edge TLS
- Edge Certificates
- Zero Trust Edge
- Edge Security Governance

The objective is not to move complete application security into the edge.

The objective is to identify, filter, restrict, authenticate, route, and observe potentially hostile traffic as early as possible while preserving defense in depth.

Application, API, identity, authorization, data, and runtime security must remain active behind the edge.

---

# Edge Security Platform Statement

> **Build a globally distributed, identity-aware, policy-governed, observable, and resilient edge security platform that blocks malicious traffic, limits abuse, protects public interfaces, verifies approved access, and preserves application-layer security at every internal destination.**

MianX.ai will operate public and private digital services across multiple products, customers, regions, APIs, integrations, and AI workloads.

# Edge Security Principles

Every Edge Security capability should follow these principles:

- Defense in Depth
- Deny Known Malicious Traffic Early
- Do Not Trust Traffic Because It Passed the Edge
- Identity Before Privileged Access

- Secure Defaults
- Managed Protection Before Custom Security Logic
- Application Security Remains Mandatory
- Protect Origins

- Validate Every Security Rule
- Minimize False Positives
- Observe Every Critical Security Decision
- Version Security Policies
- Test Before Global Enforcement
- Support Rapid Rollback
- Automate Low-Risk Enforcement

- Preserve Tenant and Product Boundaries
- Maintain Regional and Legal Compliance

# Edge Computing

Edge Computing executes approved logic close to users or external traffic before requests reach central or regional application infrastructure.

Edge Computing can reduce:

- Latency
- Origin Load
- Network Round Trips
- Repeated Request Processing
- Regional Routing Delay

It can also provide:

- Request Transformation
- Response Transformation
- Lightweight Authentication Checks
- Redirects
- Routing Decisions
- Localization
- Feature Selection
- Security Enforcement
- Token Validation
- Signed URL Validation
- Maintenance Controls

Edge Computing introduces risk because logic may run globally and affect a large percentage of traffic.

---

# Edge Computing Statement

> **Use edge computing only for bounded, deterministic, low-latency, globally distributable logic that can be safely versioned, observed, tested, and reversed.**

---

# Edge Computing Objectives

Edge Computing should:

- Reduce latency for suitable operations
- Reduce unnecessary origin requests
- Support regional request handling
- Support lightweight security enforcement
- Support routing
- Support safe personalization
- Support localization
- Support maintenance and emergency controls
- Improve customer experience
- Maintain global consistency
- Avoid moving critical state to the edge
- Preserve origin authority

---

# Edge Computing Use Cases

Suitable use cases may include:

- HTTP Redirects
- URL Rewriting
- Header Normalization
- Security Header Injection
- Locale Selection
- Regional Routing
- Product Routing
- Custom-Domain Resolution
- Signed URL Validation
- Lightweight Token Verification
- Maintenance Mode
- Feature Cohort Selection
- Basic Bot Challenge
- Cache-Key Normalization
- Image Transformation
- Public Configuration Delivery
- Static Experiment Assignment
- Emergency Request Blocking

---

# Edge Computing Non-Use Cases

Edge Computing should generally not own:

- Financial Transactions
- Payment Processing
- Authoritative Customer State
- Complex Authorization
- Tenant Membership Decisions
- Database Transactions
- Long-Running Workflows
- AI Memory
- Sensitive Business Logic
- Critical Audit State
- High-Consistency Data
- Complex Fraud Decisions
- Irreversible Operations
- Long-Running AI Inference
- Secret-Heavy Processing

---

# Edge Computing Architecture

```text
Incoming Request

↓

Edge Runtime

↓

Configuration and Policy Retrieval

↓

Bounded Edge Logic

├── Allow
├── Deny
├── Redirect
├── Rewrite
├── Route
├── Challenge
└── Return Safe Edge Response

↓

Protected Origin Where Required

↓

Logs, Metrics, and Audit
```

---

# Edge Computing Constraints

Every edge workload should define:

- Maximum Execution Time
- Memory
- CPU
- Package Size
- Network Access
- Storage Access
- Supported Runtime
- Region Availability
- Request Size
- Response Size
- Concurrency
- Cost
- Logging
- Failure Behavior

---

# Edge Compute Data Policy

Edge Compute should process only the minimum required data.

It should avoid:

- Storing Authentication Tokens
- Logging Secrets
- Logging Complete Private Payloads
- Replicating Sensitive Data Globally
- Processing Regulated Data Without Approval
- Using Customer Data Outside Approved Regions

---

# Edge Compute Failure Behavior

Failure should produce a safe result.

Possible failure behaviors include:

- Continue to Origin
- Deny Request
- Use Last-Known-Good Configuration
- Return Maintenance Response
- Use Default Region
- Disable Optional Transformation
- Trigger Alert

The selected behavior should depend on security and business risk.

---

# Edge Compute Deployment

Edge compute deployment should follow:

```text
Source

↓

Automated Tests

↓

Security Analysis

↓

Non-Production Edge Validation

↓

Limited Regional Release

↓

Limited Traffic Release

↓

Global Release

↓

Monitoring

↓

Rollback Where Required
```

# Web Application Firewall

A Web Application Firewall inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic and applies security rules before requests reach applications.

A WAF can help protect against:

- Injection
- Cross-Site Scripting
- Path Traversal
- Protocol Abuse
- Malformed Requests
- Known Vulnerability Patterns
- Suspicious Request Headers
- Automated Scanning
- Application-Layer DDoS
- Known Malicious Sources

---

# WAF Statement

> **Use managed and custom WAF controls to reduce known web threats while preserving legitimate customer traffic and maintaining application-layer security behind the firewall.**

---

# WAF Objectives

The WAF should:

- Block known attack patterns
- Detect suspicious requests
- Protect public applications
- Protect public APIs
- Protect authentication
- Support virtual patching
- Reduce origin load
- Provide security evidence
- Support emergency response
- Support product-specific rules
- Minimize false positives
- Support staged enforcement

---

```text
↓

├── Managed Rules
├── Custom Rules

├── Geographic Rules
└── Emergency Rules

↓

Allow, Log, Challenge, Rate-Limit, or Block

↓
```

# DDoS Protection

Distributed Denial-of-Service protection defends services against attempts to exhaust:

- Network Bandwidth
- Connections
- Protocol Resources
- Load Balancers
- Application Capacity
- Database Capacity
- Authentication Services
- API Capacity
- Origin Infrastructure

---

# DDoS Protection Statement

> **Absorb, filter, rate-control, or safely degrade hostile traffic before it exhausts critical MianX.ai infrastructure or prevents legitimate customer access.**

---

# DDoS Objectives

DDoS protection should:

- Protect network availability
- Protect public endpoints
- Protect edge infrastructure
- Protect load balancers
- Protect origins
- Protect authentication systems
- Protect APIs
- Maintain customer access
- Detect attacks rapidly
- Support automated mitigation
- Support escalation
- Preserve forensic evidence
- Control attack-related cost

---

# DDoS Attack Categories

## Volumetric Attacks

Attempt to consume bandwidth.

## Protocol Attacks

Attempt to exhaust network or transport resources.

## Application-Layer Attacks

Attempt to exhaust application or backend resources.

## Reflection and Amplification

Use third-party services to multiply attack traffic.

## Slow Request Attacks

Hold connections open and consume resources.

## Distributed Authentication Abuse

Target login, password-reset, or token endpoints.

```text
↓

↓

Origin Capacity Protection

↓

Incident Response
```

| DD5 | Enterprise-wide or provider-level attack |

# Rate Limiting

Rate Limiting controls how many requests, connections, operations, or units of work a source may consume during a defined period.

It protects:

- Availability
- Fairness
- Origins
- APIs
- Authentication
- Databases
- External Providers
- AI Costs
- Customer Experience

---

# Rate Limiting Statement

> **Every externally accessible or resource-sensitive service should define bounded usage based on identity, tenant, consumer, operation, risk, and capacity.**

---

# Rate Limiting Objectives

Rate Limiting should:

- Prevent abuse
- Prevent accidental overload
- Protect shared resources
- Protect authentication
- Protect expensive APIs
- Protect AI workloads
- Enforce customer plans
- Maintain tenant fairness
- Protect downstream providers
- Support predictable capacity
- Support graceful degradation
- Provide usage evidence

---

# Rate-Limit Dimensions

Limits may apply by:

- Source IP
- User
- Session
- Account
- Tenant
- Organization
- API Key
- OAuth Client
- Service Identity
- Agent
- Product
- Endpoint
- Method
- Region
- Device
- Customer Plan
- Cost Unit

IP-only limits should not be the sole control for authenticated services.

---

# Rate-Limit Algorithms

Potential algorithms include:

- Fixed Window
- Sliding Window
- Token Bucket
- Leaky Bucket
- Concurrent Request Limit
- Queue-Based Limit
- Cost-Weighted Limit

---

# Fixed Window

Counts requests during a fixed time interval.

Benefits:

- Simple
- Low Cost

Risks:

- Boundary Bursts

---

# Sliding Window

Evaluates requests across a continuously moving time range.

Benefits:

- More Accurate
- Better Burst Control

Costs:

- Higher Complexity

---

# Token Bucket

Allows controlled bursts while maintaining a sustained limit.

Useful for:

- APIs
- User Traffic
- Partner Integrations
- Mobile Clients

---

# Concurrency Limiting

Limits active operations.

Useful for:

- Long Requests
- File Processing
- AI Inference
- Reports
- Database-Heavy Queries
- WebSockets

---

# Cost-Weighted Rate Limiting

Operations may consume different units.

Example:

```text
Simple Read = 1 Unit

Complex Search = 5 Units

Report Generation = 20 Units

AI Analysis = 50 Units
```

This may protect high-cost services more effectively than request count alone.

---

# Rate-Limit Response

Rate-limit responses should provide suitable:

- HTTP Status
- Retry Guidance
- Limit Information Where Safe
- Correlation ID
- Documentation Reference

Sensitive internal limits should not be unnecessarily exposed.

---

# Rate-Limit Hierarchy

A request may be subject to:

```text
Global Limit

+

Product Limit

+

Tenant Limit

+

Consumer Limit

+

Endpoint Limit

+

Operation Cost Limit
```

Policy precedence should be documented.

---

# Authentication Rate Limits

Authentication routes should apply controls to:

- Login
- Password Reset

- Token Refresh
- Multi-Factor Challenge
- Account Recovery

Protection should balance security with legitimate recovery needs.

# Edge Authentication

Edge Authentication verifies identity before allowing traffic to reach protected applications or administrative services.

It may protect:

- Administrative Portals
- Internal Applications
- Staging Environments
- Developer Tools
- Security Consoles
- Customer-Dedicated Interfaces
- Private APIs
- Support Tools
- Preview Environments

---

# Edge Authentication Statement

> **Require strong verified identity at the edge for restricted applications while preserving application-level session and authorization controls behind the edge.**

---

# Edge Authentication Objectives

Edge Authentication should:

- Block anonymous access to restricted applications
- Integrate enterprise identity
- Support multi-factor authentication
- Support device-aware access
- Protect administrative interfaces
- Protect internal applications
- Reduce public attack surface
- Provide access audit
- Support rapid revocation
- Support temporary access
- Support customer and partner identity where approved

---

# Edge Authentication Methods

Potential methods include:

- OpenID Connect
- SAML
- OAuth
- Client Certificate
- Mutual TLS
- One-Time Code
- Identity-Aware Proxy
- Device Certificate
- Workload Identity

---

# Authentication Flow

```text
User Requests Protected Application

↓

Edge Detects Missing or Invalid Session

↓

Redirect to Approved Identity Provider

↓

Identity and Multi-Factor Authentication

↓

Edge Receives Verified Identity Claims

↓

Access Policy Evaluated

↓

Approved Identity Context Forwarded Safely

↓

Application Performs Its Own Authorization
```

---

# Identity Claims

Trusted claims may include:

- User ID
- Email
- Organization
- Role
- Group
- Device Status
- Authentication Strength
- Session Time
- Region
- Risk

Claims should be:

- Signed
- Validated
- Time-Bound
- Minimally Forwarded
- Protected From Client Modification

---

# Edge Sessions

Edge session policy should define:

- Session Duration
- Idle Timeout
- Absolute Timeout
- Refresh
- Revocation
- Cookie Security
- Device Binding Where Required
- Reauthentication
- Logout

---

# Multi-Factor Authentication

MFA should be required for:

- Administrative Access
- Security Tools
- Infrastructure Tools
- Production Management
- High-Risk Customer Operations
- Sensitive Internal Applications

---

# Edge Authentication Failure

Failure should result in:

- Deny
- Reauthentication
- Safe Error
- Security Alert Where Suspicious
- No Origin Access

---

# Edge Authentication Quality Gates

- [ ] Protected application is classified
- [ ] Identity provider is approved

- [ ] Claims are validated

- [ ] Application authorization remains active

- [ ] Recovery access is documented
- [ ] Access is tested
- [ ] Ownership is assigned

# Edge Authorization

Edge Authorization evaluates whether an authenticated identity may reach a protected application, route, region, or service.

Edge authorization should remain coarse-grained.

Fine-grained resource authorization belongs in the application.

---

# Edge Authorization Statement

> **Use edge authorization to control application and route access, not to replace domain-level and data-level authorization inside responsible services.**

---

# Edge Authorization Objectives

Edge Authorization should:

- Restrict administrative applications
- Restrict internal tools
- Restrict staging and preview environments
- Restrict customer-dedicated portals
- Restrict regional applications
- Restrict partner APIs
- Enforce group or role access
- Support temporary access
- Support device policy
- Support geographic policy
- Preserve auditability

---

# Edge Authorization Inputs

Policies may evaluate:

- Identity
- Group
- Role
- Organization
- Device
- Network
- Country
- Region
- Authentication Strength
- Time
- Application
- Route
- Risk
- Session Age

---

# Edge Authorization Actions

A policy may:

- Allow
- Deny
- Require MFA
- Require Reauthentication
- Require Managed Device
- Require Approved Network
- Require Client Certificate
- Limit Session
- Log and Review

---

# Edge Authorization Policy Example

```text
Application:
Production Infrastructure Console

Allowed Identities:
Infrastructure Operations Group

Requirements:
Multi-Factor Authentication
Managed Device
Approved Country or Network
Recent Authentication

Session:
Maximum Four Hours

Action:
Deny by Default
```

---

# Edge Authorization Limitations

Edge authorization should not decide:

- Which tenant record a user may read
- Which invoice a user may modify
- Which project a user owns
- Which database row an agent may access
- Which business action is legally allowed

These decisions remain application responsibilities.

---

# Edge Authorization Quality Gates

- [ ] Application scope is defined
- [ ] Deny-by-default is applied
- [ ] Allowed identities are documented
- [ ] MFA and device requirements are defined
- [ ] Geographic policy is justified
- [ ] Application authorization remains active
- [ ] Temporary access expires
- [ ] Logs are centralized
- [ ] Emergency access is controlled
- [ ] Policies are tested
- [ ] Ownership and review dates exist

---

# Edge TLS

Edge TLS protects communication between external clients and edge infrastructure.

TLS may also protect communication between the edge and origin.

---

# Edge TLS Statement

> **Encrypt all production traffic using supported TLS configurations, strong certificate management, secure protocol policy, and verified edge-to-origin encryption.**

---

# TLS Objectives

TLS should:

- Protect confidentiality
- Protect integrity
- Authenticate endpoints
- Prevent downgrade
- Support modern clients
- Protect API traffic
- Protect customer portals
- Protect administrative access
- Support mutual TLS where required
- Support certificate automation
- Maintain global availability

---

# TLS Architecture

```text
Client

↓

TLS Connection

↓

Edge Certificate and Protocol Validation

↓

Edge Security Processing

↓

TLS or Mutual TLS Connection

↓

Protected Origin
```

# Supported TLS Versions

MianX.ai should support approved modern TLS versions.

Deprecated or weak versions should be disabled according to compatibility and security policy.

---

# Cipher Policy

- Approved
- Modern
- Forward-Secret Where Supported
- Regularly Reviewed
- Compatible With Supported Clients
- Free From Deprecated Algorithms

- Secure Origin Communication

# HTTP Strict Transport Security

- Domain Scope
- Subdomains
- Preload
- Certificate Readiness
- Recovery Risk
- Customer Custom Domains

Incorrect HSTS configuration can cause prolonged access failure.

# Edge-to-Origin TLS

The edge should connect to origins through encrypted communication.

Validation should include:

- Certificate Trust
- Hostname
- Expiration
- Supported Protocol
- Origin Identity
- Mutual TLS Where Required

- Partner APIs

- Regulated Integrations

# Zero Trust Edge

Zero Trust Edge combines identity, device, context, network, and policy controls to protect applications and resources without assuming trust based on location.

It may protect:

- Administrative Portals
- Developer Services
- Internal Applications
- Production Tools
- Customer-Dedicated Applications
- Security Systems
- Infrastructure Consoles
- Remote Workforce Access
- Partner Access

---

# Zero Trust Edge Statement

> **No user, device, service, agent, network, or customer connection should receive access solely because it is inside a private network; every request must be explicitly verified and policy-evaluated.**

---

# Zero Trust Edge Principles

- Verify Explicitly
- Use Least Privilege
- Assume Breach
- Deny by Default
- Evaluate Identity
- Evaluate Device
- Evaluate Application
- Evaluate Context
- Use Short-Lived Access
- Monitor Continuously
- Revoke Rapidly
- Require Stronger Controls for Higher Risk

---

# Zero Trust Access Flow

```text
Access Request

↓

Identity Verification

↓

Authentication Strength Check

↓

Device or Workload Evaluation

↓

Application and Route Policy

↓

Risk and Context Evaluation

↓

Minimum Access Granted

↓

Continuous Session Monitoring

↓

Reauthentication or Revocation Where Required
```

---

# Zero Trust Identity Types

Zero Trust should support:

- Human User
- Administrator
- Contractor
- Partner User
- Customer User
- Service
- Workload
- AI Agent
- Device
- Automation Pipeline

---

# Device Context

- Risk
- Location
- Device Identity

- Threat Intelligence
- Abnormal Behavior
- Privileged Action
- Security Incident
- Stale Session

Actions may include:

- Require MFA
- Require Reauthentication
- Deny
- Limit Session
- Restrict Action
- Alert Security

---

# Zero Trust Application Access

Applications should be published through identity-aware access rather than broad VPN access where practical.

Benefits include:

- Application-Level Access
- Reduced Network Exposure
- Better Identity Context
- Better Audit
- Easier Revocation
- Reduced Lateral Movement

- Agent Identity

- Tenant
- Task
- Tool
- Risk
- Time

- Cost Limit

An AI agent should not receive general network trust.

Sessions should support:

- Idle Timeout

- Revocation
- Device Recheck
- Risk Re-evaluation
- Logout
- Emergency Termination

---

- Named Emergency Role

- Approval
- Time Limit
- Restricted Scope
- Session Audit
- Incident Reference
- Post-Use Review

# Edge Security Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| ESP0 | Basic Perimeter | TLS and limited provider protection |
| ESP1 | Standard Edge Security | Managed WAF, DDoS, basic rate limiting, certificate automation |
| ESP2 | Governed Edge Security | API protection, bot policies, policy as code, stronger monitoring |
| ESP3 | Multi-Product Zero Trust Edge | Product policies, edge identity, customer and administrative protection |
| ESP4 | Adaptive Regional Edge Security | Regional risk policies, predictive abuse detection, controlled automation |
| ESP5 | Intelligent Global Edge Security | Policy-driven global protection with bounded automation and human governance |

---

# ESP0 — Basic Perimeter

Characteristics:

- Basic HTTPS
- Public origins
- Limited WAF
- Manual certificates
- Minimal rate limiting
- Weak edge monitoring
- No bot policy
- No Zero Trust access

Exit requirements:

- Managed WAF
- Managed DDoS
- Automated certificates
- Origin protection
- Basic rate limits
- Security logging
- Ownership

---

# ESP1 — Standard Edge Security

Characteristics:

- WAF baseline
- DDoS protection
- TLS standards
- Certificate automation
- Authentication route protection
- Basic API protection
- Basic bot controls
- Basic alerts

Exit requirements:

- Policy as code
- Product-specific rules
- Formal API controls
- Bot classification
- Zero Trust access
- False-positive process
- Recovery runbooks

---

# ESP2 — Governed Edge Security

Characteristics:

- Versioned security policies
- WAF exceptions governed
- Rate-limit overrides governed
- API schema protection
- Credential abuse protection
- Edge security dashboards
- Certificate inventory
- Controlled edge functions

Exit requirements:

- Multi-product policies
- Customer-specific protection
- Administrative Zero Trust
- Regional policies
- AI endpoint protection
- Advanced security analytics

---

# ESP3 — Multi-Product Zero Trust Edge

Characteristics:

- Products inherit enterprise baseline
- Product-specific WAF and bot rules
- Customer and partner API protection
- Administrative applications protected by Zero Trust
- AI agent edge access governed
- Product-level security metrics
- Global certificate governance

Exit requirements:

- Predictive bot and abuse detection
- Adaptive rate recommendations
- Regional edge-security policy
- Automated rule validation
- Advanced incident automation
- Global security intelligence

---

# ESP4 — Adaptive Regional Edge Security

Characteristics:

- Region-aware security policies
- Predictive DDoS and bot signals
- Automated low-risk rule adjustment
- Context-aware Zero Trust
- AI-assisted incident analysis
- Advanced origin protection
- Continuous policy validation

Exit requirements:

- Reusable global security blueprints
- Enterprise-wide policy intelligence
- Automated safe recovery
- Multi-provider resilience where justified
- Strong human strategic control

---

# ESP5 — Intelligent Global Edge Security

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems inherit approved edge-security controls.
- Security decisions consider identity, device, agent, tenant, product, region, route, behavior, threat, and risk.
- Low-risk protections are automated.
- High-impact blocking, access, certificate, and failover changes remain human-approved.
- Global edge security remains explainable, observable, reversible, and auditable.
- Every incident improves enterprise protection.

---

# Edge Security Roadmap

## Phase 1 — Essential Edge Protection

- Enforce HTTPS
- Automate certificates
- Enable managed DDoS protection
- Enable managed WAF baseline
- Protect origins
- Add basic rate limits
- Centralize logs
- Assign owners

## Phase 2 — API and Abuse Protection

- Protect public APIs
- Add schema validation
- Add authentication rate limits
- Add webhook protection
- Add bot classification
- Add credential-stuffing protection
- Add API abuse alerts
- Establish false-positive process

---

## Phase 3 — Edge Identity and Zero Trust

- Protect administrative applications
- Integrate enterprise identity
- Require MFA
- Add device-aware access
- Add temporary access
- Add session controls
- Add Zero Trust logging
- Reduce broad VPN dependency

---

## Phase 4 — Multi-Product Edge Security

- Define product WAF policies
- Define product rate limits
- Define product bot policies
- Protect customer domains
- Protect partner APIs
- Protect AI endpoints
- Allocate cost by product
- Add product security dashboards

---

## Phase 5 — Regional Adaptive Security

- Add regional security policy
- Add geographic threat controls
- Add regional certificate and TLS monitoring
- Add predictive abuse analysis
- Automate low-risk responses
- Improve DDoS readiness
- Test regional edge-security failure
- Improve Zero Trust risk context

---

## Phase 6 — Intelligent Global Edge Security

- Add global threat intelligence
- Add continuous policy validation
- Add AI-assisted rule optimization
- Automate bounded recovery
- Add reusable security blueprints
- Evaluate multi-provider security resilience
- Maintain human approval for critical actions
- Integrate edge learning into enterprise security governance

# Part 14B-3C-3B Exit Criteria

Part 14B-3C-3B is complete when:

- Edge Computing use cases and limits are documented.
- Edge Functions are registered, versioned, tested, observable, and reversible.
- Sensitive and authoritative enterprise state remains outside edge runtimes unless explicitly approved.
- Edge Security layers and policy classes are defined.
- A managed WAF baseline protects public production applications.
- WAF managed rules, custom rules, exceptions, virtual patches, and false positives are governed.
- DDoS protection covers network, protocol, application, authentication, and API threats.
- Origin systems are protected from direct public bypass.
- API Protection covers authentication, methods, schemas, size limits, versions, webhooks, abuse, and AI APIs.
- Rate Limiting supports user, tenant, consumer, endpoint, concurrency, and cost-aware controls.
- Bot Protection distinguishes verified, approved, unknown, suspicious, and malicious automation.
- Credential-stuffing, scraping, scanner, and AI crawler policies are defined.
- Edge Authentication integrates approved identity and MFA.
- Edge Authorization remains limited to application and route access.
- Application-level authorization remains mandatory.
- TLS policies, protocol versions, cipher standards, HTTPS enforcement, and edge-to-origin encryption are documented.
- Certificate issuance, renewal, rotation, inventory, revocation, and customer-domain responsibilities are governed.
- Zero Trust Edge protects administrative and restricted applications.
- Human, service, workload, device, and AI-agent access are explicitly verified.
- Edge Security Governance defines ownership, policy hierarchy, risk levels, changes, access, incidents, and recovery.
- Edge security policies are version-controlled where practical.
- Logs, metrics, alerts, KPIs, risks, maturity levels, quality gates, and roadmap are documented.
- High-risk global blocking, certificate, access, and Zero Trust changes require authorized human approval.
- The architecture is ready to progress into Edge Observability, edge monitoring, logging, tracing, alerting, cost optimization, governance metrics, maturity assessment, final traffic architecture summary, and exit criteria.
