# Part 14B-3D-2 — Network Access Control

Network Access Control defines how MianX.ai grants, restricts, validates, records, reviews, and revokes network-level communication between workloads, services, products, environments, regions, customers, administrators, and external systems.

Firewall Architecture establishes the enterprise security boundaries.

Network Access Control translates those boundaries into enforceable workload, subnet, interface, service, and traffic rules.

It governs:

- Which source may initiate communication
- Which destination may receive communication
- Which protocol may be used
- Which port may be used
- Which direction is allowed
- Which environment is involved
- Which product owns the communication
- Which tenant or customer scope applies
- Which identity or security group is trusted
- How long access remains valid
- Who owns and approves the rule
- How access is monitored
- How access is removed

Network Access Control applies to:

- Security Groups
- Network ACLs
- Cloud Network Security Groups
- Virtual Network Rules
- Network Interface Rules
- Subnet Controls
- Kubernetes Network Policies
- Private Endpoints
- Managed Databases
- Managed Caches
- Message Queues
- Search Services
- Vector Databases
- Internal Load Balancers
- Public Load Balancers
- API Gateways
- Serverless Services
- Virtual Machines
- Containers
- Customer Networks
- Partner Networks
- Administrative Services
- Disaster-Recovery Environments

Network access must never be based only on convenience.

Every approved network path must have a clear purpose, limited scope, accountable ownership, controlled lifecycle, and verifiable security outcome.

---

# Network Access Control Statement

> **Permit only the minimum network communication required for an approved business or technical purpose, enforce it through layered controls, validate it continuously, and revoke it immediately when the need no longer exists.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai will operate multiple products, platforms, customer environments, AI systems, databases, shared services, cloud networks, and regional deployments.

These components require communication to function.

Examples include:

- Edge Gateway to Application Service
- Application Service to Database
- Product Service to Shared Identity Service
- AI Agent to Approved Tool API
- Monitoring Service to Workload Metrics Endpoint
- Backup Service to Storage
- Customer VPN to Integration Gateway
- Partner Network to Approved API
- Deployment Pipeline to Runtime Platform
- Administrator to Protected Management Interface

Without governed access control, communication may become excessively broad.

Examples of unsafe access include:

- All Application Servers to All Databases
- All Products to All Shared Services
- Development Networks to Production
- Internet to Administrative Interfaces
- Any Customer Network to Internal Platform Services
- Unrestricted Outbound Internet Access
- Entire Kubernetes Cluster to Sensitive Data Services
- Permanent Temporary Access
- Source Rules Based on Changing Personal IP Addresses
- Broad Port Ranges Without Justification

The preferred evolution path is:

```text
Manual IP-Based Rules

↓

Standard Security Groups

↓

Subnet and Network ACL Boundaries

↓

Product and Environment Isolation

↓

Identity-Based Network Access

↓

Automated Least-Privilege Rules

↓

Continuous Rule Validation

↓

Adaptive Enterprise Access Governance
```

The objective is not zero connectivity.

The objective is controlled connectivity.

Every communication path should be:

- Required
- Explicit
- Narrow
- Owned
- Documented
- Testable
- Observable
- Reviewable
- Revocable
- Recoverable

---

# Network Access Control Mission

The mission of Network Access Control is to enforce least-privilege communication throughout the MianX.ai enterprise infrastructure.

The access-control platform must:

- Restrict public ingress
- Restrict internal ingress
- Restrict outbound traffic
- Separate products
- Separate environments
- Separate customers
- Separate data zones
- Protect management networks
- Protect security platforms
- Protect observability systems
- Protect shared platform services
- Protect AI systems
- Protect disaster-recovery systems
- Support approved customer connectivity
- Support approved partner connectivity
- Support rapid incident isolation
- Maintain service availability
- Maintain access evidence
- Support policy automation
- Support continuous review

---

# Network Access Control Objectives

Network Access Control should:

- Enforce default deny
- Enforce least privilege
- Reduce attack surface
- Reduce lateral movement
- Prevent unauthorized public exposure
- Prevent cross-environment access
- Prevent cross-product access
- Prevent cross-customer access
- Protect production databases
- Protect administrative services
- Control internet egress
- Protect cloud-managed services
- Support workload identity
- Support temporary access
- Support automated expiration
- Detect broad rules
- Detect stale rules
- Detect duplicate rules
- Detect configuration drift
- Support incident response
- Maintain compliance evidence
- Support long-term enterprise growth

---

# Network Access Control Scope

This section covers:

- Security Groups
- Network Security Groups
- Network ACLs
- Subnet ACLs
- Ingress Rules
- Egress Rules
- Rule Management
- Rule Ownership
- Rule Lifecycle
- Rule Review
- Rule Testing
- Least-Privilege Networking
- Network Isolation
- Product Isolation
- Environment Isolation
- Tenant Isolation
- Customer Isolation
- Data-Zone Isolation
- Administrative Isolation
- Access Governance
- Change Management
- Exceptions
- Monitoring
- Logging
- Recovery
- Maturity
- Roadmap

---

# Network Access Control Non-Scope

Network Access Control does not replace:

- User Authentication
- Application Authorization
- API Authorization
- Database Roles
- Tenant-Level Permissions
- Business-Level Permissions
- Encryption
- Web Application Firewall
- DDoS Protection
- IDS or IPS
- Endpoint Security
- Secret Management
- Identity Governance
- Secure Coding

A permitted connection is not proof that the caller may perform every business action.

The destination must still enforce application, tenant, and data authorization.

---

# Network Access Control Principles

The following principles are mandatory.

---

## 1. Deny by Default

Traffic without an approved rule must be denied.

---

## 2. Least Privilege

Grant only the minimum source, destination, protocol, port, direction, and duration required.

---

## 3. Identity Over Broad Address Ranges

Where supported, use:

- Security Group Reference
- Service Identity
- Workload Identity
- Application Tag
- Managed Service Tag
- Kubernetes Service Account

instead of broad IP ranges.

---

## 4. No Unrestricted Public Access

Public exposure requires explicit registration, ownership, protection, and review.

---

## 5. No Public Production Databases

Production databases must remain private.

---

## 6. Control Both Ingress and Egress

Outbound communication must be governed as carefully as inbound communication.

---

## 7. Separate Environments

Development, testing, staging, production, and disaster recovery must have explicit boundaries.

---

## 8. Separate Products

Products should communicate through approved interfaces, not unrestricted networks.

---

## 9. Separate Customers

Customer-dedicated environments and private connections must remain isolated.

---

## 10. Protect Shared Services

Shared platform services must expose only approved ports and interfaces.

---

## 11. Temporary Rules Must Expire

Every temporary rule should include an automatic or governed expiration.

---

## 12. Every Rule Must Have an Owner

Unowned rules should be blocked from deployment or remediated.

---

## 13. Every Rule Must Have a Purpose

A rule without a documented business or technical purpose should not remain active.

---

## 14. Avoid Broad Port Ranges

Permit only required ports.

---

## 15. Avoid Broad CIDR Ranges

Large address ranges require strong justification.

---

## 16. Avoid Personal IP Rules for Long-Term Access

Administrative access should use controlled enterprise access systems.

---

## 17. Manage Rules as Code

Production rules should be version-controlled where practical.

---

## 18. Test Allow and Deny Behavior

A rule is not validated until expected successful and unsuccessful paths are tested.

---

## 19. Log Material Decisions

Critical allows, denies, and administrative changes must be observable.

---

## 20. Detect Drift

Deployed access must remain aligned with approved configuration.

---

## 21. Preserve Required Operations

Rules must not unintentionally block:

- Health Checks
- Monitoring
- Deployment
- Backup
- Recovery
- Security Telemetry
- Customer Transactions

---

## 22. Use Independent Review for High-Risk Access

Database, management, cross-region, customer, and public-access rules require elevated review.

---

## 23. Revoke Access When the Need Ends

Access removal is part of the access lifecycle.

---

## 24. AI Assistance Must Remain Bounded

AI may detect, recommend, test, and document access changes.

High-risk access must remain human-approved.

---

# Network Access Control Reference Architecture

```text
Source Workload, User, Network, or Service

↓

Source Identity or Network Classification

↓

Security Group or Workload Policy

↓

Subnet or Network ACL

↓

Central or Distributed Firewall

↓

Destination Security Group

↓

Destination Service

↓

Application Authentication and Authorization

↓

Logs, Metrics, Alerts, and Audit
```

---

# Enforcement Layers

Network Access Control should use layered enforcement.

## Layer 1 — Edge and Perimeter

Controls public and external access.

## Layer 2 — Network or Subnet Boundary

Controls communication between network segments.

## Layer 3 — Workload or Interface Boundary

Controls direct communication to workloads.

## Layer 4 — Container and Service Boundary

Controls pod, namespace, and service communication.

## Layer 5 — Application Boundary

Controls identity, permission, method, and data access.

---

# Security Groups

Security Groups are stateful, workload-oriented access controls commonly attached to:

- Virtual Machines
- Network Interfaces
- Load Balancers
- Managed Databases
- Managed Caches
- Private Endpoints
- Container Services
- Serverless Services
- Application Gateways

Security Groups should represent workload purpose rather than temporary infrastructure details.

---

# Security Group Statement

> **Use security groups as reusable workload identities that describe approved communication relationships rather than as unstructured collections of IP-based rules.**

---

# Security Group Objectives

Security Groups should:

- Protect workloads
- Protect interfaces
- Support stateful communication
- Support workload identity
- Reduce IP dependency
- Support environment separation
- Support product separation
- Support database isolation
- Support reusable patterns
- Support automation
- Support logging
- Support rapid revocation

---

# Security Group Model

```text
Source Security Group

↓

Approved Protocol and Port

↓

Destination Security Group
```

Example:

```text
restaurant-api-sg

↓

TCP 5432

↓

restaurant-database-sg
```

This is preferable to:

```text
10.0.0.0/8

↓

All Ports

↓

Database Network
```

---

# Security Group Categories

Security Groups may include:

- Public Load Balancer Group
- Private Load Balancer Group
- Web Application Group
- API Service Group
- Background Worker Group
- Database Group
- Cache Group
- Queue Group
- Search Group
- AI Service Group
- Monitoring Group
- Security Tool Group
- Administrative Gateway Group
- Customer Integration Group
- Partner Integration Group
- Backup Group
- Disaster-Recovery Group

---

# Security Group Naming

Security Group names should include:

- Environment
- Product
- Service
- Purpose
- Region Where Required

Example:

```text
prod-platform-auth-api-sg

prod-restaurant-order-db-sg

staging-poultry-web-sg
```

Avoid names such as:

```text
default-sg

temp-access

allow-all

test-rule
```

---

# Default Security Groups

Provider-created default groups should not be used for production workloads without review.

Default groups may permit broader access than intended.

Recommended controls include:

- Remove Default Inbound Rules
- Restrict Default Outbound Rules
- Prevent Production Attachment
- Detect Use Through Policy
- Replace With Named Managed Groups

---

# Security Group References

Where supported, one group should reference another group.

Benefits include:

- Reduced IP Dependency
- Better Workload Identity
- Easier Scaling
- Easier Replacement
- More Stable Rules
- Better Automation

---

# Security Group Ingress

Ingress should define:

- Approved Source Group
- Approved Source Network
- Protocol
- Port
- Purpose
- Owner
- Environment
- Product
- Expiration Where Temporary

---

# Security Group Egress

Default unrestricted egress should be reviewed.

Egress may be limited to:

- Approved Internal Services
- Approved Databases
- Approved APIs
- Approved SaaS
- Approved Model Providers
- Approved Package Repositories
- Approved DNS
- Approved Logging Systems

---

# Database Security Groups

Database groups should accept traffic only from:

- Approved Application Groups
- Approved Migration Services
- Approved Backup Services
- Approved Monitoring Services
- Controlled Administrative Gateway

They should deny:

- Public Internet
- General Employee Networks
- Development Workloads
- Unrelated Products
- Unrelated Customer Environments

---

# Load Balancer Security Groups

Public load balancers may accept approved public protocols.

Their backend targets should accept traffic only from the load balancer group.

Example:

```text
Internet

↓

Public Load Balancer Security Group

↓

Application Security Group
```

The application group should not directly allow the internet.

---

# Administrative Security Groups

Administrative groups should permit access only from:

- Zero Trust Gateway
- Bastion
- Privileged Access System
- Approved VPN
- Managed Administrative Network

---

# Monitoring Security Groups

Monitoring systems may require access to:

- Metrics Endpoints
- Health Endpoints
- Log Forwarders
- Management APIs

Their access should remain narrow and read-oriented where possible.

---

# AI Service Security Groups

AI services should allow communication only from approved:

- AI Gateway
- Agent Runtime
- Orchestration Service
- Retrieval Service
- Tool Gateway
- Monitoring Service

Direct unrestricted workload access should be avoided.

---

# Customer Integration Security Groups

Customer-specific access should use dedicated or scoped groups.

Rules should define:

- Customer
- Source Network
- Destination Gateway
- Protocol
- Port
- Contract
- Environment
- Region
- Owner
- Expiration or Review Date

---

# Security Group Limits

Provider limits may include:

- Rules per Group
- Groups per Interface
- Referenced Groups
- Prefix Lists
- Update Frequency

Excessive rules may create:

- Deployment Failure
- Operational Complexity
- Hidden Access
- Slower Review
- Provider Quota Risk

---

# Security Group Composition

Security groups should be modular.

Example:

```text
Base Application Egress Group

+

Product Application Ingress Group

+

Monitoring Access Group
```

Composition should not accidentally create excessive combined access.

---

# Security Group Quality Gates

- [ ] Group has a defined purpose
- [ ] Group has an owner
- [ ] Product and environment are identified
- [ ] Default rules are removed
- [ ] Ingress is least privilege
- [ ] Egress is reviewed
- [ ] Group references are used where appropriate
- [ ] Public access is justified
- [ ] Database access is private
- [ ] Temporary rules expire
- [ ] Rules are version-controlled
- [ ] Rule limits are monitored
- [ ] Allow and deny behavior is tested
- [ ] Logs and alerts are active

---

# Network ACLs

Network Access Control Lists are stateless controls commonly attached to subnets or network segments.

They provide an additional boundary around groups of workloads.

Network ACLs should complement rather than duplicate every Security Group rule.

---

# Network ACL Statement

> **Use Network ACLs to enforce broad subnet and segment boundaries, block prohibited traffic classes, and provide defense in depth without creating unmanageable rule duplication.**

---

# Network ACL Objectives

Network ACLs should:

- Protect subnet boundaries
- Support defense in depth
- Block prohibited networks
- Block prohibited protocols
- Separate public and private subnets
- Separate management and data networks
- Support emergency containment
- Support stateless filtering
- Provide network-level evidence

---

# Network ACL Model

```text
Source Network

↓

Inbound ACL Evaluation

↓

Subnet

↓

Workload Security Group

↓

Destination Workload
```

Return traffic must also satisfy outbound ACL behavior because ACLs are stateless.

---

# Security Groups Versus Network ACLs

| Characteristic | Security Groups | Network ACLs |
|---|---|---|
| Enforcement Level | Workload or interface | Subnet or network segment |
| State | Stateful | Usually stateless |
| Primary Use | Fine-grained workload access | Broad network boundary |
| Rule Target | Workload, group, CIDR | CIDR, protocol, port |
| Return Traffic | Often automatic | Must be considered explicitly |
| Rule Evaluation | Provider-specific | Often ordered |
| Best Use | Service relationships | Segment-level restrictions |

---

# Network ACL Categories

ACLs may protect:

- Public Subnets
- Private Application Subnets
- Data Subnets
- Management Subnets
- Security Subnets
- Monitoring Subnets
- Customer Integration Subnets
- Partner Subnets
- Disaster-Recovery Subnets
- Restricted Data Subnets

---

# Public Subnet ACL

A public subnet ACL may permit:

- Approved Public Web Traffic
- Return Traffic
- Health Checks
- Required Provider Services

It should deny:

- Database Ports
- Administrative Ports
- Unapproved Protocols
- Known Malicious Networks Where Appropriate

---

# Private Application Subnet ACL

A private application subnet may permit:

- Traffic from Approved Load Balancers
- Internal Service Traffic
- Monitoring
- Deployment
- Approved Egress

---

# Data Subnet ACL

A data subnet should allow only:

- Approved Application Networks
- Approved Backup Networks
- Approved Monitoring Networks
- Approved Administrative Gateway

---

# Management Subnet ACL

Management networks should permit only:

- Privileged Access Gateways
- Infrastructure Management
- Monitoring
- Security
- Approved Provider Control Traffic

---

# Emergency Deny Rules

Network ACLs may support rapid blocking of:

- Compromised Address Ranges
- Malicious Partner Networks
- Misconfigured Internal Networks
- Unexpected Regional Traffic
- Data-Exfiltration Paths

Emergency rules must be governed and reviewed.

---

# ACL Rule Ordering

Where ACL rules are evaluated by number or order, the organization should define:

- Numbering Ranges
- Emergency Rule Range
- Mandatory Deny Range
- Standard Allow Range
- Default Deny
- Reserved Future Range

Example:

```text
100–199:
Emergency Deny

200–399:
Mandatory Security Rules

400–699:
Approved Application Rules

700–899:
Temporary Approved Rules

900:
Default Deny
```

Exact behavior should match the selected provider.

---

# Ephemeral Ports

Stateless ACLs may require return traffic through ephemeral port ranges.

These ranges should be:

- Documented
- Provider-Compatible
- Narrow Where Practical
- Tested
- Not Mistaken for Broad Application Access

---

# ACL Complexity

ACLs should not become exact duplicates of all Security Group policies.

Overly complex ACLs may create:

- Rule Conflicts
- Failed Return Traffic
- Troubleshooting Difficulty
- Deployment Risk
- Rule-Limit Exhaustion
- Hidden Outages

---

# Network ACL Quality Gates

- [ ] Subnet purpose is defined
- [ ] ACL owner is assigned
- [ ] Inbound and outbound behavior is documented
- [ ] Stateless return traffic is considered
- [ ] Rule ordering is understood
- [ ] Public and data subnets are separated
- [ ] Administrative ports are restricted
- [ ] Emergency deny process exists
- [ ] Default deny is active
- [ ] ACLs do not duplicate unnecessary workload rules
- [ ] Rules are tested
- [ ] Configuration is version-controlled
- [ ] Logging or flow visibility is active
- [ ] Recovery configuration exists

---

# Ingress Rules

Ingress Rules define which traffic may enter a workload, interface, subnet, product, environment, region, or enterprise boundary.

Ingress should be granted only when the destination has a valid reason to receive traffic.

---

# Ingress Rule Statement

> **Permit inbound communication only from approved sources to explicitly defined destinations using the minimum required protocol and port.**

---

# Ingress Rule Components

Every ingress rule should define:

- Rule ID
- Source
- Destination
- Protocol
- Port
- Direction
- Product
- Environment
- Region
- Customer or Tenant Scope
- Purpose
- Owner
- Approver
- Logging
- Creation Date
- Expiration
- Review Date
- Related Service
- Related Change

---

# Ingress Source Types

Sources may include:

- Public Internet
- Approved CIDR
- Security Group
- Service Identity
- Customer Network
- Partner Network
- Load Balancer
- API Gateway
- Monitoring Service
- Administrative Gateway
- Backup Service
- Disaster-Recovery Environment

---

# Ingress Destination Types

Destinations may include:

- Public Load Balancer
- Private Load Balancer
- API Gateway
- Application Service
- Database
- Cache
- Queue
- Search Service
- Monitoring Endpoint
- Administrative Interface
- Customer Integration Gateway

---

# Public Ingress

Public ingress should normally terminate at:

- CDN
- WAF
- Public Load Balancer
- API Gateway
- Zero Trust Gateway
- VPN Gateway

It should not normally terminate directly at:

- Database
- Cache
- Message Queue
- Administrative Console
- Internal Application Instance
- Monitoring Tool
- Security Platform

---

# Internal Ingress

Internal ingress should use approved sources such as:

- Specific Security Group
- Specific Service Identity
- Specific Subnet
- Specific Product Gateway
- Specific Customer Integration Zone

---

# Database Ingress

Database ingress should permit only required database clients.

Example:

```text
Source:
prod-restaurant-order-api-sg

Destination:
prod-restaurant-order-db-sg

Protocol:
TCP

Port:
5432
```

---

# Administrative Ingress

Administrative ingress should require:

- Zero Trust or Private Access
- Strong Authentication
- Named Identity
- Restricted Source
- Restricted Destination
- Time-Bound Access
- Session Audit

---

# Health-Check Ingress

Health-check access should include only approved:

- Load Balancers
- Monitoring Systems
- Provider Health Checkers

Health endpoints should not unnecessarily expose sensitive data.

---

# Partner Ingress

Partner ingress should define:

- Partner
- Source
- Authentication
- Encryption
- Destination
- Protocol
- Contract
- Rate Limit
- Monitoring
- Expiration or Review

---

# Customer Ingress

Customer private access should be limited to customer-specific gateways or services.

It should not provide broad network visibility.

---

# Ingress Rule Risks

Risks include:

- Public Exposure
- Broad CIDR
- Broad Port Range
- Wrong Environment
- Wrong Product
- Wrong Customer
- Missing Expiration
- Unowned Rule
- Source Spoofing
- Bypassed Gateway
- Direct Origin Exposure

---

# Ingress Quality Gates

- [ ] Destination requires inbound access
- [ ] Source is the narrowest practical scope
- [ ] Protocol is required
- [ ] Port is required
- [ ] Public access is approved
- [ ] Product and environment are correct
- [ ] Customer scope is correct
- [ ] Gateway cannot be bypassed
- [ ] Logging is active
- [ ] Owner and review date exist
- [ ] Temporary access expires
- [ ] Deny behavior is tested
- [ ] Rollback exists

---

# Egress Rules

Egress Rules define which destinations a workload, subnet, product, environment, or service may communicate with.

Outbound access must not be treated as harmless.

A compromised workload may use unrestricted egress to:

- Exfiltrate Data
- Contact Command-and-Control Infrastructure
- Download Malware
- Access Unauthorized SaaS
- Access Unapproved AI Models
- Access Unapproved Package Repositories
- Bypass Security Inspection
- Send Spam
- Scan External Networks

---

# Egress Rule Statement

> **Allow outbound communication only to approved destinations and services required for the workload’s defined purpose.**

---

# Egress Rule Components

Every egress rule should define:

- Source
- Destination
- Protocol
- Port
- Purpose
- Product
- Environment
- Region
- Data Classification
- Owner
- Provider
- Logging
- Expiration
- Review Date

---

# Egress Destination Types

Destinations may include:

- Internal Service
- Database
- Cache
- Queue
- Object Storage
- Logging Platform
- Monitoring Platform
- Approved SaaS
- Approved Model Provider
- Package Repository
- Operating-System Update Service
- Customer API
- Partner API
- Payment Provider
- Email Provider
- DNS Resolver

---

# Default Egress

Default unrestricted egress should be reviewed and progressively reduced.

At early maturity, broad egress may be controlled through:

- Central NAT
- Central Egress Firewall
- Proxy
- DNS Filtering
- Logging
- Threat Intelligence

At higher maturity, workload-specific allowlists should be introduced.

---

# Internet Egress

Internet access should pass through approved:

- NAT Gateway
- Egress Firewall
- Secure Proxy
- Cloud Firewall
- Service Gateway

Direct public addressing should be avoided for private workloads.

---

# SaaS Egress

SaaS access should define:

- Service
- Business Owner
- Technical Owner
- Domain or Address
- Protocol
- Data Classification
- Contract
- Risk
- Review Date

---

# AI Provider Egress

AI systems should communicate only with approved:

- Model Providers
- Embedding Providers
- Vector Services
- Tool APIs

Rules should account for:

- Data Classification
- Tenant
- Project
- Region
- Cost
- Model Policy
- Logging
- Human Approval Requirements

---

# Package Repository Egress

Build and runtime systems should access only approved:

- Language Package Registries
- Operating-System Repositories
- Container Registries
- Artifact Repositories

Where practical, internal mirrors should be used.

---

# DNS Egress

Workloads should use approved DNS resolvers.

Direct communication with arbitrary public DNS servers should be restricted where possible.

---

# Email Egress

Email traffic should use approved mail services.

Direct outbound SMTP from general workloads should be blocked unless explicitly required.

---

# Egress Data Protection

Egress controls should integrate with:

- Data-Loss Prevention
- Proxy Logging
- DNS Monitoring
- Threat Intelligence
- Anomaly Detection
- Application Logs
- Security Incident Response

---

# Egress Failure Mode

When approved destinations are unavailable, workloads should not automatically fall back to unapproved public endpoints.

Fallback must be explicitly governed.

---

# Egress Quality Gates

- [ ] Outbound destination is approved
- [ ] Business purpose is documented
- [ ] Data classification is reviewed
- [ ] Protocol and port are required
- [ ] Direct internet access is justified
- [ ] Approved egress path is used
- [ ] DNS is controlled
- [ ] Model and SaaS providers are approved
- [ ] Logging is active
- [ ] Threat monitoring is active
- [ ] Temporary access expires
- [ ] Failure behavior is documented
- [ ] Owner and review date exist

---

# Rule Management

Rule Management governs the creation, naming, review, testing, deployment, monitoring, modification, expiration, and removal of network-access rules.

Rule Management prevents security controls from becoming unstructured and unmaintainable.

---

# Rule Management Statement

> **Every network-access rule must have a defined lifecycle from request to retirement, with ownership, validation, monitoring, and evidence at every stage.**

---

# Rule Lifecycle

```text
Access Need Identified

↓

Rule Request Created

↓

Business and Technical Purpose Validated

↓

Security Risk Reviewed

↓

Rule Designed

↓

Policy and Conflict Checks

↓

Testing

↓

Approval

↓

Deployment

↓

Connectivity Validation

↓

Monitoring

↓

Periodic Review

↓

Modification or Retirement
```

---

# Rule Request

A request should include:

- Requester
- Product
- Environment
- Region
- Source
- Destination
- Protocol
- Port
- Purpose
- Duration
- Customer or Tenant
- Data Classification
- Risk
- Owner
- Testing Plan
- Rollback Plan

---

# Rule Approval

Approval should consider:

- Business Need
- Technical Need
- Security Risk
- Public Exposure
- Data Access
- Customer Impact
- Product Impact
- Availability
- Compliance
- Duration
- Existing Alternative

---

# Rule Naming

Rule names should communicate:

- Environment
- Product
- Source
- Destination
- Protocol or Purpose

Example:

```text
prod-platform-api-to-audit-service-https

prod-poultry-worker-to-event-queue-tls

customer-acme-vpn-to-acme-gateway-https
```

---

# Rule Documentation

Every rule should be linked to:

- Service
- Architecture
- Change
- Business Requirement
- Customer Contract Where Relevant
- Incident Where Relevant
- Risk or Exception Where Relevant

---

# Rule Ownership

The rule owner should confirm:

- Access is still required
- Source still exists
- Destination still exists
- Port is still correct
- Environment is still correct
- Customer or partner relationship is active
- Temporary access has expired or been renewed

---

# Rule Validation

Validation should include:

- Syntax Check
- Policy Check
- Conflict Check
- Duplicate Check
- Shadowing Check
- Public Exposure Check
- Cross-Environment Check
- Cross-Product Check
- Customer Isolation Check
- Port Check
- Expiration Check
- Owner Check

---

# Rule Testing

Testing should verify:

## Positive Test

Approved source can reach the approved destination.

## Negative Test

Unapproved source cannot reach the destination.

## Scope Test

The source cannot reach unrelated services.

## Environment Test

Non-production cannot reach production unless explicitly approved.

## Customer Test

One customer cannot reach another customer’s environment.

## Egress Test

The source cannot reach unapproved external destinations.

---

# Rule Deployment

Rule deployment should use:

- Infrastructure as Code
- Reviewed Pull Request
- Automated Validation
- Approved Pipeline
- Controlled Change Window
- Monitoring
- Rollback

---

# Rule Propagation

The system should understand:

- Provider Propagation Time
- Partial Deployment Behavior
- Region Propagation
- Failure Behavior
- Rollback Time

---

# Rule Recertification

Rules should be reviewed based on risk.

| Rule Type | Suggested Review |
|---|---|
| Emergency Rule | After incident and within days |
| Temporary Rule | Before expiration |
| Public Ingress | Quarterly |
| Database Access | Quarterly |
| Administrative Access | Quarterly |
| Customer or Partner Access | Quarterly or contract review |
| Standard Internal Access | Semiannually |
| Low-Risk Stable Rule | Annually |

---

# Rule Expiration

Temporary rules should be removed automatically where possible.

Expiration controls should include:

- Expiration Date
- Owner Notification
- Renewal Request
- Approval
- Automatic Deletion
- Post-Deletion Validation

---

# Stale Rule Detection

A rule may be stale when:

- No Traffic Matches
- Service Is Retired
- Source No Longer Exists
- Destination No Longer Exists
- Product Is Retired
- Customer Contract Ends
- Temporary Need Ends
- Rule Is Replaced

---

# Unused Rule Analysis

Unused does not always mean unnecessary.

A disaster-recovery rule may be rarely used but still required.

Review should consider:

- Service Purpose
- Recovery Need
- Seasonal Use
- Emergency Use
- Contractual Need

---

# Duplicate Rules

Duplicate rules should be consolidated to reduce:

- Complexity
- Review Burden
- Provider Limits
- Hidden Access
- Configuration Drift

---

# Shadowed Rules

Shadowed rules should be detected because they may create:

- False Security Assumptions
- Inconsistent Behavior
- Unnecessary Complexity

---

# Rule Conflict

A conflict may occur when:

- One rule allows and another denies.
- One product policy conflicts with an enterprise policy.
- A temporary rule bypasses a required gateway.
- A regional rule violates residency requirements.
- An egress rule permits a prohibited destination.

---

# Rule Removal

Removal should include:

- Impact Analysis
- Owner Confirmation
- Dependency Review
- Controlled Deployment
- Connectivity Validation
- Rollback
- Evidence

---

# Emergency Rule Management

Emergency rules may be created to:

- Block Attack Traffic
- Isolate a Workload
- Stop Data Exfiltration
- Restore Critical Connectivity
- Protect a Customer
- Support Disaster Recovery

They must be:

- Narrow
- Time-Bound
- Logged
- Approved
- Reviewed
- Reconciled Into Code
- Removed When No Longer Needed

---

# Rule Management Quality Gates

- [ ] Rule request is complete
- [ ] Owner is assigned
- [ ] Purpose is documented
- [ ] Source and destination are narrow
- [ ] Protocol and port are required
- [ ] Policy checks pass
- [ ] Duplicate and shadow checks pass
- [ ] Positive test passes
- [ ] Negative test passes
- [ ] Customer and environment isolation are validated
- [ ] Deployment is controlled
- [ ] Monitoring is active
- [ ] Expiration exists where temporary
- [ ] Rollback exists
- [ ] Evidence is retained

---

# Least-Privilege Networking

Least-Privilege Networking ensures that every workload receives only the network access required for its defined responsibilities.

It reduces the damage possible from:

- Compromised Credentials
- Vulnerable Applications
- Malware
- Misconfiguration
- Insider Threat
- Compromised AI Agent
- Supply-Chain Attack
- Stolen Workload Identity

---

# Least-Privilege Networking Statement

> **A workload should communicate only with the specific services required to complete its approved function and nothing more.**

---

# Least-Privilege Dimensions

Access should be minimized by:

- Source
- Destination
- Protocol
- Port
- Direction
- Environment
- Product
- Region
- Tenant
- Customer
- Identity
- Time
- Frequency
- Data Classification

---

# Role-Based Network Access

Network access may align with workload roles such as:

- Web Frontend
- API Service
- Background Worker
- Database
- Cache
- Queue
- Monitoring
- Security Tool
- AI Agent Runtime
- Backup Service

---

# Service-to-Service Least Privilege

A service should not receive access to an entire platform network when it requires only one API.

Preferred pattern:

```text
Order Service

↓

HTTPS

↓

Payment Service
```

Avoid:

```text
Order Service

↓

All Ports

↓

Entire Shared Platform Network
```

---

# Database Least Privilege

Database access should be limited by:

- Application Service
- Database
- Port
- Environment
- Region
- Administrative Path

Database authorization should further restrict:

- Schema
- Table
- Operation
- Role

---

# Administrative Least Privilege

Administrators should receive:

- Time-Bound Access
- Specific Environment
- Specific Service
- Specific Port
- Audited Session
- Approval
- Automatic Revocation

---

# AI Agent Least Privilege

AI agents should receive network access based on:

- Agent Identity
- Department
- Role
- Task
- Project
- Tenant
- Tool
- Model
- Time
- Risk
- Human Approval

Agents should not receive broad internal network access.

---

# Least-Privilege Discovery

To reduce excessive access, the organization may analyze:

- Actual Traffic
- Service Maps
- Distributed Traces
- Flow Logs
- Application Documentation
- Dependency Graphs
- Deployment Manifests

Observed traffic should support decisions but should not automatically authorize unknown communication.

---

# Access Reduction Process

```text
Current Access Inventoried

↓

Actual Required Paths Identified

↓

Unused or Broad Access Classified

↓

Replacement Rules Designed

↓

Controlled Narrowing

↓

Application Validation

↓

Monitoring

↓

Old Access Removed
```

---

# Least-Privilege Exceptions

Exceptions should define:

- Why Narrow Access Is Not Possible
- Compensating Controls
- Monitoring
- Risk
- Owner
- Expiration
- Remediation Plan

---

# Least-Privilege Quality Gates

- [ ] Access is tied to a defined workload purpose
- [ ] Source is narrow
- [ ] Destination is narrow
- [ ] Port is narrow
- [ ] Environment is explicit
- [ ] Product is explicit
- [ ] Customer or tenant scope is explicit
- [ ] Time boundary exists where appropriate
- [ ] Administrative access is temporary
- [ ] AI access is task-bounded
- [ ] Broad access has an approved exception
- [ ] Actual usage is reviewed
- [ ] Unnecessary access is removed

---

# Network Isolation

Network Isolation separates workloads, environments, products, tenants, customers, data zones, management systems, and security capabilities.

Isolation limits attack propagation and protects enterprise boundaries.

---

# Network Isolation Statement

> **Separate workloads according to trust, product, environment, customer, data sensitivity, operational function, and regional requirement so that compromise in one domain does not create unrestricted access to another.**

---

# Isolation Objectives

Network Isolation should:

- Reduce lateral movement
- Protect production
- Protect customer environments
- Protect tenant data
- Protect sensitive data
- Protect management systems
- Protect security systems
- Protect shared services
- Support incident containment
- Support regional compliance
- Support recovery
- Reduce blast radius

---

# Isolation Dimensions

Isolation may be based on:

- Environment
- Product
- Customer
- Tenant
- Region
- Data Classification
- Workload Type
- Administrative Function
- Security Function
- Recovery Function
- Compliance Boundary

---

# Environment Isolation

Separate:

- Development
- Testing
- Staging
- Production
- Recovery

Controls may include:

- Separate Accounts
- Separate Virtual Networks
- Separate Subnets
- Separate Security Groups
- Separate Identities
- Separate Credentials
- Separate Routing
- Separate DNS

---

# Product Isolation

Products should have:

- Product Networks or Segments
- Product Security Groups
- Product Routes
- Product Policies
- Product Observability
- Product Ownership

Communication with shared services should pass through approved interfaces.

---

# Customer Isolation

Customer-dedicated environments may require:

- Dedicated Network
- Dedicated Subnet
- Dedicated Security Group
- Dedicated Gateway
- Dedicated Private Endpoint
- Customer-Specific Routing
- Customer-Specific Monitoring

---

# Tenant Isolation

Shared multi-tenant products may use common infrastructure.

Network controls should complement:

- Tenant Identity
- Application Authorization
- Database Row-Level Security
- Tenant Data Partitioning

Network controls alone cannot provide complete logical tenant isolation.

---

# Data-Zone Isolation

Sensitive data zones should be separated from:

- Public Networks
- General Application Networks
- Development
- General Employee Access
- Unapproved Analytics
- Unapproved AI Services

---

# Management Isolation

Management systems should remain in restricted networks.

They may include:

- Infrastructure Management
- Kubernetes Control Access
- Database Administration
- Monitoring Administration
- Security Tools
- CI/CD Control Plane
- Secret Management
- Backup Administration

---

# Security-System Isolation

Security systems may require broad visibility but should remain protected from modification by general product workloads.

---

# Observability Isolation

Logging, metrics, and tracing systems should:

- Accept Telemetry From Approved Sources
- Restrict Administrative Access
- Prevent Product Workloads From Altering Evidence
- Support Separate Read and Write Paths

---

# Recovery Isolation

Disaster-recovery infrastructure should not be exposed unnecessarily during normal operations.

It should remain:

- Secure
- Synchronized
- Monitored
- Testable
- Operationally Accessible When Required

---

# Internet Isolation

Private workloads should avoid direct public addresses.

Outbound access should use controlled gateways.

---

# Kubernetes Isolation

Kubernetes isolation may use:

- Cluster Separation
- Namespace Separation
- Network Policies
- Service Accounts
- Ingress Controllers
- Egress Policies
- Node Pools
- Service Mesh
- Admission Controls

---

# Serverless Isolation

Serverless services should define:

- Public or Private Ingress
- Service Identity
- VPC Integration
- Egress Policy
- Private Endpoint Access
- Environment
- Product
- Region

---

# Isolation Validation

Isolation should be tested through:

- Connectivity Tests
- Deny Tests
- Cross-Environment Tests
- Cross-Product Tests
- Cross-Customer Tests
- Database Access Tests
- Administrative Access Tests
- Incident Containment Tests

---

# Isolation Failure

An isolation failure may include:

- Development Reaching Production
- One Product Reaching Another Product’s Database
- One Customer Reaching Another Customer’s Gateway
- Public Workload Reaching Management Systems
- Product Workload Modifying Security Logs
- AI Agent Reaching Unapproved Tools

---

# Network Isolation Quality Gates

- [ ] Environments are separated
- [ ] Products are separated
- [ ] Customer environments are isolated
- [ ] Tenant-sensitive paths are protected
- [ ] Data zones are restricted
- [ ] Management systems are isolated
- [ ] Security systems are isolated
- [ ] Observability evidence is protected
- [ ] Recovery environments are controlled
- [ ] Kubernetes policies are defined
- [ ] Serverless ingress and egress are defined
- [ ] Cross-boundary deny tests pass
- [ ] Incident containment is tested

---

# Access Governance

Access Governance defines how Network Access Control policies, rules, ownership, changes, exceptions, reviews, evidence, automation, and lifecycle are managed.

---

# Access Governance Statement

> **Network access must remain centrally standardized, locally accountable, continuously reviewed, technically validated, operationally observable, and formally revoked when no longer required.**

---

# Access Governance Objectives

Access Governance should:

- Maintain enterprise standards
- Assign accountability
- Control public exposure
- Control internal communication
- Control egress
- Govern temporary access
- Govern customer and partner access
- Prevent rule sprawl
- Prevent configuration drift
- Maintain access evidence
- Support compliance
- Support incident response
- Support recovery
- Govern AI-assisted access decisions
- Improve maturity

---

# Access Governance Structure

```text
Enterprise Security Governance

↓

Network and Cloud Security Architecture

↓

Platform and Infrastructure Engineering

↓

Product and Application Owners

↓

Security Operations and SRE

↓

Compliance and Audit

↓

Human and AI Contributors
```

---

# Access Ownership

Every access rule should define:

- Business Owner
- Technical Owner
- Security Owner
- Operational Owner
- Product Owner
- Customer Owner Where Applicable
- Documentation Owner
- Review Owner

---

# Access Roles

Potential roles include:

- Access Viewer
- Rule Requester
- Non-Production Rule Editor
- Production Rule Editor
- Security Reviewer
- Network Approver
- Emergency Access Operator
- Audit Reader
- Policy Administrator

---

# Privileged Access

Privileged network-access administration should require:

- Enterprise Identity
- MFA
- Named Accounts
- Least Privilege
- Just-in-Time Access Where Possible
- Approval
- Session Logging
- Access Review
- Rapid Revocation

---

# Automation Access

Automation should receive only the permissions required to:

- Create Approved Rule Types
- Modify Approved Environments
- Read Current State
- Validate Drift
- Remove Expired Rules

Automation should not receive unrestricted authority across all products and environments.

---

# AI-Assisted Access Governance

AI agents may support:

- Rule Risk Analysis
- Duplicate Detection
- Stale Rule Detection
- Policy Validation
- Dependency Mapping
- Access Recommendation
- Rule Documentation
- Review Summaries
- Incident Correlation

AI agents should not independently:

- Expose a Production Service Publicly
- Grant Database Access

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|

# NAC-L0 — Uncontrolled Access

Characteristics:

- Default groups
- Broad CIDR rules
- unrestricted egress
- no ownership
- manual console changes
- no expiration
- weak isolation
- limited logs

Exit requirements:

- Named groups
- default deny
- basic environment separation
- database isolation
- ownership
- logging
- initial rule inventory

---

# NAC-L1 — Standardized Access

Characteristics:

- Security Group standards
- basic network ACLs
- production separation
- public access inventory
- basic egress controls
- rule naming
- basic reviews

Exit requirements:

- Rule lifecycle
- temporary expiration
- infrastructure as code
- negative testing
- product isolation
- access governance
- drift detection

---

# NAC-L2 — Governed Access

Characteristics:

- Formal rule requests
- risk-based approval
- recurring reviews
- policy checks
- egress governance
- stale-rule detection
- rule evidence
- recovery configuration

Exit requirements:

- Multi-product isolation
- customer isolation
- regional controls
- AI traffic controls
- identity-aware rules
- continuous compliance

---

# NAC-L3 — Multi-Product Isolation

Characteristics:

- Products have dedicated rule patterns
- shared services expose controlled interfaces
- customer environments are isolated
- regional access is governed
- customer and partner access are reviewed
- unit-level visibility exists

Exit requirements:

- Workload identity
- dynamic policy validation
- automated stale-rule removal
- attack-aware access response
- AI-assisted analysis

---

# NAC-L4 — Identity-Aware Access

Characteristics:

- Service identity replaces broad address rules
- workload context is evaluated
- access is continuously validated
- temporary access expires automatically
- unused access is recommended for removal
- incident isolation is accelerated
- AI assists rule analysis

Exit requirements:

- Global policy intelligence
- reusable access blueprints
- bounded automated access reduction
- explainable decisions
- enterprise learning

---

# NAC-L5 — Intelligent Access Governance

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems inherit approved access-control blueprints.
- Access decisions consider identity, product, environment, tenant, customer, region, service, protocol, risk, and business purpose.
- Low-risk validation, cleanup, and expiration are automated.
- High-risk grants and public exposure remain human-approved.
- Access remains observable, explainable, auditable, recoverable, and reversible.
- Every incident improves access policy and enterprise knowledge.

# Part 14B-3D-2 Exit Criteria

Part **14B-3D-2 — Network Access Control** is complete when:

## Security Groups

- Security Group standards are documented.
- Groups are aligned with workload purpose.
- Default groups are restricted.
- Group-to-group references are preferred over broad IP rules where supported.
- Database, load-balancer, administrative, monitoring, AI, customer, and partner group patterns are defined.
- Ingress and egress behavior are governed.
- Provider limits are monitored.
- Security Groups are version-controlled and testable.

## Network ACLs

- Subnet and segment ACL responsibilities are documented.
- Stateful and stateless behavior is understood.
- Public, private, data, management, customer, and recovery subnet patterns are defined.
- Inbound and outbound return paths are tested.
- Rule ordering and numbering are governed.
- ACL complexity remains manageable.
- Emergency deny capability exists.
- ACL recovery is documented.

## Ingress Rules

- Every ingress path has an approved source, destination, protocol, port, purpose, owner, environment, region, and lifecycle.
- Public ingress terminates at approved gateways.
- Direct public access to databases and administrative services is prohibited.
- Internal, partner, customer, administrative, database, and health-check ingress patterns are documented.
- Public, broad, temporary, and high-risk rules receive elevated review.
- Positive and negative ingress tests pass.

## Egress Rules

- Internet egress uses approved gateways.
- Outbound destinations are identified and approved.
- SaaS, AI providers, package repositories, DNS, email, customer APIs, and partner APIs are governed.
- Data classification is considered before granting egress.
- Unrestricted egress is reduced according to maturity.
- Egress logging, threat monitoring, and failure behavior are defined.
- Temporary egress rules expire.

## Rule Management

- A complete rule lifecycle exists.
- Rule requests include business and technical purpose.
- Naming, documentation, ownership, review, testing, deployment, expiration, and retirement standards are defined.
- Duplicate, stale, shadowed, broad, and conflicting rules are detected.
- Rule deployment is controlled and reversible.
- Emergency rules are reconciled and reviewed.
- Evidence is retained.

## Least-Privilege Networking

- Access is reduced by source, destination, protocol, port, environment, product, region, tenant, customer, identity, and time.
- Service-to-service communication uses approved paths.
- Database access is workload-specific.
- Administrative access is time-bound and audited.
- AI-agent access is task- and project-bounded.
- Broad access requires approved exception and remediation.
- Actual traffic is reviewed to identify excessive access.

## Network Isolation

- Development, testing, staging, production, and recovery environments are separated.
- Products are isolated.
- Customer-dedicated environments are isolated.
- Tenant-sensitive paths are protected.
- Data, management, security, observability, and recovery zones are controlled.
- Kubernetes and serverless isolation patterns are defined.
- Cross-boundary deny tests pass.
- Incident containment is tested.

## Access Governance

- Access ownership and roles are defined.
- Privileged administration uses strong identity and least privilege.
- Automation rights are bounded.
- AI assistance remains bounded and auditable.
- Access risk levels NAC0–NAC5 are approved.
- Review cadences are defined.
- Exceptions are time-bound and monitored.
- Audits cover public, database, administrative, customer, partner, environment, and egress access.
- Monitoring, alerts, incidents, recovery, KPIs, risks, maturity, and roadmap are documented.
- High-risk access decisions remain human-governed.

---

# Part 14B-3D-2 Summary

Network Access Control converts the MianX.ai firewall and segmentation strategy into precise, enforceable communication rules.

The complete access-control lifecycle is:

```text
Communication Need Identified

↓

Source, Destination, Identity, Product, Environment, Region, and Purpose Defined

↓

Least-Privilege Rule Designed

↓

Security and Policy Validation

↓

Approval

↓

Controlled Deployment

↓

Positive and Negative Testing

↓

Monitoring and Review

↓

Narrowing, Renewal, or Revocation
```

The architecture is built around eight connected capabilities:

```text
Security Groups
Protect workloads and interfaces through stateful access controls

Network ACLs
Protect subnet and segment boundaries through stateless filtering

Ingress Rules
Control traffic entering services and networks

Egress Rules
Control outbound communication and data paths

Rule Management
Governs the complete access-rule lifecycle

Least-Privilege Networking
Limits communication to the minimum required paths

Network Isolation
Separates products, environments, customers, data, and management systems

Access Governance
Controls ownership, reviews, exceptions, monitoring, and recovery
```

MianX.ai Network Access Control must remain:

- Default-Deny
- Least-Privilege
- Identity-Aware
- Workload-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Environment-Aware
- Tenant-Aware
- Customer-Aware
- Region-Aware
- Ingress-Controlled
- Egress-Controlled
- Isolated
- Observable
- Testable
- Auditable
- Revocable
- Recoverable
- Version-Controlled
- Policy-Governed
- AI-Compatible
- Human-Accountable
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to create security groups and ACLs.

The objective is to ensure that every network connection in the MianX.ai enterprise exists for a validated reason, reaches only the correct destination, remains active only for the required duration, and can be explained, tested, monitored, revoked, and recovered.

# Part 14B-3D-3A — Zero Trust Foundation

Zero Trust Foundation defines the strategic, architectural, and operational basis through which MianX.ai verifies every user, device, workload, service, AI agent, application, and network request before granting access to enterprise resources.

Traditional network security often assumes that systems located inside a private network are trustworthy.

Zero Trust rejects this assumption.

A user, device, service, workload, application, AI agent, or network connection must not receive access merely because it is:

- Inside a Corporate Network
- Connected Through a VPN
- Running in a Private Subnet
- Hosted in the Same Cloud Account
- Located in the Same Kubernetes Cluster
- Connected to the Same Virtual Network
- Operating From an Approved Office
- Using an Internal IP Address
- Part of an Existing Customer Environment
- Previously Authenticated
- Managed by an Internal Team
- Created by an Automation System
- Registered as an AI Agent

Every access request must be evaluated according to current evidence.

That evidence may include:

- Identity
- Authentication Strength
- Device Trust
- Workload Identity
- Service Identity
- Product
- Environment
- Tenant
- Customer
- Project
- Region
- Network Context
- Resource Sensitivity
- Request Purpose
- Session State
- Time
- Behavior
- Risk
- Security Posture
- Human Approval Where Required

Zero Trust does not mean that every request must be blocked.

It means that no request receives implicit trust.

The complete model is:

```text
Never Trust Implicitly

↓

Verify Explicitly

↓

Grant Minimum Required Access

↓

Observe Continuously

↓

Re-Evaluate Continuously

↓

Revoke When Risk or Need Changes
```

---

# Zero Trust Foundation Statement

> **Build an identity-centered, context-aware, continuously verified, least-privilege, policy-enforced, observable, and human-governed network architecture in which no user, device, service, workload, customer, tenant, or AI agent receives access through implicit trust.**

---

# Executive Summary

MianX.ai will operate a distributed enterprise ecosystem containing:

- Human Employees
- Contractors
- Administrators
- Customers
- Partners
- Developers
- Support Teams
- AI Agents
- AI Workforce Departments
- Applications
- APIs
- Microservices

- Cloud Services
- Customer-Dedicated Environments
- Private Integrations
- Marketplace Plugins
- Developer Tools
- Security Platforms
- Observability Platforms
- Regional Infrastructure
- Disaster-Recovery Infrastructure

These identities and systems will communicate across:

- Public Internet
- Private Networks
- Virtual Networks
- Cloud Accounts
- Multiple Regions
- Kubernetes Clusters
- Customer Networks
- Partner Networks
- Developer Devices
- Administrative Systems
- Edge Infrastructure
- Service Meshes
- API Gateways
- Private Endpoints

A traditional perimeter-only model cannot safely govern such an environment.

Once an attacker, compromised workload, malicious insider, stolen credential, or unsafe AI agent enters a trusted network, unrestricted internal access may enable:

- Lateral Movement
- Privilege Escalation
- Data Exfiltration
- Cross-Tenant Access
- Cross-Customer Access
- Cross-Environment Access
- Database Compromise
- Administrative-System Compromise
- Security-Platform Compromise
- AI Tool Abuse
- Unauthorized Model Access
- Supply-Chain Compromise
- Business-Continuity Disruption

Zero Trust reduces this risk by replacing network-based trust with explicit identity, policy, context, and continuous verification.

The preferred Zero Trust evolution path is:

```text
Traditional Network Perimeter

↓

Strong Identity and MFA

↓

Application-Level Access

↓

Device and Workload Trust

↓

Least-Privilege Network Segmentation

↓

Continuous Verification

↓

Context-Aware Policy Enforcement

↓

Multi-Product Zero Trust Platform

↓

Adaptive Enterprise Zero Trust
```

The objective is not to eliminate all networks, firewalls, VPNs, or security groups.

The objective is to stop treating those controls as proof of trust.

Zero Trust works with:

- Firewalls
- Security Groups
- Network ACLs
- Identity Providers
- Zero Trust Access Gateways
- Service Meshes
- API Gateways
- Workload Identity
- Mutual TLS
- Endpoint Security
- Device Management
- Policy Engines
- Monitoring
- Security Analytics

The complete security model should remain layered:

```text
Identity Verification

+

Device or Workload Verification

+

Network Policy

+

Application Authorization

+

Data Authorization

+

Continuous Monitoring

+

Governance
```

---

# Zero Trust Mission

The mission of the Zero Trust Network is to ensure that every access request to MianX.ai resources is explicitly verified, minimally authorized, continuously observed, and rapidly revocable.

The Zero Trust architecture must:

- Eliminate implicit network trust
- Verify human identities
- Verify service identities
- Verify workload identities
- Evaluate device posture
- Evaluate request context
- Enforce least privilege
- Restrict lateral movement
- Protect applications
- Protect APIs
- Protect databases
- Protect administrative services
- Protect customer environments
- Protect tenant boundaries
- Protect AI tools and agents
- Protect multi-cloud environments
- Support remote access
- Support regional access
- Support customer private connectivity
- Support continuous risk evaluation
- Support rapid access revocation
- Produce complete audit evidence
- Preserve human oversight for critical access

---

# Zero Trust Objectives

Zero Trust should:

- Remove trust based solely on network location
- Reduce broad VPN access
- Reduce lateral movement
- Reduce standing privilege
- Reduce shared access
- Reduce long-lived credentials
- Improve administrative security
- Improve application isolation
- Improve product isolation
- Improve customer isolation
- Improve tenant isolation
- Improve service-to-service security
- Improve AI-agent access control
- Improve session security
- Improve access evidence
- Improve incident containment
- Improve revocation speed
- Support regional and regulatory requirements
- Support enterprise-scale automation
- Maintain operational usability
- Maintain service availability

---

# Zero Trust Scope

Zero Trust Foundation applies to:

- Human User Access
- Administrative Access
- Developer Access
- Customer Access
- Partner Access
- Contractor Access
- Service-to-Service Access
- Workload-to-Workload Access
- AI Agent Access
- API Access
- Database Access

- Remote Workforce Access
- Multi-Cloud Communication

- Disaster-Recovery Access
- Security-System Access
- Observability-System Access
- Deployment-System Access
- Secret-Management Access

---

# Zero Trust Non-Scope

Zero Trust does not replace:

- Secure Coding
- Application Authorization
- Database Authorization
- Data Encryption
- Firewalls
- Security Groups
- Network ACLs
- Endpoint Protection
- Vulnerability Management
- DDoS Protection
- WAF
- API Security
- Secret Management
- Backup
- Disaster Recovery
- Business Continuity
- Security Awareness
- Compliance Governance

Zero Trust coordinates and strengthens these controls.

It should not become a marketing label applied to ordinary VPN or identity systems.

---

# Zero Trust Philosophy

Zero Trust Philosophy defines the beliefs guiding every access decision across the MianX.ai enterprise.

---

# Zero Trust Philosophy Statement

> **Trust must never be inherited from location, network, device ownership, previous authentication, organizational role, or system origin; trust must be continuously earned through verified identity, approved context, minimum privilege, and observable behavior.**

---

# Never Trust Implicitly

No identity or system should receive automatic trust because it is:

- Internal
- Private
- Corporate
- Cloud-Hosted
- Managed
- Previously Approved
- Located in Production
- Connected Through VPN
- Created by an Administrator
- Created by an AI Workflow
- Part of a Trusted Product

Every request must be evaluated independently.

---

# Verify Explicitly

Verification should use all relevant available signals.

For human users, signals may include:

- Identity
- Passwordless or Strong Authentication
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Device
- Location
- Risk
- Role
- Session Age
- Requested Resource
- Privileged Action
- Behavior

For workloads and services, signals may include:

- Service Identity
- Workload Identity
- Certificate
- Deployment
- Product
- Environment
- Region
- Namespace
- Service Account
- Runtime
- Image
- Security Posture
- Requested Resource

For AI agents, signals may include:

- Agent Identity
- Agent Role
- Department
- Project
- Tenant
- Task
- Tool
- Model
- Budget
- Human Approval
- Risk Classification
- Execution Context

---

# Least Privilege by Default

Access should be limited to:

- Required Resource
- Required Action
- Required Environment
- Required Product
- Required Tenant
- Required Region
- Required Duration
- Required Protocol
- Required Data
- Required Tool

Access should not be granted based on broad organizational membership alone.

---

# Assume Breach

Zero Trust architecture should assume that:

- Credentials may be stolen
- Devices may be compromised
- Workloads may be vulnerable
- Internal networks may be penetrated
- Service identities may be abused
- Administrators may make mistakes
- Partners may be compromised
- AI agents may act incorrectly
- Security tools may fail
- Cloud accounts may be misconfigured

Architecture should therefore limit blast radius.

---

# Continuous Verification

Trust should not remain valid indefinitely after one successful authentication.

Access should be re-evaluated when:

- Session Age Increases
- Device Posture Changes
- User Role Changes
- Risk Increases
- Location Changes
- Behavior Changes
- Resource Sensitivity Changes
- Privileged Action Is Requested
- Security Incident Occurs
- Workload Version Changes
- Certificate Changes
- Agent Task Changes
- Tenant Context Changes

---

# Access Is Contextual

An identity may be permitted to access one resource but denied another.

Example:

```text
Developer

Allowed:
Staging Application Logs

Denied:
Production Customer Database
```

Similarly:

```text
AI Support Agent

Allowed:
Customer Support Knowledge Base

Denied:
Production Billing Database
```

---

# Identity Is Not Authorization

Authentication proves who or what an identity is.

Authorization determines what it may do.

A valid identity does not automatically receive broad access.

---

# Networks Are Transport, Not Trust

Private networks remain useful for:

- Isolation
- Traffic Control
- Performance
- Compliance
- Reduced Public Exposure

However, private network location is not proof of authorization.

---

# Sessions Are Temporary

Sessions should be:

- Time-Bound
- Revocable
- Risk-Aware
- Resource-Aware
- Device-Aware
- Audited

Long-lived sessions should not remain valid without re-evaluation.

---

# Access Must Be Explainable

Every critical access decision should answer:

- Who requested access?
- Which identity was verified?
- Which device or workload was used?
- Which resource was requested?
- Which policy applied?
- Which context was evaluated?
- Why was access allowed or denied?
- How long was access granted?
- Who approved privileged access?
- How can access be revoked?

---

# Human Accountability

Zero Trust automation must not remove accountability.

High-impact actions such as:

- Global Administrative Access
- Production Database Access
- Security-Control Changes
- Disaster-Recovery Activation
- Cross-Customer Access
- AI Agent Privilege Expansion
- Certificate Authority Access
- Identity-Provider Administration

should retain authorized human approval.

---

# Zero Trust Principles

The following Zero Trust Principles are mandatory.

---

## 1. Never Trust Based on Location

Private network location does not establish trust.

---

## 2. Verify Every Identity

Human, service, workload, device, customer, partner, and AI-agent identities must be verifiable.

---

## 3. Deny by Default

Access without an approved policy must be denied.

---

## 4. Grant Least Privilege

Access should remain limited to the minimum necessary scope.

---

## 5. Use Strong Authentication

Privileged and sensitive access should require strong authentication.

---

## 6. Use Multi-Factor Authentication

MFA should be required for:

- Administrators
- Security Teams
- Infrastructure Teams
- Production Access
- Sensitive Customer Operations
- High-Risk Actions

---

## 7. Use Short-Lived Credentials

Prefer:

- Short-Lived Tokens
- Temporary Credentials
- Rotating Certificates
- Federated Identity
- Workload Identity

over long-lived static secrets.

---

## 8. Verify Device or Workload Posture

Identity alone may be insufficient for sensitive access.

---

## 9. Separate Authentication and Authorization

A valid identity must still pass resource-specific authorization.

---

## 10. Continuously Re-Evaluate Access

Access should adapt to changing risk and context.

---

## 11. Protect East-West Traffic

Internal service-to-service communication should be authenticated and authorized.

---

## 12. Protect North-South Traffic

External and administrative traffic must pass through approved policy enforcement.

---

## 13. Use Application-Level Access

Where practical, provide access to applications rather than broad networks.

---

## 14. Reduce Broad VPN Access

VPN access should not automatically expose entire internal networks.

---

## 15. Use Service Identity

Services should authenticate through approved machine identities.

---

## 16. Use Workload Identity

Cloud, container, Kubernetes, and serverless workloads should avoid shared static credentials.

---

## 17. Encrypt Communication

Sensitive and production traffic should use approved encryption.

---

## 18. Segment Continuously

Products, environments, customers, tenants, workloads, and data zones should remain isolated.

---

## 19. Observe Every Critical Decision

Authentication, authorization, denial, elevation, and revocation events should be logged.

---

## 20. Revoke Rapidly

Compromised or unnecessary access should be removable immediately.

---

## 21. Use Just-In-Time Privilege

Privileged access should be granted only when needed and for a limited time.

---

## 22. Avoid Shared Identities

Every human and workload should use a distinct accountable identity.

---

## 23. Protect the Identity Plane

Identity providers, policy engines, certificate authorities, and access gateways are critical infrastructure.

---

## 24. Validate Policy Continuously

Policies should be tested, monitored, and compared with deployed behavior.

---

## 25. Preserve Availability

Zero Trust controls should be highly available and recoverable.

---

## 26. Provide Safe Failure Behavior

Failure behavior should be defined for identity, policy, device, and access systems.

---

## 27. Maintain Break-Glass Access

Emergency access should exist but remain:

- Restricted
- Strongly Authenticated
- Time-Bound
- Audited
- Reviewed

---

## 28. Govern AI-Agent Access

AI agents must receive bounded, task-specific, tenant-specific, and tool-specific access.

---

## 29. Automate Low-Risk Enforcement

Policy validation, session expiration, stale-access detection, and evidence collection may be automated.

---

## 30. Retain Human Approval for Critical Access

High-risk privilege and policy decisions must remain human-governed.

---

# Zero Trust Architecture

Zero Trust Architecture defines how identity, devices, workloads, policies, enforcement points, applications, networks, and monitoring systems work together.

---

# Zero Trust Reference Architecture

```text
User, Device, Service, Workload, Customer, Partner, or AI Agent

↓

Identity and Credential Verification

↓

Device or Workload Posture Evaluation

↓

Context and Risk Evaluation

↓

Policy Decision

├── Deny
├── Require Stronger Authentication
├── Require Device Compliance
├── Require Human Approval
├── Grant Limited Access
└── Grant Temporary Privileged Access

↓

Policy Enforcement Point

↓

Application, API, Service, Tool, or Data Resource

↓

Application and Data Authorization

↓

Continuous Session and Behavior Monitoring

↓

Re-Evaluation, Restriction, or Revocation
```

---

- Session Management

# Zero Trust Control Flow

```text
Access Request

↓

Identity Validation

↓

Credential Validation

↓

Device or Workload Validation

↓

Context Collection

↓

Risk Evaluation

↓

Policy Decision

↓

Policy Enforcement

↓

Resource-Level Authorization

↓

Session Monitoring

↓

Continuous Re-Evaluation
```

---

# Zero Trust Architecture Layers

## Layer 1 — Identity

Answers:

- Who or what is requesting access?

---

## Layer 2 — Device or Workload

Answers:

- From which device, workload, runtime, or execution context?

---

## Layer 3 — Network and Location

Answers:

- Through which network, region, gateway, or connection?

Location is context, not trust.

---

## Layer 4 — Application and Service

Answers:

- Which application, API, service, or tool is requested?

---

## Layer 5 — Data

Answers:

- Which data class, tenant, customer, project, or record is involved?

---

## Layer 6 — Policy

Answers:

- Which rule permits or denies the request?

---

## Layer 7 — Monitoring and Response

Answers:

- Is the session behaving safely?
- Should access remain active?

# Fail-Open Versus Fail-Closed

The failure mode should reflect resource criticality.

## Fail Closed

Suitable for:

- Security Platforms
- Sensitive Databases
- Privileged APIs
- Customer Data

## Controlled Degraded Access

May be suitable for:

## Fail Open

Should remain exceptional and strongly justified.

# Zero Trust Networking

Zero Trust Networking applies Zero Trust principles to network communication.

It replaces broad network trust with identity-aware, service-aware, application-aware, and context-aware access.

---

# Zero Trust Networking Statement

> **Network connectivity should be granted to specific identities for specific services under specific conditions rather than to entire users, devices, subnets, products, or networks.**

---

# Zero Trust Networking Objectives

Zero Trust Networking should:

- Reduce implicit trust
- Reduce flat networks
- Reduce broad VPN access
- Restrict lateral movement
- Improve service identity
- Improve workload identity
- Improve micro-segmentation
- Improve administrative access
- Protect shared services
- Protect databases
- Protect customer environments
- Protect AI tools
- Support continuous verification
- Support rapid isolation
- Maintain traffic visibility

---

# Traditional Network Access

A traditional model may operate as:

```text
User Connects to VPN

↓

User Enters Internal Network

↓

User Can Reach Many Internal Services
```

This creates excessive trust.

---

# Zero Trust Network Access

A Zero Trust model should operate as:

```text
User Requests Specific Application

↓

Identity Verified

↓

Device and Context Evaluated

↓

Application Policy Evaluated

↓

Access Granted Only to That Application
```

The user does not automatically enter the complete internal network.

---

# Application-Level Access

Application-level access should be preferred for:

- Administrative Portals
- Internal Applications
- Developer Tools
- Security Dashboards
- Customer Support Tools
- Staging Environments
- Product Management Systems
- Infrastructure Consoles

---

# Network-Level Access

Network-level access may still be required for:

- Legacy Protocols
- Database Administration
- Infrastructure Management
- Customer Private Integration
- Specialized Tools

Such access should remain:

- Narrow
- Temporary Where Possible
- Identity-Aware
- Monitored
- Audited

---

# Zero Trust Segmentation

Zero Trust Networking should segment by:

- Product
- Environment
- Customer
- Tenant
- Region
- Workload
- Service
- Data Classification
- Administrative Function
- Security Function
- Recovery Function

---

East-west traffic is communication between internal workloads or services.

It should require:

- Service Identity
- Workload Identity
- Mutual Authentication
- Authorization
- Encryption
- Network Policy
- Logging
- Continuous Monitoring

---

North-south traffic is communication entering or leaving a controlled environment.

It should pass through approved:

- Edge Gateway

- DDoS Protection
- Rate Limiting
- Authentication

# Zero Trust Foundation Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| ZTF0 | Implicit Trust | Network location and VPN provide broad access |
| ZTF1 | Identity Foundation | Strong identity, MFA, and basic application access |
| ZTF2 | Governed Zero Trust | Device, workload, policy, least privilege, and continuous reviews |
| ZTF3 | Multi-Product Zero Trust | Product, customer, tenant, region, and AI access are governed |
| ZTF4 | Adaptive Zero Trust | Continuous risk evaluation and automated low-risk enforcement |
| ZTF5 | Intelligent Enterprise Zero Trust | Policy-driven global access with bounded AI assistance |

---

# ZTF0 — Implicit Trust

Characteristics:

- Broad VPN access
- private-network trust
- shared accounts
- long-lived credentials
- limited MFA
- flat networks
- limited service identity
- weak session monitoring

Exit requirements:

- Central identity
- MFA
- named accounts
- application inventory
- basic access gateway
- initial segmentation
- access logging

---

# ZTF1 — Identity Foundation

Characteristics:

- Enterprise identity
- MFA for administrators
- basic identity-aware access
- named service accounts
- initial device management
- limited application-level access
- basic session controls

Exit requirements:

- Workload identity
- device posture
- policy decision model
- just-in-time access
- stronger segmentation
- continuous verification
- access reviews

---

# ZTF2 — Governed Zero Trust

Characteristics:

- Zero Trust policies
- application-level access
- service identity
- workload identity
- device posture
- short-lived credentials
- privileged access governance
- continuous logs
- revocation processes

Exit requirements:

- Multi-product policies
- customer and tenant controls
- AI-agent identity
- regional context
- unified policy enforcement
- adaptive risk signals

---

# ZTF3 — Multi-Product Zero Trust

Characteristics:

- Products inherit Zero Trust standards
- customers and tenants are isolated
- shared services require identity
- AI agents use task-bound access
- regional access is governed
- administrative access is just-in-time
- service-to-service identity is standard

Exit requirements:

- Continuous risk scoring
- automated policy validation
- behavioral signals
- adaptive sessions
- automated low-risk response
- centralized policy intelligence

---

# ZTF4 — Adaptive Zero Trust

Characteristics:

- Access decisions use dynamic risk
- sessions are continuously re-evaluated
- non-compliant access is automatically restricted
- low-risk remediation is automated
- AI assists policy analysis
- privileged access is continuously monitored
- workload behavior influences access

Exit requirements:

- Global policy intelligence
- reusable Zero Trust blueprints
- bounded automated containment
- explainable AI decisions
- enterprise-wide learning

---

# ZTF5 — Intelligent Enterprise Zero Trust

Characteristics:

- New Industry Operating Systems inherit approved Zero Trust blueprints.
- Access decisions consider identity, device, workload, product, tenant, customer, project, task, region, resource, behavior, and risk.
- Low-risk access validation, expiration, and restriction are automated.
- High-risk privilege and policy changes remain human-approved.
- Every decision remains explainable, observable, auditable, reversible, and recoverable.
- Every incident improves Zero Trust policy and enterprise knowledge.

# Zero Trust Foundation Roadmap

## Phase 1 — Identity and Access Foundation

- Centralize identity
- require MFA for privileged users
- remove shared administrative accounts
- inventory internal applications
- inventory service accounts
- establish access logging
- assign ownership
- define initial Zero Trust policy

---

## Phase 2 — Application-Level Access

- Deploy identity-aware access gateway
- protect administrative applications
- protect staging and internal tools
- reduce broad VPN access
- define session policies
- define break-glass access
- add device posture for privileged access
- integrate revocation

---

## Phase 3 — Service and Workload Identity

- Introduce workload identity
- introduce short-lived service credentials
- implement mutual TLS where justified
- protect Kubernetes workloads
- protect serverless workloads
- reduce static secrets
- add service authorization
- centralize identity telemetry

---

## Phase 4 — Multi-Product Zero Trust

- Define product access blueprints
- define customer access patterns
- define tenant access patterns
- govern AI-agent identities
- protect shared platform services
- add regional policy
- add customer-dedicated controls
- strengthen administrative access

---

## Phase 5 — Continuous and Adaptive Verification

- Add risk-based access
- add behavioral signals
- add continuous session validation
- automate credential and session revocation
- add device and workload re-evaluation
- add policy drift detection
- automate low-risk access restriction
- improve incident isolation

---

## Phase 6 — Intelligent Enterprise Zero Trust

- Add AI-assisted policy analysis
- create reusable Zero Trust blueprints
- automate evidence collection
- automate stale-access removal within guardrails
- support global multi-region policy
- add bounded automated containment
- preserve human approval for critical access
- continuously improve through operational learning

---
