# Intelligence Engine Quality Gates

Before an intelligence capability becomes production-ready:

- [ ] Business purpose is documented.
- [ ] Intelligence owner is assigned.
- [ ] Source systems are approved.
- [ ] Metric definitions are standardized.
- [ ] Data quality is validated.
- [ ] Product and tenant isolation are tested.
- [ ] Model or rule version is recorded.
- [ ] Evidence is traceable.
- [ ] Confidence is measurable.
- [ ] Assumptions and limitations are visible.
- [ ] Explainability is available.
- [ ] Bias and fairness are evaluated where relevant.
- [ ] Security and privacy controls are active.
- [ ] Human approval is defined for high-risk use.
- [ ] Monitoring is operational.
- [ ] Drift detection exists where required.
- [ ] Outcomes can be measured.
- [ ] Rollback or retirement is defined.
- [ ] Recovery is tested.
- [ ] Documentation is complete.

---

# Exit Criteria

Part **20 — Intelligence Engine Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified Enterprise Intelligence Architecture is defined.
- Data, knowledge, memory, automation, product, customer, research, and operational sources are integrated through governed interfaces.
- Enterprise metric definitions are standardized.
- Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive, strategic, operational, product, customer, security, and AI Workforce intelligence models are defined.
- Insight, Forecasting, Recommendation, Risk, Opportunity, Scenario, Optimization, and Decision Support services are established.
- Product, tenant, customer, regional, and permission boundaries are enforced.
- Every material intelligence result preserves evidence, context, confidence, assumptions, limitations, model version, and ownership.
- Forecast and recommendation outcomes are measurable.
- Model validation, drift detection, monitoring, rollback, and retirement are operational.
- Intelligence supports AI agents without granting uncontrolled authority.
- High-risk intelligence requires accountable human review.
- Security, privacy, bias, and access controls are enforced.
- Multi-product and Industry Operating System intelligence blueprints are reusable.
- Intelligence remains explainable, evidence-based, governed, auditable, recoverable, and long-term maintainable.

# Final Summary

The Intelligence Engine Roadmap establishes the enterprise decision-support capability of MianX.ai.

The complete intelligence lifecycle is:

```text
Enterprise Question or Signal Identified

↓

Trusted Data, Knowledge, Memory, and Research Retrieved

↓

Quality, Context, Permissions, and Freshness Validated

↓

Analysis, Model, or Rule Executed

↓

Insight, Forecast, Risk, Opportunity, or Recommendation Produced

↓

Evidence, Confidence, Assumptions, and Limitations Attached

↓

Authorized Human or Workflow Reviews the Intelligence

↓

Decision or Approved Action Occurs

↓

Actual Outcome Measured

↓

Future Intelligence Improved
```

The Intelligence Engine connects:

```text
Data Platform
Provides governed enterprise data

Knowledge Platform
Provides approved organizational knowledge

Memory Engine
Provides historical context and experience

Automation Platform
Executes approved responses

Intelligence Engine
Transforms evidence into understanding and decision support

Human Leadership
Provides accountability, judgment, and final authority
```

MianX.ai Intelligence must remain:

- Evidence-Based
- Explainable
- Context-Aware
- Source-Linked
- Confidence-Aware
- Time-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Tenant-Aware
- Customer-Aware
- Permission-Aware
- Secure
- Privacy-Preserving
- Bias-Aware
- Measurable
- Governed
- Auditable
- Recoverable
- AI-Compatible
- Human-Accountable
- Continuously Improving

The objective is not merely to display reports or generate AI predictions.

The objective is to create one governed enterprise intelligence system that helps every authorized human, AI agent, product, department, customer operation, and future Industry Operating System understand current conditions, anticipate future outcomes, detect risks and opportunities, evaluate possible scenarios, and make better decisions.

# Part 21 — Marketplace Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The Marketplace Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will create, operate, secure, govern, monetize, and scale a trusted ecosystem for distributing reusable enterprise capabilities.

The MianX.ai Marketplace will allow approved internal teams, developers, technology partners, industry experts, implementation partners, and AI solution providers to publish reusable assets that extend the MianX.ai Enterprise AI Operating System without modifying or fragmenting its core architecture.

Marketplace assets may include:

- AI Agents
- Agent Skills
- Workflows
- Automation Templates
- Plugins
- Integrations
- Connectors
- Industry Modules
- Business Templates
- Knowledge Packs
- Reports
- Dashboards
- AI Models
- Prompt Packages
- Developer Tools
- Design Assets
- Compliance Packs
- Data Connectors
- Operational Playbooks

The Marketplace will connect:

```text
MianX Core Platform

+

AI Operating System

+

Plugin Framework

+

Developer Platform

+

Partner Ecosystem

+

Industry Expertise

↓

Governed Marketplace

↓

Reusable Enterprise Capabilities
```

The Marketplace must not become an uncontrolled collection of scripts, prompts, agents, plugins, or third-party applications.

Every marketplace asset must have:

- Verified Publisher
- Unique Identity
- Defined Purpose
- Version
- Compatibility Range
- Declared Permissions
- Security Review
- Quality Review
- License
- Documentation
- Support Policy
- Update Policy
- Deprecation Policy
- Usage Metrics
- Audit History

Trust, security, compatibility, quality, transparency, and enterprise governance are the foundations of the Marketplace.

The objective is to build an ecosystem where MianX.ai and approved partners can create a capability once and distribute it safely across multiple products, tenants, customers, industries, and regions.

```text

↓
```

# Marketplace Principles

## 1. Trust Before Growth

Marketplace growth must not weaken enterprise security, quality, privacy, reliability, or customer trust.

---

## 2. Verified Publishers

Only approved identities should publish assets to production marketplace channels.

---

## 3. Security Before Publication

Marketplace assets must complete risk-appropriate security validation before public or enterprise distribution.

---

## 4. Permissions Must Be Transparent

Customers must understand which:

- Data
- APIs
- Tools
- Services
- AI Models
- External Systems

an asset can access.

---

## 5. Least-Privilege Installation

Marketplace assets should receive only the permissions required for their documented purpose.

---

## 6. Compatibility Must Be Explicit

Every asset must declare supported:

- Platform Versions
- API Versions
- Products
- Environments
- Regions
- Dependencies
- Runtime Requirements

---

## 7. Assets Must Be Versioned

Every published asset must use controlled versioning.

---

## 8. Updates Must Be Governed

An asset update must not silently gain new permissions or introduce breaking behavior.

---

## 9. Customer Control Must Remain

Customers should control:

- Installation
- Configuration
- Update Policy
- Access
- Disablement
- Removal

subject to enterprise policy.

---

## 10. Tenant Isolation Is Mandatory

Assets must not access another tenant’s data, memory, workflows, configurations, or resources.

---

## 11. Core Platform Integrity Must Be Protected

Marketplace extensions should use stable APIs, events, SDKs, and plugin contracts rather than modifying core code.

---

## 12. Documentation Is Mandatory

Every production asset must include sufficient installation, configuration, operation, security, support, and removal guidance.

---

## 13. Publishers Remain Accountable

Publishers are responsible for:

- Security
- Quality
- Maintenance
- Compatibility
- Support
- Licensing
- Incident Cooperation

---

## 14. Reviews Must Be Authentic

Ratings and reviews must come from valid marketplace usage and remain protected from manipulation.

---

## 15. High-Risk Assets Require Stronger Review

Agents, models, security integrations, financial workflows, healthcare modules, and production-management tools require enhanced review.

---

## 16. Marketplace Assets Must Be Observable

Important marketplace assets should expose:

- Health
- Errors
- Usage
- Performance
- Cost
- Security Events
- Version

---

## 17. Removal Must Be Safe

Asset removal should define:

- Data Handling
- Dependency Impact
- Configuration Cleanup
- Credential Revocation
- Workflow Migration
- Retention
- Recovery

---

## 18. Marketplace Revenue Must Be Transparent

Pricing, fees, commissions, taxes, refunds, and publisher payouts must be clearly documented.

---

## 19. Regional Requirements Must Be Respected

Distribution should account for:

- Data Residency
- Regulations
- Language
- Currency
- Tax
- Licensing
- Product Availability

---

## 20. Human Governance Remains

AI may assist review, categorization, support, fraud detection, and recommendations, but high-risk approval and enforcement remain human-governed.

# Marketplace Asset Identity

Every asset should have:

- Marketplace Asset ID
- Package ID
- Display Name
- Publisher ID
- Asset Type
- Product Scope

Asset identity should remain stable across versions.

---

# Marketplace Package Standard

A marketplace package should contain an approved manifest.

Example:

```yaml
asset:
  id: com.mianx.example.asset
  name: Example Asset
  type: workflow
  version: 1.0.0

publisher:
  id: verified-publisher-id

compatibility:
  platform: ">=1.0.0 <2.0.0"
  products:
    - restaurant-os

permissions:
  - workflow.read
  - notification.send

runtime:
  type: managed

security:
  classification: standard

support:
  channel: publisher
  policy: standard
```

The exact format should be defined by the Plugin Framework and Marketplace standards.

# Marketplace Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| MK-L0 | Internal Asset Sharing | Assets are shared manually without a formal marketplace |
| MK-L1 | Governed Internal Catalog | Internal assets use identity, metadata, versions, and review |
| MK-L2 | Partner Marketplace | Verified partners publish approved assets |
| MK-L3 | Public Enterprise Marketplace | Customers discover, purchase, install, update, and review assets |
| MK-L4 | Multi-Industry Marketplace | Industry, regional, public, and private marketplace channels operate |
| MK-L5 | Global Intelligent Ecosystem | A governed global ecosystem continuously distributes enterprise intelligence and capabilities |

Before an asset becomes production-ready:

- [ ] Publisher identity is verified.
- [ ] Asset identity is unique.

- [ ] Asset type is correctly classified.
- [ ] Version is defined.
- [ ] Compatibility is declared.
- [ ] Dependencies are declared.

- [ ] Quality review is complete.

- [ ] Documentation is complete.
- [ ] Support policy exists.

# Exit Criteria

Part **21 — Marketplace Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified Marketplace architecture is defined.
- Marketplace asset types and package standards are documented.
- Public, private, internal, industry, and regional marketplace patterns are defined.
- Publisher registration, verification, trust levels, responsibilities, and enforcement are established.
- Asset submission, validation, review, publication, installation, update, rollback, deprecation, suspension, and removal lifecycles are established.
- Security, quality, AI, compatibility, legal, compliance, and commercial reviews are risk-based.
- Marketplace packages use unique identities, versions, signatures, checksums, provenance, dependencies, permissions, licenses, documentation, and support policies.
- Search, discovery, categories, filters, ratings, reviews, recommendations, and moderation are defined.
- Installation is tenant-aware, permission-controlled, compatible, auditable, and recoverable.
- New permissions require renewed customer consent.
- Pricing, licensing, billing, entitlements, trials, refunds, revenue sharing, and publisher payouts are governed.
- Private enterprise marketplaces allow customers to control approved assets, publishers, permissions, updates, and spending.
- Marketplace integration exists with the Plugin Framework, API Platform, SDK, CLI, Developer Portal, Billing Platform, AI Governance, and Security Platform.
- Marketplace assets cannot modify the core platform through unapproved methods.
- Vulnerability management, emergency suspension, publisher compromise, and customer communication procedures are operational.
- Marketplace health, adoption, revenue, security, quality, compatibility, and customer outcomes are measurable.
- Human accountability remains mandatory for high-risk publication and enforcement decisions.
- The Marketplace can support all current and future MianX.ai Industry Operating Systems.

**Part 22 — Plugin Framework Roadmap**

# Part 22 — Plugin Framework Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The Plugin Framework Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will enable internal teams, customers, developers, and approved partners to extend the Enterprise AI Operating System without modifying, duplicating, or destabilizing the core platform.

The Plugin Framework will provide controlled extension points through which developers can add:

- Product Capabilities
- Industry Capabilities
- User Interface Extensions
- Workflow Actions
- Event Handlers
- Data Connectors
- External Integrations
- AI Tools
- Agent Skills
- Reports
- Dashboards
- Notifications
- Automation Steps
- Validation Rules
- Business Rules
- Import and Export Providers
- Authentication Providers
- Payment Providers
- Search Providers
- Knowledge Sources

The target model is:

```text
MianX Core Platform

+

Stable Extension Contracts

+

Plugin Runtime

+

Permission and Security Controls

+

Developer Tools

+

Marketplace Distribution

=

Extensible Enterprise Platform
```

Plugins must operate through explicit and governed boundaries.

They must not receive unrestricted access to:

- Core Databases
- Other Tenants
- Internal Secrets
- AI Memory
- Knowledge Repositories
- Infrastructure
- Administrative APIs
- Customer Data
- Production Runtime

The Plugin Framework must protect:

- Core Platform Stability
- Tenant Isolation
- Product Isolation
- Customer Trust
- Data Security
- API Compatibility
- Operational Reliability
- Long-Term Maintainability

The objective is not to make every internal function customizable.

The objective is to expose carefully designed extension points that allow safe ecosystem growth without creating uncontrolled architecture fragmentation.

---

# Plugin Framework Vision

Build one secure, modular, versioned, sandboxed, observable, and developer-friendly Plugin Framework that enables MianX.ai products and Industry Operating Systems to be extended through stable contracts rather than direct core modification.

---

# Plugin Framework Mission

Provide governed extension interfaces, runtimes, permissions, lifecycle controls, testing tools, documentation, and distribution mechanisms through which reusable plugins can be developed, validated, installed, operated, updated, and retired safely.

---

# Plugin Framework Purpose

The Plugin Framework exists to:

- Protect the MianX.ai core
- Prevent customer-specific code forks
- Enable partner innovation
- Support industry extensions
- Increase platform adaptability
- Accelerate integration development
- Reduce repeated customization
- Support Marketplace distribution
- Standardize extension development
- Improve developer experience
- Create reusable plugin capabilities
- Enable customer configuration
- Support global ecosystem growth

---

# Strategic Objectives

The Plugin Framework should:

- Establish stable extension contracts
- Separate plugins from core implementation
- Provide strong plugin identity
- Provide a standard plugin package
- Support secure installation
- Support tenant-aware execution
- Support product-aware execution
- Provide least-privilege permissions
- Provide sandboxed runtime options
- Support synchronous and asynchronous plugins
- Support internal and external plugins
- Support versioning and compatibility
- Support dependency management
- Support automated validation
- Support observability
- Support safe updates and rollback
- Support plugin certification
- Integrate with the Marketplace
- Integrate with SDK and CLI
- Integrate with the Developer Portal
- Support plugin monetization
- Maintain human governance over high-risk extensions

---

---

# Plugin Philosophy

The Plugin Framework follows this philosophy:

```text
Extend Through Contracts

Not Through Core Modification

Request Capabilities

Not Unrestricted Access

Operate in Isolation

Not Shared Trust

Version Every Change

Test Every Integration

Observe Every Execution

Retire Extensions Responsibly
```

---

# Plugin Framework Principles

## 1. Core Platform Integrity

Plugins must not modify MianX.ai core source code or internal platform state through undocumented methods.

---

## 2. Explicit Extension Points

Plugins may operate only through approved:

- APIs
- Events
- Hooks
- UI Slots
- Workflow Actions
- Tool Interfaces
- Data Contracts

---

## 3. Least Privilege

Every plugin receives only the capabilities required for its declared purpose.

---

## 4. Deny by Default

Undeclared access must be denied.

---

## 5. Tenant Awareness

Every plugin execution must include trusted tenant context where applicable.

---

## 6. Product Awareness

Plugins must declare which products and modules they support.

---

## 7. Environment Isolation

Development, testing, staging, and production plugin environments must remain separated.

---

## 8. Runtime Isolation

One plugin must not interfere with:

- Another Plugin
- Core Platform Runtime
- Another Tenant
- Another Product
- Host Infrastructure

---

## 9. Stable Contracts

Extension interfaces should be documented, versioned, tested, and governed.

---

## 10. Backward Compatibility

Compatible plugin versions should continue working during supported platform upgrades.

---

## 11. Transparent Permissions

Administrators must understand what a plugin can access and perform before installation.

---

## 12. Secure Secrets

Plugin credentials must use approved secret-management services.

---

## 13. No Direct Database Access by Default

Plugins should access platform data through governed APIs and services.

---

## 14. Observable Execution

Plugin calls, errors, latency, resource use, and security events must be measurable.

---

## 15. Controlled Failure

A plugin failure should not cause uncontrolled failure of the core platform.

---

## 16. Safe Updates

Plugin updates must preserve compatibility, permissions, configuration, and rollback capability.

---

## 17. Complete Lifecycle

Every plugin must support:

- Registration
- Validation
- Installation
- Activation
- Operation
- Update
- Suspension
- Deprecation
- Removal

---

## 18. Publisher Accountability

Plugin publishers remain responsible for security, maintenance, documentation, and support.

---

## 19. Marketplace Readiness

Plugins intended for distribution must meet Marketplace trust and package standards.

---

## 20. Human Control of High-Risk Plugins

Plugins with financial, security, infrastructure, medical, legal, or destructive capabilities require stronger human approval.

---

# Plugin Identity

Every plugin must have a globally unique identity.

Example:

```text
com.mianx.publisher.plugin-name
```

Plugin identity should remain stable across versions.

---

# Plugin Identity Record

The Plugin Registry should maintain:

- Plugin ID
- Display Name
- Publisher ID
- Plugin Type
- Current Version
- Supported Versions
- Product Scope
- Industry Scope
- Risk Level
- Review Status
- Marketplace Status
- Lifecycle Status

---

# Plugin Manifest

Every plugin package must include a machine-readable manifest.

Example:

```yaml
plugin:
  id: com.example.restaurant-inventory
  name: Restaurant Inventory Connector
  version: 1.2.0
  type: integration
  description: Connects RestaurantOS with an approved inventory provider

publisher:
  id: verified-publisher-id

compatibility:
  platform: ">=1.0.0 <2.0.0"
  products:
    - restaurant-os
  api_versions:
    - v1

runtime:
  type: sandboxed
  entrypoint: src/index.js
  timeout_seconds: 30

permissions:
  - inventory.read
  - inventory.update
  - events.order.completed.subscribe

configuration:
  schema: config.schema.json

network:
  outbound:
    - api.approved-provider.example

security:
  risk_level: PLG2

support:
  documentation: docs/
  policy: standard
```

---

# Manifest Requirements

The manifest should declare:

- Plugin Identity
- Name
- Description
- Publisher
- Version
- Plugin Type
- Runtime
- Entry Point
- Extension Points
- Compatibility
- Dependencies
- Permissions
- Configuration
- Network Access
- Data Access
- Secrets
- Resource Requirements
- Support
- License
- Deprecation

---

- Dependencies
- Vulnerabilities
- Deprecation

Potential extension points include:

- UI Slot

- Event Subscriber
- Validation Hook
- Report Provider
- Search Provider

- Export Provider

Every extension point should define:

- Output Schema

- Timeout
- Error Behavior
- Permission Requirements
- Compatibility Version
- Observability
- Deprecation Policy

# Hooks

Hooks may execute:

- Before Action
- After Action
- Before Validation
- After Validation
- Before Save
- After Save

- After Workflow Step

Hooks should not allow uncontrolled modification of core behavior.

# Event-Based Plugins

Event-based integration is preferred where synchronous modification is unnecessary.

```text
Platform Event

↓

Event Authorization and Filtering

↓

Plugin Event Queue

↓

Plugin Execution

↓

Result, Retry, or Dead Letter

↓

Monitoring and Audit
```

# Event Requirements

Plugins should handle:

- Duplicate Events
- Delayed Events
- Out-of-Order Events
- Retry
- Dead-Letter Events
- Schema Versioning
- Idempotency

---

# Synchronous Plugins

Synchronous plugin execution may be appropriate for:

- Validation
- Data Lookup
- User-Initiated Action
- Authentication
- Immediate Calculation

Synchronous plugins require strict:

- Timeout
- Performance
- Availability
- Error Isolation
- Circuit Breaking

---

# Asynchronous Plugins

Asynchronous plugins are preferred for:

- Notifications
- Data Synchronization
- File Processing
- Reporting
- Analytics
- Long-Running Work
- External Integration

# Plugin Runtime Models

## Managed Runtime

MianX.ai hosts and operates the plugin.

Benefits:

- Standard Monitoring
- Controlled Security
- Resource Governance
- Easier Installation

---

## Sandboxed Runtime

The plugin runs in a restricted execution environment.

Controls may include:

- CPU Limit
- Memory Limit
- Execution-Time Limit
- File-System Restrictions
- Network Restrictions
- Process Restrictions
- Read-Only Runtime
- Termination

---

## External Runtime

The plugin runs on the publisher’s infrastructure and communicates through approved APIs and webhooks.

Requirements include:

- Strong Authentication
- Endpoint Verification
- Availability
- Data Processing Disclosure
- Regional Compliance
- Audit
- Retry
- Revocation

---

## Customer-Hosted Runtime

Enterprise customers may host approved plugins within their controlled infrastructure.

This model should define:

- Deployment Responsibility
- Version Support
- Monitoring
- Security
- Connectivity
- Data Ownership
- Support Boundaries

---

# Runtime Isolation

Runtime isolation should prevent plugins from:

- Reading host process memory
- Accessing unrestricted file systems
- Calling unapproved network endpoints
- Accessing another plugin’s data
- Accessing another tenant
- Executing administrative operations
- Escaping resource limits
- Modifying core packages

---

# Capability-Based Security

Plugins should receive explicit capabilities rather than broad system roles.

Example:

```text
orders.read

orders.create

inventory.read

inventory.update

notifications.send

workflow.action.execute

knowledge.search

ai.tool.invoke
```

- Network Access

- Risk Level

## PLG0–PLG1

Requires functional, security, and compatibility review.

## PLG3

Requires product, security, operational, and customer-impact review.

## PLG4

Requires enhanced security, privacy, compliance, and human approval.

Requires multi-party enterprise authorization and strict operational controls.

# Exit Criteria

Part **22 — Plugin Framework Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified Plugin Framework architecture is defined.
- Plugins extend the platform through explicit APIs, events, hooks, UI slots, workflow actions, and tool contracts.
- Plugins cannot modify core platform code through unsupported methods.
- Plugin identity, manifest, registry, package, signing, and provenance standards are established.
- Managed, sandboxed, external, and customer-hosted runtime models are defined.
- Runtime, tenant, product, environment, data, and network isolation are enforced.
- A capability-based permission model is operational.
- Plugin identities use least-privilege workload credentials.
- Plugin data access occurs through governed services rather than unrestricted databases.
- Plugin configuration and secrets are secure, validated, scoped, and auditable.
- Registration, validation, installation, activation, execution, update, rollback, suspension, deprecation, removal, and archival lifecycles are operational.
- APIs, events, hooks, schemas, permissions, and runtimes are versioned.
- Compatibility and dependency management are testable.
- Plugin failures remain isolated from the core platform and unrelated tenants.
- SDK, CLI, Developer Portal, Sandbox, testing tools, and local development workflows support plugin developers.
- Automated security, quality, compatibility, and tenant-isolation validation is operational.
- Plugin certification and Marketplace publication processes are defined.
- Plugin health, usage, performance, security, cost, compatibility, and customer outcomes are measurable.
- Private, partner, public, product-specific, industry-specific, and regional plugin patterns are supported.
- High-risk plugins require accountable human approval.
- The Plugin Framework can support all current and future MianX.ai Industry Operating Systems.

---

# Final Summary

The Plugin Framework Roadmap establishes the controlled extensibility layer of MianX.ai.

The complete plugin lifecycle is:

```text
Extension Need Identified

↓

Approved Extension Point Selected

↓

Plugin Developed Through SDK and Stable Contracts

↓

Manifest, Permissions, Dependencies, and Compatibility Declared

↓

Plugin Tested and Validated

↓

Package Signed and Registered

↓

Administrator Reviews Scope and Permissions

↓

Plugin Installed and Activated

↓

Execution Is Isolated, Authorized, and Monitored

↓

Plugin Updated, Rolled Back, Suspended, Deprecated, or Removed

↓

Framework and Ecosystem Improve
```

The Plugin Framework connects:

```text
MianX Core Platform
Provides stable enterprise capabilities

Extension Contracts
Define safe customization boundaries

Plugin Runtime
Executes isolated extension logic

SDK and CLI
Support plugin development and operations

Developer Portal
Provides documentation and testing guidance

Marketplace
Distributes governed plugins

Customers and Partners
Extend products without fragmenting the core
```

MianX.ai Plugin Framework must remain:

- Core-Protecting
- Contract-Based
- Modular
- Versioned
- Compatibility-Aware
- Permission-Based
- Least-Privilege
- Tenant-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Environment-Aware
- Region-Aware
- Sandboxed
- Observable
- Auditable
- Recoverable
- Developer-Friendly
- Marketplace-Ready
- Customer-Controlled
- Human-Governed
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not to allow unlimited customization.

The objective is to create one governed extensibility framework through which developers, internal teams, customers, and partners can safely add integrations, workflows, AI tools, industry capabilities, reports, interfaces, and business logic without weakening the security, stability, maintainability, or architectural integrity of the MianX.ai Enterprise AI Operating System.

# Part 23 — SDK Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The SDK Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will provide secure, consistent, typed, documented, versioned, and developer-friendly Software Development Kits for accessing and extending the complete MianX.ai Enterprise AI Operating System.

The SDK platform will allow:

- Internal Engineering Teams
- Product Teams
- AI Engineering Teams

- Industry Solution Developers

to integrate with MianX.ai without repeatedly implementing:

- Retries

```text
MianX.ai APIs, Events, AI Services, and Platform Capabilities

↓

Machine-Readable Contracts

↓

Generated and Curated SDK Core

↓

Language-Specific SDK Packages
```

The SDK is not merely an automatically generated API wrapper.

# SDK Non-Scope

The SDK does not replace:

- API Platform
- CLI
- Developer Portal
- Plugin Framework
- Marketplace
- Workflow Engine
- Authentication Platform
- Business Logic
- Customer Authorization
- Server-Side Validation
- API Governance

The SDK simplifies access to these capabilities but does not move authoritative business rules into client applications.

---

# SDK Philosophy

The SDK follows this philosophy:

```text
Simple for Common Work

Explicit for Sensitive Work

Secure by Default

Consistent Across Languages

Generated From Contracts

Curated for Developers

Versioned for Stability

Observable in Production

Documented Through Examples
```

---

# SDK Principles

## 1. API Contracts Are the Source

SDK behavior must originate from approved and versioned:

- OpenAPI Contracts
- Event Schemas
- Webhook Schemas
- GraphQL Schemas Where Used
- Plugin Contracts
- AI Tool Schemas

---

## 2. Secure Defaults

SDK defaults should prefer:

- Encrypted Connections
- Short-Lived Credentials
- Safe Timeouts
- Limited Retries
- Tenant Validation
- Input Validation
- Secret Redaction

---

## 3. Consistent Developer Experience

Equivalent operations should use similar concepts across all supported languages.

---

## 4. Strong Typing Where Available

Languages supporting static typing should provide:

- Typed Requests
- Typed Responses
- Typed Errors
- Typed Events
- Typed Configuration

---

## 5. Tenant Context Must Be Explicit

Multi-tenant operations must include trusted and clearly defined tenant context.

---

## 6. Product Context Must Be Preserved

SDK calls should identify which product or Industry Operating System is being accessed where required.

---

## 7. No Hidden Privilege

The SDK must not silently request or use broader permissions than the operation requires.

---

## 8. Server Remains Authoritative

Client-side SDK validation improves experience but never replaces server-side authorization and validation.

---

## 9. Predictable Errors

Errors should be structured, documented, and actionable.

---

## 10. Safe Retries

Retries should occur only for approved transient failure classes.

---

## 11. Idempotency for Sensitive Operations

Sensitive creation, payment, provisioning, and workflow operations should support idempotency.

---

## 12. Backward Compatibility

Breaking changes require controlled major-version transitions.

---

## 13. Minimal Language Differences

Language-specific idioms are encouraged, but platform concepts should remain consistent.

---

## 14. Observable Requests

SDK operations should support:

- Correlation IDs
- Request IDs
- Tracing
- Metrics
- Debug Logging

---

## 15. Secrets Must Never Be Logged

Tokens, passwords, keys, and sensitive headers must be automatically redacted.

---

## 16. Documentation Is Part of the Product

A feature without SDK documentation and examples is not developer-ready.

---

## 17. Generated Code Must Be Reviewed

Automated generation reduces repetition but does not remove quality ownership.

---

## 18. Package Integrity Must Be Verifiable

Official SDK packages should be signed or otherwise distributed through trusted and protected publishing systems.

---

## 19. Deprecation Must Be Gradual

Deprecated operations require:

- Warning
- Replacement
- Migration Guidance
- Support Window
- Removal Timeline

---

## 20. SDK Success Is Measured by Developer Outcomes

Success should be measured through:

- Integration Speed
- Error Reduction
- Adoption
- Reliability
- Developer Satisfaction
- Customer Value

---

# SDK Architecture

The SDK platform should use a layered architecture.

```text
MianX.ai Service APIs, Events, and AI Contracts

↓

Contract Registry

↓

SDK Code Generation and Validation

↓

Shared SDK Design Standards

↓

Language-Specific SDK Core

↓

Domain and Service Clients

↓

Developer Applications, Integrations, Plugins, and Automations

↓

Telemetry, Support, Compatibility, and Governance
```

# SDK Client Initialization

A common conceptual initialization model is:

```typescript
const client = new MianXClient({
  baseUrl: process.env.MIANX_API_URL,
  credentialProvider: workloadCredentialProvider,
  tenantId: "tenant-id",
  product: "restaurant-os",
  timeoutMs: 30000
});
```

Actual SDK interfaces should follow language-specific conventions.

The SDK should support explicit environments:

- Local
- Development
- Testing
- Staging
- Production

- Customer-Dedicated

Production should never be selected accidentally through an unsafe default.

# Authentication

The SDK may support approved authentication methods such as:

- OAuth 2.0
- OpenID Connect
- Service Accounts
- Workload Identity

# Credential Providers

Credential providers may retrieve credentials from:

- Environment Variables
- Secret Vault
- Workload Identity
- Local Developer Configuration
- Secure Operating-System Storage
- Managed Cloud Identity

---

# Credential Security

The SDK should:

- Avoid plaintext credential storage
- Avoid credential logging
- Support token refresh
- Support revocation
- Validate expiration
- Redact secrets
- Prefer short-lived credentials
- Provide secure local-development guidance

---

# Authorization

The SDK should not assume that authentication grants authorization.

Authorization remains controlled by the server through:

- Roles
- Permissions
- Attributes
- Tenant Context
- Product Context
- Resource Ownership
- Policies

---

# Tenant Context

Tenant-aware requests should use trusted SDK context.

Example:

```typescript
const tenantClient = client.forTenant("tenant-id");
```

The server must still verify that the calling identity may access that tenant.

---

# Context Isolation

SDK clients should avoid mutable global tenant context in concurrent applications.

Safer models include:

- Immutable Client Context
- Request-Scoped Context
- Dedicated Tenant Client
- Explicit Context Parameters

---

# Product Context

Product context may identify:

- MianX Core
- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- RetailOS
- HealthcareOS
- EducationOS
- ManufacturingOS
- LogisticsOS

---

```text

Message

HTTP Status

Request ID

Correlation ID

Retryable

Details
```

# Error Safety

Errors must not expose:

- Secrets
- Internal Stack Traces
- Database Details
- Private Customer Data
- Internal Network Information
- Encryption Material

---

# Retry Strategy

The SDK may retry:

- Temporary Network Failures
- Selected Timeouts
- Rate Limits With Retry Guidance
- Temporary Service Unavailability

The SDK should not automatically retry:

- Validation Failures
- Authorization Failures
- Permanent Business Conflicts
- Unsafe Non-Idempotent Operations

---

# Retry Configuration

Retry policy should define:

- Maximum Attempts
- Backoff
- Jitter
- Retryable Status Codes
- Maximum Delay
- Total Time Budget
- Cancellation

---

# Timeouts

Timeouts should support:

- Connection Timeout
- Request Timeout
- Read Timeout
- Streaming Timeout
- Overall Operation Timeout

No request should wait indefinitely.

---

# Cancellation

Supported languages should allow cancellation through native patterns such as:

- Abort Signals
- Cancellation Tokens
- Context Cancellation
- Async Task Cancellation

---

# Idempotency

SDK helpers should support idempotency for operations such as:

- Payments
- Orders
- Resource Provisioning
- Task Creation
- Workflow Starts
- Customer Onboarding
- Notifications

---

# Rate-Limit Handling

The SDK should expose:

- Rate Limit
- Remaining Requests
- Reset Time
- Retry Guidance

Applications should not need to parse raw provider-specific headers.

---

# Pagination

The SDK should support consistent pagination patterns.

Potential styles include:

- Cursor Pagination
- Page Pagination
- Async Iteration
- Automatic Collection With Limits

Example:

```typescript
for await (const task of client.tasks.listAll()) {
  console.log(task);
}
```

Automatic pagination should include safeguards against unbounded memory use.

# SDK Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|

| SDK-L1 | Generated Clients | Basic generated API clients are available |

| SDK-L4 | Global Ecosystem SDKs | Enterprise, partner, marketplace, mobile, and regional SDK capabilities mature |
| SDK-L5 | Intelligent Composable SDK Ecosystem | SDKs dynamically support reusable enterprise capability composition |

# SDK Quality Gates

Before an SDK release becomes production-ready:

- [ ] SDK owner is assigned.
- [ ] Language support is approved.
- [ ] API contracts are approved.
- [ ] Generated code is reproducible.
- [ ] Authentication is secure.
- [ ] Tenant context is explicit.
- [ ] Product context is supported.
- [ ] Requests and responses are typed where possible.
- [ ] Error behavior is standardized.
- [ ] Retry behavior is safe.
- [ ] Timeouts are configured.
- [ ] Cancellation is supported where appropriate.
- [ ] Idempotency is supported where required.
- [ ] Pagination is tested.
- [ ] Rate-limit handling is tested.
- [ ] File operations are tested.
- [ ] Webhook verification is tested.
- [ ] Event compatibility is tested.
- [ ] Secrets are redacted.
- [ ] Dependencies are scanned.
- [ ] Package integrity is verifiable.
- [ ] Contract tests pass.
- [ ] Cross-language conformance passes.
- [ ] Documentation is complete.
- [ ] Examples are validated.
- [ ] Compatibility matrix is updated.
- [ ] Release notes are published.
- [ ] Migration guidance exists where required.
- [ ] Monitoring is active.
- [ ] Support ownership is confirmed.

---

# Exit Criteria

Part **23 — SDK Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified SDK architecture is defined.
- SDKs are formally positioned within the Developer Platform.
- SDK design, generation, language, security, versioning, compatibility, documentation, and release standards are approved.
- TypeScript/JavaScript and Python are evaluated as initial official SDK priorities.
- Additional language support follows measurable demand and long-term ownership.
- Core, AI, Automation, Agent, Workflow, Plugin, Marketplace, and Industry SDK boundaries are defined.
- Authentication, credential providers, tenant context, product context, requests, responses, errors, retries, timeouts, cancellation, idempotency, rate limits, pagination, files, events, webhooks, and streaming follow consistent standards.
- SDK clients use governed APIs rather than unsupported internal interfaces.
- SDK and API versions remain independently managed and compatible.
- Breaking changes require major versions, migration guides, testing, and controlled deprecation.
- Official packages use protected registries, secure release pipelines, dependency scanning, integrity verification, and supply-chain controls.
- Contract tests and cross-language conformance tests are operational.
- SDK documentation, quick starts, references, tutorials, recipes, migration guides, and examples are maintained with each release.
- Developer sandbox, test utilities, mocks, and failure simulations are available.
- SDK requests support tracing and safe telemetry.
- Adoption, reliability, compatibility, security, documentation, and developer experience are measurable.
- SDKs support internal teams, customers, partners, plugin developers, marketplace publishers, AI developers, and Industry Operating Systems.
- The SDK ecosystem remains secure, stable, typed, documented, observable, governed, and long-term maintainable.

---

# Final Summary

The SDK Roadmap establishes the programmatic developer-access layer of MianX.ai.

The complete SDK lifecycle is:

```text
Platform Capability Approved

↓

API, Event, or Tool Contract Defined

↓

Contract Registered and Versioned

↓

SDK Models and Clients Generated

↓

Developer-Friendly Behavior Added

↓

Authentication, Errors, Retries, Context, and Security Validated

↓

SDK Tested Across Supported Languages

↓

Documentation and Examples Published

↓

Signed Package Released

↓

Developer Adoption and Reliability Monitored

↓

SDK Updated, Deprecated, Migrated, or Retired
```

The SDK Platform connects:

```text
MianX.ai APIs and Events
Provide governed platform capabilities

SDK Contract Layer
Defines stable machine-readable interfaces

SDK Core
Provides authentication, transport, errors, retries, and observability

Language SDKs
Provide language-native developer experiences

Developer Portal and Sandbox
Provide documentation, examples, and testing

Plugin Framework and Marketplace
Use SDKs to create and distribute extensions

Products, Customers, and Partners
Build reliable integrations without duplicating platform complexity
```

MianX.ai SDKs must remain:

- Contract-Driven
- Secure by Default
- Typed
- Consistent
- Tenant-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Permission-Aware
- Versioned
- Compatible
- Testable
- Observable
- Documented
- Developer-Friendly
- Package-Secure
- Marketplace-Ready
- Plugin-Compatible
- AI-Compatible
- Multi-Language
- Governed
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to generate client libraries.

The objective is to create one trusted developer-access ecosystem through which internal teams, customers, partners, AI developers, plugin publishers, and Industry Operating Systems can securely consume MianX.ai capabilities with less complexity, fewer defects, faster integration, and predictable long-term compatibility.

# Part 24 — CLI Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The CLI Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will provide a secure, consistent, scriptable, developer-friendly, and enterprise-governed Command-Line Interface for interacting with the complete MianX.ai ecosystem.

The MianX.ai CLI will provide one terminal-based interface for:

- Developers
- Platform Engineers
- Product Engineers
- AI Engineers
- Infrastructure Engineers
- Security Engineers
- Data Engineers
- Marketplace Publishers
- Plugin Developers
- Enterprise Administrators
- Automation Systems
- CI/CD Pipelines
- Approved AI Engineering Agents

The CLI will simplify tasks such as:

- Authentication
- Environment Selection
- Tenant and Product Context
- Project Setup
- Local Development
- Service Discovery
- API Exploration
- Resource Management
- Workflow Operations
- AI-Agent Operations
- Plugin Development
- Marketplace Publishing
- Deployment
- Monitoring
- Logs
- Configuration
- Testing
- Diagnostics
- Support Bundles

The target model is:

```text
Developer or Automation System

↓

MianX CLI

↓

Identity, Context, Policy, and Validation

↓

MianX APIs, SDKs, Events, Workflows, and Platform Services

↓

Audited Enterprise Operation
```

The CLI must not become a collection of unrelated scripts.

It must operate as a governed Developer Platform product with:

- Stable Command Structure
- Secure Authentication
- Tenant Awareness
- Product Awareness
- Environment Awareness
- Permission Enforcement
- Predictable Output
- Structured Errors
- Automation Support
- Compatibility Management
- Auditability
- Long-Term Maintenance

The CLI should enable self-service without providing unrestricted access.

The objective is to make approved platform operations fast and repeatable while protecting production systems, customer data, enterprise security, and architectural standards.

---

# CLI Vision

Build one secure and unified command-line interface through which developers, operators, partners, CI/CD systems, and approved AI agents can discover, develop, test, deploy, operate, and extend MianX.ai capabilities through governed and repeatable commands.

---

# CLI Mission

Convert complex enterprise platform operations into clear, safe, scriptable, documented, and auditable command-line workflows while preserving identity, permissions, environment boundaries, tenant isolation, and human approval.

---

# CLI Purpose

The CLI exists to:

- Improve developer productivity
- Reduce repetitive manual operations
- Standardize platform interaction
- Improve onboarding
- Support local development
- Enable governed self-service
- Automate common engineering tasks
- Improve release consistency
- Support CI/CD
- Support plugin development
- Support marketplace publishing
- Support AI-agent operations
- Reduce direct infrastructure access
- Improve troubleshooting
- Generate verifiable execution evidence
- Preserve operational auditability

- Provide consistent command naming
- Support interactive and non-interactive operation
- Support human and machine users

- Support tenant, product, project, region, and environment context
- Standardize output and exit codes
- Support scripting and CI/CD

- Integrate with the Marketplace
- Support local and remote development

- Support controlled updates

- Measure CLI adoption and success
- Remain maintainable for the long term

# CLI Non-Scope

- SDKs
- Developer Portal
- Web Administration
- Infrastructure as Code
- Workflow Engine

- Security Policies
- Business Authorization
- Human Approval
- Incident Command

The CLI provides a controlled interface to these systems.

---

# CLI Philosophy

The CLI follows this philosophy:

```text
Discover Before Execute

Validate Before Change

Preview Before Destruction

Automate Repetition

Preserve Human Approval

Return Predictable Results

Generate Evidence

Remain Scriptable and Secure
```

---

# CLI Principles

## 1. Secure by Default

The CLI must use secure authentication, encrypted communication, protected credentials, and safe defaults.

---

## 2. Explicit Context

Every material command should operate within clearly visible:

- Organization
- Tenant
- Product
- Project
- Environment
- Region
- User or Workload Identity

---

## 3. Production Must Be Deliberate

The CLI must not silently assume production.

Production operations should require explicit context.

---

## 4. Least Privilege

CLI access must use server-enforced roles, permissions, policies, and resource ownership.

---

## 5. Human and Machine Modes

The CLI should support:

- Interactive Human Use
- Non-Interactive Automation
- CI/CD Pipelines
- Approved AI-Agent Execution

---

## 6. Predictable Commands

Equivalent resources and actions should use consistent command patterns.

---

## 7. Structured Output

Commands should support machine-readable output for automation.

---

## 8. Stable Exit Codes

Scripts must be able to determine whether a command:

- Succeeded
- Failed
- Was Denied
- Timed Out
- Partially Completed
- Requires Approval

---

## 9. Safe Destructive Actions

Delete, revoke, production deployment, migration, and infrastructure operations require stronger safeguards.

---

## 10. Dry Run Where Practical

High-impact changes should support preview before execution.

---

## 11. Idempotent Automation

Repeated commands should avoid duplicate side effects where the platform supports idempotency.

---

## 12. Secrets Must Remain Protected

Secrets must not appear in:

- Command History
- Logs
- Process Lists
- Error Messages
- Telemetry
- Output Files

---

## 13. Server Remains Authoritative

CLI validation improves usability, but the server remains responsible for authorization and business rules.

---

## 14. Documentation Must Match Commands

CLI help and Developer Portal documentation must remain synchronized.

---

## 15. Backward Compatibility

Breaking command changes require major-version governance and migration guidance.

---

## 16. Observable Execution

Material commands should provide:

- Request ID
- Correlation ID
- Status
- Evidence
- Audit Reference
- Failure Reason

---

## 17. Commands Must Be Testable

Commands should support automated testing in development and sandbox environments.

---

## 18. Self-Service Is Governed

The CLI should reduce platform-team bottlenecks without bypassing security or ownership.

---

## 19. AI-Agent Use Is Bounded

AI agents may execute CLI commands only through approved identities, policies, scopes, limits, and evidence requirements.

---

## 20. Simplicity Before Command Volume

The CLI should favor clear and composable commands over thousands of inconsistent commands.

---

# CLI Architecture

The CLI should use a layered architecture.

```text
Human, Script, CI/CD, or AI Agent

↓

CLI Command Parser

↓

↓

↓

Input Validation and Safety Controls

↓

↓

↓

Output, Evidence, Logging, and Audit
```

# CLI Command Structure

The primary executable should use a stable name.

Conceptual example:

```bash
mianx <domain> <resource> <action> [flags]
```

Examples:

```bash
mianx auth login

mianx tenant list

mianx project create

mianx workflow run

mianx agent inspect

mianx plugin validate

mianx marketplace publish
```

---

# Command Hierarchy

A recommended hierarchy is:

```text
mianx

├── auth
├── config
├── context
├── organization
├── tenant
├── workspace
├── project
├── task
├── file
├── workflow
├── automation
├── ai
├── agent
├── knowledge
├── memory
├── intelligence
├── data
├── environment
├── deployment
├── service
├── infrastructure
├── security
├── plugin
├── marketplace
├── logs
├── metrics
├── diagnostics
└── version
```

---

# Command Naming Standards

Commands should use consistent actions such as:

- `list`
- `get`
- `create`
- `update`
- `delete`
- `describe`
- `inspect`
- `validate`
- `run`
- `start`
- `stop`
- `pause`
- `resume`
- `cancel`
- `deploy`
- `rollback`
- `logs`
- `status`

Avoid multiple words for the same action without justification.

---

# Command Options

Common options may include:

```text
--profile

--organization

--tenant

--product

--workspace

--project

--environment

--region

--output

--timeout

--request-id

--dry-run

--yes

--verbose

--quiet

--no-color

--help
```

---

# Global Flags

Global flags should behave consistently across commands.

Example:

```bash
mianx task list \
  --tenant tenant-123 \
  --product restaurant-os \
  --environment production \
  --output json
```

---

# CLI Profiles

Profiles should store non-secret operational context.

A profile may contain:

- Profile Name
- API Endpoint
- Organization
- Default Tenant
- Default Product
- Default Environment
- Default Region
- Output Format
- Credential Provider Reference

---

# Profile Commands

Potential commands include:

```bash
mianx config profile create

mianx config profile list

mianx config profile use

mianx config profile inspect

mianx config profile delete
```

---

# Profile Security

Profiles should not store plaintext:

- Passwords
- Long-Lived Tokens
- Client Secrets
- Private Keys
- Encryption Keys

---

# Context Management

The CLI should display and manage current context.

Example:

```bash
mianx context show
```

Output may include:

```text
Profile:        production-admin
Organization:   mianx
Tenant:         tenant-123
Product:        restaurant-os
Environment:    production
Region:         pk-primary
Identity:       user@example.com
```

---

# Context Precedence

Context may be resolved through:

```text
Explicit Command Flag

↓

Environment Variable

↓

Active Profile

↓

Safe Default
```

Production should not be selected through an ambiguous default.

---

# Authentication Commands

Potential commands include:

```bash
mianx auth login

mianx auth login --device

mianx auth status

mianx auth whoami

mianx auth refresh

mianx auth logout
```

---

# Human Authentication

Human authentication should support:

- Browser-Based Login
- Device Authorization
- SSO
- MFA
- Short-Lived Sessions
- Session Revocation

---

# Machine Authentication

CI/CD and automation should use:

- Workload Identity
- Short-Lived Federated Credentials
- Approved Service Accounts
- Scoped Tokens Where Required

Long-lived static credentials should be avoided.

---

# Authentication Status

The CLI should clearly show:

- Identity
- Authentication Method
- Session Expiration
- Organization
- Active Permissions
- Credential Provider

It should never print secret token values.

---

# Authorization

The CLI must rely on platform authorization.

CLI command visibility may be permission-aware, but hidden commands must not be considered a security boundary.

---

# Output Formats

For automation and integration.

## Table

For list and summary commands.

Returns only the required value.

# Output Standard

A structured response may include:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "requestId": "req_123",
  "data": {},
  "warnings": [],
  "evidence": []
}
```

---

# Output Stability

Machine-readable output is an interface contract.

Fields should not be removed or renamed without compatibility governance.

---

# Error Output

Structured errors should include:

```json
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "PERMISSION_DENIED",
    "message": "The current identity cannot deploy to production.",
    "requestId": "req_123",
    "retryable": false
  }
}
```

---

# Exit Codes

A standard exit-code model may include:

| Code | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | General failure |
| 2 | Invalid command or input |
| 3 | Authentication failure |
| 4 | Authorization failure |
| 5 | Resource not found |
| 6 | Conflict |
| 7 | Timeout |
| 8 | Partial success |
| 9 | Approval required |
| 10 | Compatibility failure |

Exact codes should be formally standardized.

# CLI Risk Levels

| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| CLI0 | Read-only local or informational command |
| CLI1 | Read-only remote enterprise command |
| CLI2 | Standard non-destructive resource change |
| CLI3 | Customer-impacting or production change |
| CLI4 | Security, financial, bulk, privileged, or infrastructure change |
| CLI5 | Irreversible, destructive, global, or safety-critical operation |

---

# Risk-Based Controls

## CLI0–CLI1

May run with standard authentication and authorization.

## CLI2

Requires explicit context and normal audit.

## CLI3

Requires production warning, impact validation, and suitable approval.

## CLI4

Requires dry run, strong identity, enhanced audit, and accountable approval.

## CLI5

Requires multi-party authorization, impact evidence, recovery plan, and strict execution control.

| CLI-L0 | Manual and Scripted Operations | Teams use unrelated scripts and manual commands |
| CLI-L1 | Basic Platform CLI | Authentication and basic resource commands exist |
| CLI-L2 | Governed Developer CLI | Context, security, output, testing, versioning, and audit are standardized |
| CLI-L3 | Multi-Product Self-Service CLI | Development, deployment, AI, workflow, plugin, and marketplace operations are integrated |
| CLI-L4 | Enterprise Automation CLI | CI/CD, policy automation, diagnostics, and regional operations are mature |
| CLI-L5 | Intelligent Enterprise Control Interface | Humans and governed AI agents operate composable enterprise capabilities safely through one interface |

# CLI Quality Gates

Before a CLI release becomes production-ready:

- [ ] CLI owner is assigned.
- [ ] Command architecture is approved.
- [ ] Command naming is consistent.
- [ ] Authentication is secure.
- [ ] Credentials are protected.
- [ ] Tenant context is explicit.
- [ ] Product context is explicit.
- [ ] Environment and region are explicit.
- [ ] Production is not an unsafe default.
- [ ] Permissions are server-enforced.
- [ ] Inputs are validated.
- [ ] Errors are structured.
- [ ] Output formats are stable.
- [ ] Exit codes are standardized.
- [ ] Timeouts are defined.
- [ ] Retries are safe.
- [ ] Cancellation is supported where required.
- [ ] Idempotency is supported where required.
- [ ] Dry run exists for suitable high-impact commands.
- [ ] Destructive confirmations are tested.
- [ ] Non-interactive behavior is deterministic.
- [ ] CI/CD authentication is supported.
- [ ] Logs and telemetry exclude secrets.
- [ ] Cross-platform tests pass.
- [ ] API compatibility tests pass.
- [ ] Installation packages are trusted.
- [ ] Release integrity is verifiable.
- [ ] Documentation is complete.
- [ ] Examples are tested.
- [ ] Upgrade and rollback are tested.
- [ ] Deprecation guidance exists.
- [ ] Support ownership is confirmed.

---

# Exit Criteria

Part **24 — CLI Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified enterprise CLI architecture is defined.
- CLI is formally positioned within the MianX.ai Developer Platform.
- Command, argument, flag, context, output, error, exit-code, configuration, versioning, compatibility, and documentation standards are approved.
- Authentication supports humans, service identities, CI/CD systems, and approved AI agents.
- Credentials are short-lived where practical, securely stored, redacted, revocable, and never printed.
- Organization, tenant, product, project, environment, region, and identity context are visible and controlled.
- Production cannot be selected accidentally through unsafe defaults.
- Interactive, non-interactive, scripting, CI/CD, and bounded AI-agent modes are supported.
- Core Platform, development, testing, deployment, workflow, automation, AI, agent, data, security, plugin, marketplace, monitoring, and diagnostic command domains are defined.
- Machine-readable output and stable exit codes support reliable automation.
- Dry run, impact preview, confirmation, approval, idempotency, retry, timeout, cancellation, and partial-failure behavior are standardized.
- High-risk and destructive commands use risk-based controls.
- The CLI relies on official SDKs and governed platform interfaces.
- Installation, update, release-channel, signing, provenance, compatibility, deprecation, and retirement processes are established.
- macOS, Linux, and Windows support is evaluated and governed.
- CLI documentation, help, examples, troubleshooting, migration guides, and command references are synchronized.
- Cross-platform, security, compatibility, destructive-operation, and automation tests are operational.
- CLI telemetry remains privacy-aware and excludes secrets and customer data.
- CLI usage, reliability, performance, security, adoption, compatibility, and developer outcomes are measurable.
- The CLI supports all current and future MianX.ai Industry Operating Systems without bypassing enterprise governance.
- High-risk operations remain under accountable human authority.

---

# Final Summary

The CLI Roadmap establishes the terminal-based self-service and automation interface of MianX.ai.

The complete CLI lifecycle is:

```text
Developer or Automation Need Identified

↓

Approved Command Selected

↓

Identity Authenticated

↓

Organization, Tenant, Product, Project, Environment, and Region Resolved

↓

Inputs, Permissions, Risk, and Compatibility Validated

↓

Dry Run or Approval Completed Where Required

↓

Command Executed Through Governed Platform Interfaces

↓

Structured Result, Evidence, Request ID, and Audit Recorded

↓

Operation Monitored, Repeated, Improved, or Recovered
```

The CLI connects:

```text
Developers and Operators
Need fast and repeatable platform access

MianX CLI
Provides consistent commands and safe execution

SDK
Provides secure and typed platform communication

Platform APIs
Provide authoritative enterprise capabilities

Developer Portal
Provides documentation and guidance

Plugin Framework and Marketplace
Provide extensibility and ecosystem operations

Security and Governance
Control identity, permissions, risk, audit, and approval
```

MianX.ai CLI must remain:

- Secure by Default
- Context-Aware
- Tenant-Aware
- Product-Aware
- Environment-Aware
- Region-Aware
- Permission-Controlled
- Scriptable
- Interactive
- CI/CD Compatible
- AI-Agent Compatible
- Predictable
- Versioned
- Backward-Compatible
- Testable
- Observable
- Auditable
- Recoverable
- Cross-Platform
- Developer-Friendly
- Human-Governed
- Long-Term Maintainable

The objective is not merely to provide terminal commands.

The objective is to create one trusted enterprise control interface through which developers, operators, automation systems, partners, publishers, and governed AI agents can safely develop, test, deploy, inspect, extend, and operate the complete MianX.ai ecosystem with less friction, fewer errors, stronger evidence, and consistent enterprise control.

# Developer Portal Principles

## 1. One Authoritative Entry Point

Developers should not need to search unrelated repositories, chat messages, personal notes, and outdated documents to understand the platform.

---

## 2. Documentation Is Part of the Product

Documentation must be planned, reviewed, tested, versioned, and released with platform capabilities.

---

## 3. Developer Journeys Before Document Volume

Content should be organized around developer objectives rather than internal organizational structure alone.

---

## 4. Search Before Navigation Complexity

Developers should be able to locate relevant content quickly through reliable search.

---

## 5. Role-Aware Experience

The portal should adapt guidance for:

- Internal Engineer
- Customer Developer
- Plugin Developer
- Marketplace Publisher
- Partner
- Administrator
- AI Engineer
- Data Engineer
- Operations Engineer

---

## 6. Product-Aware Experience

Documentation should distinguish between:

- MianX Core
- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- RetailOS
- HealthcareOS
- EducationOS
- ManufacturingOS
- LogisticsOS

---

## 7. Version Awareness

Developers must know which platform, API, SDK, CLI, plugin, and product versions documentation applies to.

---

## 8. Secure by Default

The portal must not expose internal, customer-specific, privileged, or security-sensitive documentation to unauthorized users.

---

## 9. Self-Service With Governance

Developers should be able to request access, environments, credentials, templates, and services through governed workflows.

---

## 10. Executable Examples

Examples should be tested automatically where practical.

---

## 11. Clear Ownership

Every service, API, SDK, guide, and standard should have an identified owner.

---

## 12. Freshness Must Be Visible

Users should be able to see:

- Last Updated Date
- Version
- Owner
- Review Date
- Deprecation Status

---

## 13. Documentation Must Match Implementation

Documentation and implementation should be validated against each other.

---

## 14. Accessibility Is Mandatory

The portal should support accessible navigation, content, examples, forms, and interactive tools.

---

## 15. Search Results Must Respect Permissions

Search must not reveal restricted titles, snippets, paths, or metadata.

---

## 16. Examples Must Be Safe

Examples must not include:

- Real Secrets
- Real Customer Data
- Unsafe Permissions
- Unbounded Production Commands
- Insecure Defaults

---

## 17. Feedback Must Create Work

Developer feedback should create measurable documentation, tooling, platform, or support improvements.

---

## 18. Internal and External Experiences May Differ

Internal users may receive deeper operational content, while external users receive approved public or customer-scoped documentation.

---

## 19. Human Accountability Remains

AI may assist search, documentation generation, explanation, and troubleshooting, but authoritative content remains owner-governed.

---

## 20. Developer Success Is the Primary Outcome

Portal success should be measured through developer outcomes rather than page count alone.

# Content Risk Levels

| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| DOC0 | Public general documentation |
| DOC1 | Authenticated developer documentation |
| DOC2 | Customer or product-scoped documentation |
| DOC3 | Internal operational or architecture documentation |
| DOC4 | Security-sensitive, privileged, or customer-confidential content |
| DOC5 | Critical secrets, keys, or highly restricted evidence |

DOC5 content should not be stored as ordinary portal documentation.

---

# Publishing Approval

## DOC0–DOC1

May use standard editorial and technical review.

## DOC2

Requires product, access, and customer-scope validation.

## DOC3

Requires internal ownership and security review where applicable.

## DOC4

Requires strict access control, security approval, retention, and audit.

## DOC5

Must use approved secure systems rather than ordinary portal publishing.

# Developer Portal Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| DP-L0 | Fragmented Documentation | Developer information exists across unrelated systems |
| DP-L1 | Central Documentation Portal | Basic documentation and navigation are centralized |
| DP-L2 | Governed Developer Portal | Ownership, service catalog, APIs, SDKs, CLI, versioning, search, and support are governed |
| DP-L3 | Self-Service Developer Platform | Sandbox, API Explorer, access requests, templates, plugins, and Marketplace workflows are integrated |
| DP-L4 | Intelligent Developer Ecosystem | Personalized guidance, AI assistance, predictive support, and ecosystem analytics operate |
| DP-L5 | Global Enterprise Developer Platform | Developers and governed AI agents can compose Industry Operating Systems through trusted self-service capabilities |

- A unified Developer Portal architecture is defined.

- Private, customer-specific, internal, partner, and public documentation remain correctly isolated.
- The Developer Portal supports every current and future MianX.ai Industry Operating System.

# Part 26 — Enterprise Platform Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The Enterprise Platform Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will consolidate its Core Platform, Shared Enterprise Services, AI Operating System, Business Platform, Developer Platform, Marketplace, and Industry Operating Systems into one governed enterprise ecosystem.

The Enterprise Platform is the permanent operating foundation through which MianX.ai will support:

- Multiple Organizations
- Multiple Tenants
- Multiple Products
- Multiple Industries
- Multiple Customer Environments
- Multiple Regions
- Human Teams
- AI Workforce Teams
- Developers
- Partners
- Marketplace Publishers
- Enterprise Administrators

The target model is:

```text
Enterprise Governance

↓

MianX Core Platform

↓

Shared Enterprise Services

↓

AI Operating System

↓

Business Platform

↓

Industry Modules

↓

Customer Configuration

↓

Integrations, Plugins, and Marketplace Assets

↓

Complete Industry Operating Systems
```

The Enterprise Platform is not one application, dashboard, database, or administrative panel.

It is the complete governed platform layer through which MianX.ai can:

- Build Products
- Operate Products
- Extend Products
- Secure Products
- Scale Products
- Integrate Products
- Govern Products
- Measure Products
- Continuously Improve Products

This roadmap does not replace the earlier Core Platform Roadmap.

The Core Platform Roadmap defines foundational technical capabilities.

The Enterprise Platform Roadmap defines how those capabilities mature into a complete enterprise-grade, multi-product, multi-tenant, AI-native, ecosystem-enabled operating platform.

The objective is to ensure that every new Industry Operating System begins with a secure and production-ready enterprise foundation rather than rebuilding authentication, tenancy, permissions, files, notifications, workflows, billing, reporting, integrations, AI, security, and operations.

---

# Enterprise Platform Vision

Build one secure, modular, multi-tenant, AI-native, API-first, event-ready, observable, extensible, and globally scalable enterprise platform capable of powering every current and future MianX.ai Industry Operating System.

---

# Enterprise Platform Mission

Provide reusable, governed, configurable, and production-ready enterprise capabilities that allow MianX.ai teams, customers, developers, partners, and AI agents to create and operate intelligent business systems without duplicating foundational architecture.

---

# Enterprise Platform Purpose

The Enterprise Platform exists to:

- Prevent foundational rebuilding
- Eliminate architectural fragmentation
- Standardize enterprise capabilities
- Accelerate product delivery
- Support multiple products simultaneously
- Support multiple customers securely
- Support AI Workforce execution
- Provide reusable business capabilities
- Enable configuration before customization
- Provide stable integration interfaces
- Support developers and partners
- Enable Marketplace extensions
- Improve enterprise reliability
- Improve security and compliance
- Reduce long-term platform cost
- Support regional and global expansion

---

# Strategic Objectives

The Enterprise Platform Roadmap should:

- Establish one authoritative MianX Core Platform
- Establish reusable Shared Enterprise Services
- Integrate the AI Operating System
- Establish reusable Business Platform capabilities
- Support modular Industry Operating Systems
- Enforce tenant and product isolation
- Support configuration-driven customer variation
- Provide standardized APIs and events
- Provide governed workflows and automation
- Provide enterprise data and reporting
- Provide billing, subscription, and payment capabilities
- Provide developer self-service
- Support SDK, CLI, and Developer Portal access
- Support plugins and Marketplace assets
- Provide centralized security and compliance
- Provide unified observability and audit
- Support multi-region operations
- Maintain backward compatibility
- Control platform cost
- Support long-term enterprise composition

# Enterprise Platform Non-Scope

The Enterprise Platform does not place every product-specific capability inside the Core Platform.

The following should remain outside the Core unless broadly reusable:

- Restaurant-Specific Workflows
- Poultry-Specific Trading Logic
- Healthcare-Specific Clinical Logic
- School-Specific Academic Logic
- Retail-Specific Point-of-Sale Logic
- Customer-Specific Custom Code
- One-Off Integration Behavior
- Temporary Business Experiments

Industry-specific capabilities belong in modular Industry Operating Systems.

Customer-specific differences should be managed through configuration, workflows, approved plugins, and bounded extensions wherever possible.

---

# Enterprise Platform Principles

## 1. Platform Before Product Duplication

Shared capabilities must be implemented once and reused across products.

---

## 2. Configuration Before Customization

Customer variation should be handled through:

- Configuration
- Feature Flags
- Rules
- Workflows
- Templates
- Plugins

before custom product forks are considered.

---

## 3. Secure by Default

Security controls must be embedded into every platform capability.

---

## 4. Tenant-Aware by Design

Every tenant-scoped operation must preserve trusted tenant context.

---

## 5. Product-Aware by Design

Shared services must understand which product is consuming them.

---

## 6. API-First

Platform capabilities should expose stable and governed service interfaces.

---

## 7. Event-Ready

Important platform changes should generate versioned enterprise events.

---

## 8. Modular Architecture

Capabilities must have clear boundaries, owners, interfaces, and dependencies.

---

## 9. Stable Contracts

Products should consume documented and versioned contracts rather than internal implementation details.

---

## 10. Shared Identity

Human users, AI agents, services, plugins, workflows, and integrations must operate through recognized identities.

---

## 11. Least Privilege

Every identity receives only the capabilities required for its approved responsibility.

---

## 12. Observable by Default

Every critical service should expose:

- Logs
- Metrics
- Traces
- Health
- Cost
- Audit Events

---

## 13. Recoverable by Design

Every critical capability must define backup, restoration, failover, and recovery procedures.

---

## 14. Backward Compatibility

Platform evolution must not unnecessarily break existing products and customers.

---

## 15. Documentation With Delivery

Architecture, APIs, configuration, security, deployment, and operational documentation must change with implementation.

---

## 16. AI Through Governance

Products must consume approved AI services rather than create uncontrolled independent AI systems.

---

## 17. Extension Through Contracts

Plugins, Marketplace assets, and integrations must extend the platform through explicit boundaries.

---

## 18. Evidence Before Maturity

Platform maturity must be demonstrated through implementation, testing, adoption, security, reliability, and customer outcomes.

---

## 19. Cost-Aware Operations

Platform cost should be visible by service, product, tenant, environment, workflow, and region.

---

## 20. Human Strategic Authority

High-risk, legal, security, financial, ethical, and irreversible decisions remain under accountable human authority.

---

# Platform Decision Framework

A capability belongs in the Core Platform when it:

- Is required by several products
- Has stable reusable behavior
- Requires centralized governance
- Benefits from one shared implementation
- Has enterprise-wide security requirements
- Can be exposed through stable contracts

A capability belongs in an Industry Module when it:

- Represents domain-specific business behavior
- Is not required by most products
- Has industry-specific workflows
- Has industry-specific terminology
- Can evolve independently

A capability belongs in customer configuration when it:

- Changes values or rules rather than architecture
- Does not require new core behavior
- Can be expressed through approved settings
- Remains tenant-specific

# Enterprise Platform Maturity Model

| Level | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| EP-L0 | Fragmented Applications | Products rebuild foundational capabilities independently |
| EP-L1 | Shared Core | Basic identity, tenancy, work, files, audit, and configuration are shared |
| EP-L2 | Governed Enterprise Platform | Shared services, contracts, ownership, security, reliability, and governance operate |
| EP-L3 | Multi-Product AI Platform | Multiple Industry Operating Systems and AI teams consume one platform |
| EP-L4 | Ecosystem Enterprise Platform | Developers, partners, plugins, and Marketplace safely extend the platform |
| EP-L5 | Composable Enterprise Platform | New Industry Operating Systems are assembled from governed reusable capabilities |

# Exit Criteria

Part **26 — Enterprise Platform Roadmap** is complete when:

- A unified Enterprise Platform architecture is defined.
- The distinction between Core Platform, Shared Enterprise Services, AI Operating System, Business Platform, Industry Modules, and Customer Configuration is clear.
- Shared capabilities are implemented once and consumed by multiple products.
- Organization, tenant, product, workspace, project, environment, and region boundaries are defined.
- Identity and authorization support humans, services, AI agents, plugins, workflows, and integrations.
- Tenant and product isolation are enforced and tested.
- Core Platform modules provide stable reusable foundations.
- Shared Enterprise Services have owners, contracts, versions, documentation, monitoring, service-level objectives, recovery procedures, and deprecation policies.
- RestaurantOS, PoultryOS, and future Industry Operating Systems can inherit shared platform capabilities.
- Customer differences are handled primarily through configuration, rules, workflows, and approved extensions.
- APIs, events, SDKs, CLI, Developer Portal, Plugin Framework, and Marketplace provide governed platform access.
- Data, knowledge, memory, intelligence, automation, and AI capabilities remain integrated but correctly governed.
- Platform security, observability, reliability, audit, cost, capacity, and recovery are measurable.
- Platform changes follow architecture, security, compatibility, documentation, release, and migration governance.
- Multi-region, localization, data-residency, and regional-compliance patterns are defined.
- New products can be launched without rebuilding enterprise foundations.
- Platform maturity is demonstrated through reuse, adoption, security, reliability, customer outcomes, and sustainable economics.
- High-risk and strategic decisions remain under accountable human authority.
- The Enterprise Platform is capable of supporting the complete long-term MianX.ai ecosystem.

# Part 27 — Business Platform Roadmap

## Executive Summary

The Business Platform Roadmap defines how MianX.ai will design, build, govern, operate, scale, and continuously improve reusable enterprise business capabilities shared across multiple Industry Operating Systems.

The Business Platform sits between the MianX Enterprise Platform and industry-specific product modules.

The target model is:

```text
MianX Core Platform

+

Shared Enterprise Services

+

AI Operating System

↓

Business Platform

↓

Industry-Specific Modules

↓

Customer Configuration

↓

Complete Industry Operating System
```

The Business Platform will provide reusable capabilities for:

- Customer Relationship Management
- Sales
- Marketing
- Finance
- Human Resources
- Procurement
- Inventory Foundations
- Billing
- Subscription Management
- Customer Success
- Customer Support
- Vendor Management
- Approval Management
- Business Rules
- Business Reporting
- Business Intelligence

These capabilities should be developed once and reused across:

- RestaurantOS
- PoultryOS
- RetailOS
- HealthcareOS
- EducationOS
- ManufacturingOS
- LogisticsOS
- HospitalityOS
- Real EstateOS
- ConstructionOS
- AgricultureOS
- Future Industry Operating Systems

The Business Platform is not intended to create one large and inflexible ERP.

It should provide modular, configurable, API-first, event-ready, AI-enabled, and independently adoptable business capabilities.

An Industry Operating System should be able to consume only the business modules it requires.

For example:

```text
RestaurantOS

may consume:

CRM
+
Sales
+
Procurement
+
Inventory
+
Finance
+
Customer Support
```

```text
PoultryOS

may consume:

CRM
+
Sales
+
Procurement
+
Vendor Management
+
Inventory
+
Finance
+
Collections
```

The Business Platform must preserve clear boundaries between:

- Core Platform Capabilities
- Shared Business Capabilities
- Industry-Specific Capabilities
- Customer-Specific Configuration
- Approved Extensions

The objective is to prevent every product from rebuilding the same CRM, finance, sales, procurement, support, approval, reporting, and administrative foundations.
